MADGE. This young Princess is very tall, graceful, and handsome and according to all accounts, is likely to be well en- dowed with this world's goods. Queen Victoria provided amply for all the children of Princess Henry of Batten- berg, and it is an open secret that Princess Ena will inherit much of the ex-Empress Eugenie's wealth. Princess En& sings and plays brilliantly, speaks several languages, and is a really brilliant and accomplished girl. October's Stone.—The foolish prejudice against the opal—the stone of the present month,—is happily, like much in the way of superstition, disappearing, and it is .now quite a fashionable gem. There are three prin- cipal varieties of opal, namely, the Oriental, the fire and the common opal. The first mentioned and most valuable, is found mostly in Hungary, though Honduras, Mexico and Australia, have furnished beauti- ful specimens. Black opals, which have the glow of a ,ruby seen through a mist, are found in Egypt, but they are very few and far between. The finest opals in the world are those which form part of the Austrian Crown jewels, but Queen Alexandra possesses some very fine •specimens, which she often wears. Lady Curzon.—lt is given to few to possess the love .and esteem enjoyed by Lady Curzon, and her very wide circles of friends have passed a very anxious time lately. That she has pulled through her dangerous illness is little short of marvellous, but there is now every hope that the patient's convalescence will by no means prove a tedious one. Lady Curzon is a very beautiful woman, with glorious eyes and hair, and a ssNeet and somewhat •sad smile. She is a devoted wife and mother, and is never so happy as when away from all affairs of State, and 'living a simple, free, and open-air life, with her ,husband and children. Lord and Lady Curzon have three daughters, the youngest to whom the Queen is godmother, being but six months old. Colours and Nerves.—The idea that the colours in a room have considerable effect upon a patient suffering from any nervous disorder, has possibly much in it. We all know that a crude, or unharmonious apartment jars, and makes us feel out of harmony with ourselves, and.the would generally, and that an artist, restful room has just the opposite effect. A specialist in men- tatdiseases it of opinion that white is not to be thought of,except side by side with shades less dazzling,and that yellow should only set off other hues. Mauves, lilacs, greys, and soft greens, are all restful he says, while red makes for cheeriness and brightness. Blue is calming encouraging cool reasoning, and temperate opinions. It is comparatively easy for those people starting in house- keeping, to have everything artistic and restful about them, to attain to " one harmonious whole' but less fortunate individuals who have to work ih old furniture,old hangings and old carpets, have sometimes a more difficult task. 'lt is however a simple and inex- pensive matter to get hangings and carpets dipped, and the clever housewife can do much in the furniture cov- ering department for herself, so there is really little excuse nowadays for crude, hard colourings and rooms that jar. New Shades in Millinery.—Milliners are growing weary of tangerine, and vert mousse, and have taken a new shade—which almost baffles description—into favour. This suggests petunia, mauve, clear Parma -violet, and Pontifical purple and yet, is quite distinct from any of these colours. 'Never before have we seen more daring and startling shades, as in leading show- rooms this autumn, but though they are very. charming and fascinating when shown eff on "dummies," great care needs to be exercised in the selection of a hat or toque. Not one complexion in twenty can successfully stand the proximity of these new brilliant tints,and we should do well to remember that it is better to be less np-to-date,than to weer what is absolutely unbecoming. Modish Sleeves.—Sleeves are as varied in style that it is possible for every woman te select a becoming fashion. The sleeve with a stiff series of puffs—the Tudor sleeve—is perhaps the one preferred by the smart dresser, but the quite tight sleeve with the puff at the top is also a great favorite. The tightly-fitting variety with the baggy elbow to wrist arrangement. still _obtains, but for all dressy afternoon functions, the sleeve terminates in billowy frills nt the elbow. Tailor's sleeves are all of the tightly-fitting persuasion, only the slightest spring being allowed at the cuff.

div.p: SUMMER THINS THE BLOOD. Winter Finds Weak Places.
BILE HANS STRENGTHEN THE SYSTEM.

Do you feel chilly? If so, have you thought why? It is not merely because the weather is a little cooler. Summer heat thins out the blood. The hotter the summer, the thinner and poorer becomes the blood. A hot summer just affects your blood sufficient to make you feel chilly when Autumn comes, however mild. Now is the time when unless the blood is thoroughly nourished and brought up to its winter standard, disease creeps in. Bile Beans ensure that all food taken is turned into rich red blood, and a course of them will prepare you for the trying winter season. . "My blood was so thin, and my circulation so feeble, that sometimes my hands and feet were numb with cold," so says Mrs. M.H. Hughes, of Dake-street,Stoke. "Being so run down I began to suffer from wind,spasras, palpitation, indigestion and general weakness. Wind would collect round my heart, and give me great pain, accompanied' by a burning sensation. The attacks were so frequent,that I was always in a sinking and exhausted condition. Indeed, I was so bad, that several times I I thought I was really going to die. I had treatment on several occasions from different doctors but medical attention was very expensive, and did not: give me any lastinn. benefit. "We saw Bile Beans spoken highly of in the 'Sentinel,' and thinking that the symptoms described by some of the sufferers were very much like those I experienced, I thought I would try them. lam glad I did so. "I felt an improvement very soon. The wind began to go from round my heart, and I began to feel stronger and less depressed. I persevered with the Beans, and when one box was done got another, and then a third. Without going into all the details, I may say that their result has been to change me from the wretched con- dition I was in when I began to take them, to what you 1 ' see lam to-day. lam not now like the same woman. You will readily understand how well and strong I feel, when I tell you that I can do all my housework myself, look after my_ seven children, and attend also to my husband's shop. RETIRED FARMER'S SUICIDE. On Saturday, at the Bull Inn, Ditton, Mr. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest touching the death of Henry Willcox, a retired farmer, of Ditton.—The e dence was to the effect that deceased had lived unhappily with his wife. On Thursday he took up a poker to touch the fire. The wife said, "Don't', it will soon burn up." Without further provocation deceased attacked her, and struck her twice on the head with the poker. He then went out, returning later without coat and cap and with his other garments wet. He twice asked his wife to forgive him.-- -Dr. Eatock was called to the woman, and whilst attending her deceased cut his throat 'faith a sharp clasp knife, and was found by the doctor sitting on the bed with a terrible gash in his throat, from which he expired almost immediately.—Police-constable Bretherton said he questioned deceased during the morning as to why he assaulted his wife. Deceased replied," I don't know. My head is bad."—The constable also found decsa..:3d's clothing by the side of a neighbouring pit. There we every evidence that deceased had tried to drown him- self.—Several of the jurors said the man was addicted to drink, and that he had not worked regularly at all for three years.--fhe jury returned a verdict of i" Suicide," adding that they believed deceased to be sane.

div.head: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.
div.p: FASHIONS OF TO-DAY.

There are no pleasanter hours in all the day, I fancy, than whes. the hall door closes on us after perhaps a busy and hardworked day, when every minute has been occupied in the pursuit of pleasure or in the more dreary round of money seeking then one can revel in the comfort of a neglige of some sort, and rest contented in the blaze of •a cosy fire, which is more a luxury than a necessity just yet. In these days of paper patterns the cost of a cosy tea-gown is greatly reduced, and this modern but delightful wrap is quite within the means of most girls who can employ their leisure minutes in transforming yards of warmly coloured flannel or Zenana cloth into a becoming garment. A few years ago a gown of this kind would have been con- sidered not only extravagant, but unsuitable to any one save an invalid, but a more ea-

div.head: TAILOR-MADE.
div.p: A TAILOR-MADE.

lightened age has seen and recognised the fact that not only is a neglige style of dress restful and therefore conducive to good health when not overdone,but it is also an economy, for it saves the outdoot gown considerably as nothing loses its look sooner than a dress which is made to do duty both in and out of doors. Zenana cloth is certainly not cheap to begin with but it is a much better invest- ment than many of the less costly materials, for it stands any amount of hard wear as its tough but silky surface does not rub, while the woolly underside renders a lining un- necessary, and is delightfully warm. A cosy and easily slipped on gown of this style con- trasts vividly with the severe lines of the simple but smart tailor-made in my first sketch, but each mode is suited to the hours of the day when it is to be worn. For morning wear the smart little coat and skirt,sketched is just the thing whether for town or country, for when designed in a nice navy blue serge or Scotch cheviot it looks very modish and distinctly serviceable. A lining of silk, of course, enhances its charms, and a touch of the fashionable orange yellow velvet on the narrow coat collar and plain cuffs is highly successful. The skirt is cut short and is neatly, strapped and flat gold buttons are arranged in groups of three at either side of the front, which is fastened by invisible hooks and eyes and can therefore be worn open or closed as desired. The back aiid sides of the coat fit closely, while the front is a little pouched over the band. The peaked cap is of the same material as the dress.
SHIONABLE HAT.

Orange in varying depths of tone is much worn thil autumn, although it is no novelty on the other side of the Channel, as yellow was quite the rage among the Parisiennes. It is, of course, a brilliant and rich colour and nrust be used in moderation. A touch of it in the hat and in the costume together with a frilly silk underskirt of the same tone brighten up a dark toilette wonderfully, and many girls will be able in this manner to coax an old gown to appear almost as good as new. My second sketch depicts the charms of the most fashionable hat of the moment. The shape is a mushroom,. which, together with the long sloping shoulders,has made a success- ful reappearance in an improved form. The newest mushroom hat is lifted off the head by a bandeau Covered generally with flat ribbon bows of velvet, and this has certainly the result of making it vastly more becoming to the majority of faces than when it is low on the head. The trimming in this instance consists of a full silk ruche arranged round the crown. These ruches can be purchased in a variety of colours ready for tacking, to the crown. I have seen some very pretty ones of the same style but made of feathers dyed to pretty shades ot, every colour. • These fea- ther ruches look very well on the rough;' furry surfaced felts which will be very fashionable throughout the autumn and winter seasons These not only look warm, but are delightfully cosy to wear, and a 'hat like the one sketched can be evolved for little cost by purchasing the trimming and lining ready made. The reign of the blouse beautiful continues, and one cannot wonder at it when viewing .the many pretty models on view at such a moderate cost that it baffles the home worker to understand how, it is done.
L'IZETTY BI
,OUSE

The pretty blouse illustrated is of vel- veteen in a soft mouse-colour with a yoke of lace over silk. Some pretty gauging,s allow the velveteen to fall in pretty folds. The mode is a simple one but it is not wise to attempt any elaborations in velvet or velveteen as the material is too weighty. A nice flannel would also make up into a pretty morning blouse in this fashion. I have seen some new and very pretty designs in flannel for blouses, and perhaps the nicest of all shows spots through which a silk stripe runs. Stripes and spots individually or in con- junction look smarter for blouses to my mind than some of the more elaborate floral designs These latter in pale colours on a cream or white ground look certainly dressy and have

many admirers. Large pictnre .hats are likely to be worn throughout all the winter, and are mostly of the Gainsborough style, in rniroir satin or drawn silk in either black or delicate shades. such as pearl gray or biscuit. They are in all cases trimmed with large ostrich plumes of the same colour as the hat itself, with some- times the addition of some fine lace as a cache-pagne behincld Z.1.1.i COQUETTE J I

div.head: DEATH OF SIR WILLIAM HARCOURT.
div.p: DEATH OF SIR WILLIAM HARCOURT.

By the death of Sir William Harcourt one mf the most distinguished politicians of the Victorian Era passes away. The deceased gentleman has been in indifferent health since his retirement, but his demise was quite un- expected, Lady Harcourt being the only relative in the house when he breathed his last. He died at his seat at Nuneham,
Oxfordshire, a place where he had always expressed a wish to live and die. Sir William Harcourt, it can be 'truly said, . was

in the front rank as a debater, not, ined, for readiness, for his speeches were always elaborately prepared, but for clear exposition, for brilliant phrasing and biting epigram. His command of language and his forensic instincts sometimes ran away with him ; an Irishman once remarked that he was as vehement when proposing tl4e Hares and Rabbits Bill as when urging coercive legis- lation for Ireland. But behind the fierce partisanship and unsparing oratory there lay qualities which gained for him the respect and good-will of members of all political parties. He was a friend of Lord Beacons- field, and Mr. Balfour, with whom he always maintained cordial relations, has testified to his freedom from bitterness and his devotion to great public ends. The skill with which he led the House of Commons in the memor- able Session of 1894, and especially the tact and patience which he exhibited in the management of the most contentious financial measure of modern times, came as a surprise to many who had seen in Sir William Har- court no more than an accomplished and unsparing partisan. Sir William's last speech was delivered on the 28tb July this year at the National Liberal Club on the occasion of the Club's annual At Home." He then said, in reference to his retirement from Parlia- ment: "It is not because I was weary of the fight or because I was lukewarm in the cause. It is because I did hot think it for the public advantage that people should attempt to fulfil the duties of a task which they are un- able to perform." The funeral took place on Thursday at Nuneham Park and was largely attended by many of his old colleagues and political opponents.
SIR WILLIAM HARCOURT.

div.head: LONDON'S NEW LORD MAYOR.
div.p: LONDON'S NEW LORD MAYOR.

Last week the formality of electing the new Lord Mayor of London took place at the Guildhall, and Alderman Pound, whose name came first in rotation, was unanimously chosen for the post. Prior to the election the Lord Mayor, Sir J. T. Ritchie, with the Sheriffs and Aldermen, attended service at St. Lawrence Jewry in state, complying for the five hundredth time with a custom which originated at the election of the famous Dick Whittington in 1404. Afterwards the procession adjourned to the Common Hall of the Guildhall, where the list of candidates was read, and the names of Alderman Pound (leatherseller ) and Alderman Vaughan Morgan (cutler) were selected. Then the Lord :Mayor and the Aldermen who had passed the chair adjourned to the Court of Aldermen and were followed in due course by the other Aldermen, and after a few minutes it was

div.head: ALDERMAN POUND.
div.p: ALDERMAN POUND.

announced that Alderman Pound - hnd been unanimously elected: The announcement was received, with loud cheering, and the Lord Mayor Elect took the usual oath. In re- turning thanks he promised that during his tenure of office hug speeches shouli not be the order of the. day, and he was followed by Sir J. Williams Watson, who -proposed a. vote of thanks to Sir J. T. Ritchie, which was carried unanimously. The Lord Mayor Elect, who assumes office on the ninth of November, is a, very handsome , and dignified old man of seventy-five with white hair, beard, and • moustache, who will look Most imposing in his robes. He is the head of the firm of , John Pound and Co. and a member -of .the Leather Sellers' Company - and was educated at Christ's Hospital.

div.head: SIR HERBERT CHERMSIDE RETIRES.
div.p: SIR HERBERT CHERMSIDE RETIRES.

Much regret will be felt in Brisbane by the resignation of Major - General Sir Herbert Chermside, Governor of Queensland. Sir Herbert was appointed Governor in December, Igor, and both he and Lady Chermside have been extremely popular with all classes. The late Governor married in 1899 the younger daughter of the late Mr. Wil- liam Frederick Webb. She brought him as her marriage portion New- stead Abbey, in Not tin gham- shire, and with it an estate of 4,000 acres. The Abbey, founded about 1170 by Henry 11., was formerly the re- sidence at Lord Byron, having been granted to his family in 1546, Sir John Byron, knight, being the grantee. Lord Byron, the poet, succeeded to the Abbey at the age Qf six, but at that time it had fallen largely into decay. It is not the least tragic of the many tragic episodes of the life of the poet that at the very time when he was constrained by lack of money to sell the estate to his friend. Colonel Wildman, there was that beneath it which, had he known it, would have mad?, him one of the richest men in England at that date, for the estate lay over one of the finest coalfields in the county. The retiring Governor served with distinction in the Egyptian campaign of 1882, was commander in Crete in 180, and in 1900 nent to South Africa in command of the 3rd Division in succession to Sir William Gatacre. He was made K.C.M.G in 1399.

div.head: KING OF SPAIN AND MATRIMONY;
div.p: KING OF SPAIN AND MATRIMONY;

It is now announced that the King 01 Spain, who is quite the most interesting young bachelor in Europe, is soon to quit that state for matrimony, and the announce- ment has- been very cordially received on all sides. The bride whom he has chosen is the Grand Duchess Marie Antoinette of Mecklen- burg-Schwerin, whom he met as A boy when travelling in Austria and Italy with his tutors: The young King is now eighteen years of age and his bride is just two years older than he is. She was born in Venice and is strongly Latin in her sympathies,
ALFONSO AND PRINCESS MARIE

and the 'Continental papers announce that it is • a love-match, which has been brought about by the King's own insistence. It is well known that the young King, who is shortly to pay a .visit to this country, is a very !.4.rong character, and shows signs of dominating his ministers and his country in no half-hearted fashion. From his very earliest day' he has shown himself born to rule, and many stories are told of him as a child, which go to prove this fact. Yet though strong and inclined at times to be imperious, King Alfonso is generous and kind to all with whom he comes into contact, but he will not brook too much interference with his plans and ideas. He is decidedly a boy with a strong will and precocious grasp of the responsibilities and requirements of his position, and in many ways he recalls the Kaiser as a young man. He it is whom he emulates in many respects, especially in his devotion to military science and his deter- ,inination to bring the Spanish Army to a pitch of perfection in organisation and equipment. With his fearlessness, ambition, and energy it is' possible that King Alfonso may bring Spain back to her former high place amongst the powers, and it is certain that he will not allow the grass to grow under his feet. He is a Hapsburg in appearance with his fair hair and blue eyes, taking after his mother's family, and looks quite at his best on horseback, being a fine and fearless rider. His visit to England is being eagerly looked forward to, as this country is anxious to see this rising young ruler of a_friendly country.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, October 8, 1904. HOCKEY. I HARVEST FESTIVALS.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, October 8, 1904. HOCKEY. I HARVEST FESTIVALS.
STOCKTON HEATH 2ND V. BANKFIKLD 2ND.

This match was played at Grappenhall-road, and re- sulted in a win for the Heathens by eight goals to four. For the home team the scorers were—NV. G. Longdin (four), D. Skelton (three), R. Monks (one). LATCEIFORD IsT, v. BIRKENHEAD PARK IsT Latchford Ist xi. opened the season on Saturday at Latchford by playing 'Birkenhead Park Ist. and defeated the visitors by 2 goals to nil. Although it had rained rather heavily the previous night, the ground was in good condition, and the teams had a pleasant and fast game in consequence. Considering that this was the first match of the season, the home team played very well, all showing form which augues well for another successful season. The visitors were strong in the backs, but their forwards hardly gained the ground which might have been gained with a little more dash and individual effort. Frequent chances in the circle to score were missed, particularly by the home front rank, but no doubt this was due to over eagerness, and will be remedied when they have settled down to the game. No score was registered up to half-time, although as above indicated, several chances were missed by the home team, but Pearson and Banks each shot goals in the second half, and when the whistle was blown for time the score read :—Latchford, 2; Birkenhead Park, nil. BANKFIELD v. STOCKTON HEATH.

These teams met at Bankfleld,the weather being bright but chilly. L. Fairclough won the toss, and elected to play with the breeze. From the bully off Stockton Heath at once assumed the upper hand, and after some good work by the inside men, S. Baxter opened the scoring with a good shot. The Bankfield backs could not hold the visiting forwards, and it was not long before R. Pierpoint added a second goal. Shortly after this Bankfield broke away, and entered the Stockton circle for the first time,only to be robbed before shoot- ing. After this the Heathens again attacked by good passing among the forwarcLs,and S. Baxter added another with a hot shot. It was not long before W. Richardson who had bsen playing a sound game, added a fourth goat and before half-time a fifth. Half-time score, 5-0- Upon the restart the visitors again attacked, and follow- ing up a good shot by R. Pierpoint, W. Richardson toilk the ball as it rebounded from the goalkeeper's pads, and banged it into the net. Mention should be made of the Bankfield goalkeeper, who played a fine game, and it was only through his play that the score was not doubled. Before the whistle sounded five more goals were added, W. Richardson, two ; R. Pierpoint, two.; and C. H. Bond, one. As a final effort Bankfield for- wards dashed down the field, and scored with their first and last shot. Result : 11-1 LA.TCEIFORD "A " v. BIRKENHEAD PARK_ "A.

Latchford "A" opened their season successfully on Saturday after a good game by defeating Birkenhead Park on their own ground by two goals to one. Latch- ford were the smarter team all through, and on Satur- days' form should at least have as successful a season as the last. The forwards got through some very good work especially D. Knight at centre, and Calton and Jones on the right wing, the passing being very clean , and accurate, whilst the backs were sound I and reliable, C. Hale at full back show- ing fine form and clearing well on two or three critical occasions. Knight scored in the first half I with a good swift shot which was the only point registered up to half time. The second half was much the same as the first, play again ruling in favour of the Latchford eleven, although on several occasions the Park became dangerous. However, after pressing for some time Jones put another through for the visitors, to which Hard shortly afterwards replied with one for the home team. After the bully off, the visitors again pressed, but owing to poor play in the circle no further score was added, and when time was called the score was as indicated above: Latchford A, 2; Birkenhead Park A, 1. Both teams meet Eccles to-day, and the players selec- ted are as follow :—Latchford Ist v. Eccles Ist, at Eccles: Goal, I. Wilkinson; full backs, R. Hallows, J. R. Conway; half backs, W. Knight, Cl. Heald, T. Dixon; forwards, W. Spenseley, E. T. Cliffe, W. H. Banks, J. Pearson, A. Albinson. Latchford 2nd v. Eccles 2nd, at Latchford: Goal, W. Unsworth •' full backs, C. Hale, T. Young; half backs, W. B. Cobb, J. B. I Wilkinson, B. H. Rathbone ; forwards, J. Callon, R. Jones, D. Knight, T. Wilkinson, J. Rathbone..

div.head: ST. CROSS, APPLETON.
div.p: ST. CROSS, APPLETON.

The services at this church were continued on Sunday. In the evening the church was crowded. The preaeher was the Rev. Charles Morgan, rector of Rhoscrowther, Pembroke. Special music was rendered, Mr. T. Reeves presiding at the organ. The church was beautifully and tastefully decorated by the ladies of the congregation.

div.head: MOORE WESLEYAN CHURCH.
div.p: MOORE WESLEYAN CHURCH.

A large congregation assembled for the harvest, thanksgiving services. The Rev. G. H. Carnson was the preacher and took for his subject at morning service "Sowing and reaping." A specially interesting address to the young was drawn from the word "Harvest." In the evening the sermon was based on Psalm i. The decorations were as usual, of a very tasteful character, and were carried out by the ladies of the congregation. Special music was rendered effectively by the choir, the anthem being "Fear not, 0 land." On Monday evening the school children and teachers were entertained to a substantial tea by Mr. and Mrs. Birch, and a most enjoyable evening was spent. PRESTON BROOK PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHURCH.

At this place of worship on Sunday, harvest thanks- giving services were held, when Pastor T: Grady, of Warrington, occupied the pulpit at both the afternoon and evening service. The Sunday school teachers and other friends had worked hard in tastefully decorating the interior with corn, fruit, vegetables, plants, Sze. The choir, under the direction of Miss N. Cowap, rendered special hymns and the anthems, "Thou shall keep the feast of harvest "and "Sing to the Lord of harvest," in a, creditable manner. The offertories were on behalf of the Sunday School funds.

div.head: WARRINGTON RAGGED SCHOOL MISSION.
div.p: WARRINGTON RAGGED SCHOOL MISSION.

The harvest festival services were held on Sunday at the above Mission. Addresses were delivered in the afternoon by Mr. Llewelyn and in the evening by Mrs. Moores. The augmented choir, under the leadership of Mr. F. J. Owen, were ably assisted by several members of Miss B. Turner's Ladies' Orchestra, and rendered several hymns and solos in a very effective manner. The mission, which has recently been beautified through- out, was prettily decorated with flowers, fruit and. vegetables. The collection realised LI Bs. 2d. On Mon- day evening there was a fruit banquet, and a splendid entertainment, contributed to mainly by Miss Turner's excellent Ladies' Orchestra of violins and mandoline s Songs were also sung by Mrs. Barlow and others, a cornet solo by Mr. Booth, a Lancashire dialect reading by Mr. J. W. Howarth, and a recitation by Miss Wright A most enjoyable evening was thoronghty appreciate by both the children and adults present. ST. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH.

The annual harvest thanksgiving services were held at St. John's on Sunday, when the minister of the church, the Rev. J. L. Milne, M.A.,8.D., preached morn- ing and evening and addressed a gathering of Sunday school scholars in the afternoon. The building was beautifully and tastefully decorated for the occasion with a large quantity of corn, fruit and vegetables, suitably relieved with flowers and greeneu. The scheme of decoration reflected great credit on tfie ladies of the congregation by whom it was carried out, and was much admired by those attending the services. The singing was led by an augmented choir, while the newly-appointed organist, Mr. J. W. Jowett, presided at the organ. In the morning Mr. Milne preached from St. John, chap. vi. ver. 11. the words ".Having given thanks." In the evening, when there was a large con- gregation, the preacher chose for the subject of discourse the account of our Lord's cursing the unfruitful fig tree (St. Mark, chap. xi. vers.l2 to 14.) Mr. Milne said this was a miracle round which there had raged great discussion, though exactly why that was so it were diffi- cultleolturderstand.The two questions to which he wished to direct attention were, Ist. Why Jesus came to the tree? and 2nd. Why, he spoke the word that destroyed it? When Jesus saw the tree he f.either knew or did not know whether there was fruit on it. If he knew there was not fruit his conduct was hard to understand , and looked like acting, which was an unpleasant thought. If he did not know there was no fruit his conduct was intelligible enough. It was his (the preacher's) own opinion that Jesus did not know. Jesus' knowledge in this world, though the very Son of God, was limited. How other were they to explain His growth in wisdom? They were told He" grew in wisdom and in stature." In Greek the word standing for "'mew" signified knowledge gained by enquiry. Jesus knew what was in man because he had observed man. He learned by observation as they did, though perhaps he learned more than they did. His divine knowledge was limited in some way they could not understand. It was thus then that Jesus went to the fig tree, not knowing there was no fruit thereon. He went hoping to find fruit as they might have done, and• finding none he spoke the word ithat destroyed the tree. Then as to why Jesus destroyed the tree. The remarks that had been made concerning this aspect of the matter only went to show how much men had felt this action of their Lord's and how they had tried to explain it. But the difficulty was not so great after all. The tree made a pretence. The probability was that had it been healthy there would have been fruit. There was a profession of fruit-bearing, and to teach the disciples a lesson they had need to learn, Jesus spoke the word that destroyed the tree, the appearance of which was a lie. The un- fruitful one would be destroyed and that was the lesson Jesus meant to teach. Fruit-bearing was necessary if men were to be spared. There was nothing in the world but that bore fruit—nothing absolutely useless. The most disappointing of God's works was his greatest •work—man. The world should be better for their Christianity which was not a gift to the individual alone but to the world through the individual. Fruit- bearing was a mark of discipleship; it was more valuable than believing and conduct more important than creed. Mr. A. Griffiths gave a very fine rendering of the solo "The Good Shepherd," while the anthem "Great and marvellous" was sung by the choir. Very satisfactory collections were obtained.

div.head: MOTOR NOTES.
div.p: MOTOR NOTES.
It is stated that a ten-miles anlhour limit for motor cars in the City of London is a foregone conclusion.

At first sight this may not appear to be a very grea t hardship, since the congested state of the traffic renders that, or even a slightly lower speed, a dangerous one in many parts. Indeed, at present, very few motor car drivers would care to travel at a consistent ten miles an hour speed through Holborn or portions of Piccadill y. Where the shoe pinches is,if this limit be enforced, the greater facility thus afforded to the police for stopping and summoning motor car drivers .on an alleged in- fringement of that limit, although their chances of judging the speed accurately would be re.luced to a minimum.

As we have repeatedly stated, Section 1 of the Motor Car Act is quite stringent enough to deal with any case of furious or reckless driving, irrespective of the speed at which the car is actually travelling at the time. This gives the police ample powers to act should occa- sion arise, so that any speed limit is 'really quite super- fluous and totally unnecessary.

We note that a petrol tramcar has been co nstructed by a Birmingham firm and is so designed as to accom- modate about thirty passengers as well as a ton of baggage. Petrol driven trams are certainly to be preferred to the electric type, where either an extra rail is needed for the cable,or else overhead wires—frequently with the standards in the. centre of the roadway—are in
requisition.

The pioneers of the first practicable petrol tram were the Societe Decauville, of Paris, who exhibited one at the Automobile Show a year ago. This was greatly admired, for it was at once seen that it would beespeci- ally useful in those districts where there is little or no railway inter-communication between villages, whilst its adoption would not entail a large original outlay upon the ratepayers. Upon the other hand, the future undoubtedly seems to lie with the petrol motor omni- bus, which needs no rails to be laid for its accommoda- tion and, therefore, causes no danger or inconvenience to other traffic. Tram lines are always a certain menace, whilst the vehicles themselves, are not suitable for running on a high road.

In spite of this, however, almost all our main thoroughfares out of London are now cut up with tram lines. In many of the large provincial towns, too, they are a prominent danger, some of the streets in which they are laid actually being so narrow that there is no room for a trap to draw up before a shop or house at which it is proposed to call. In addition to this, many of them are in connection with the electric system, so that it is impossible- for the drivers to pill up so quickly as they would be able to do with the old horse drawn type of vehicle. It is true that tram cars are a great convenience to those who use them ; but, surely, even the convenience of the many should not be gained by absolute danger to what is really a large minority.

Under no circumstances should fresh petrol be poured into the tank without being rur through a funnel having a gauze strainer attached, or, at any rate, if such a one is not handy, through a muslin placed across the mouth of the ordinary pattern. Fragments of dirt and some- times even tiny insects will frequently be found in the spirit, and these if not carefully prevented from enter- ing the petrol tank with the spirit, will assuredly lead to complication and perhaps, will even cause a lengthy delay on the road before the trouble is lccated.

BY CISSIE LOFTUS,
Author of "Jim's Ida," "*Buttonhead'e Brother," &c.

"It seems to me," said tanjo, with more rThemence than appeared necessary, "that e woman who could love a man and tell him so, and then throw him over for another, is absolutely and utterly contemptible. I could make no excuse for such a woman. She must be contemptible to be able to change so. If I loved a man I should love him for ever; nothing could ever make me change." "Would you, little. girl ? " asked the man. "Oh, yes," she replied readily, as she took up her book and left the room.

"It is your birthday to-c:ay, Banjo" he said, looking at her with interest. "How old are you ? " "Sixteen," she answered proudly. "And is that pretty new belt you have on a birthday present ? " "Yes." How he notices things ! she thought. "Well," he said to her gently, "I have no gift for you, but you have my very sincere wishes for your happiness, little girl, .and I hope you will have as many more birthdays as you would like to have."
"I'm not a little girl any longer. I'm grown up!" and she elevated her head a little in a vain endeavour to make herself look tall. 111.

"I am going to be present at your singing-lesson to-day," he said. "Are you?" she answered nervously. "Oh, I shall be so frightened, and I kn,ow I shan't be able to sing a note ! " "Well, do your best," he told her kindly, and he went away. After the lesson they met in the passage.

He took her hand and held it in both his own. "You did very well indeed," he said, "but you have one little fault which you must try to correct." Her heart was beating fast, because he still held her hand. "You don't open your mouth wide enough when you sing. Now, you have a very pretty mouth "—he looked at it smilingly—"so yot. mustn't be afraid to open it." "I'll try," she murmured.
"He thinks I have a pretty mouth ! " she told herself all that day. "Fancy a grown-up man like that taking notice of me! Ido like him 1"
Iv. "It is my birthday to-day," he told her a week or two later. "Are you going to give me any- thing ? "
"I haven't anything to give you," she said, looking up at him shyly. "I didn't know about it." "Would you have given me anything if you had known ? "
"I don't know," doubtfully. "I should have liked tn."
After a pause:. "Will you give me a kiss, little girl ? "
He took her hands and drew her gently to him. "Give me a kiss, my sweet I"

"You are not half a sweetheart!" she wrote to him jokingly. "Here is Christmas Day, and every- one has given me something but you! For shame! They met the same day, and he clasped round her thin arm a fine gold bangle from which hung the letters of her pet name in diamonds. Banjc looked a pretty name in diamonds. "How lovely! " she exclaimed. "How beauti- ful! But oh, what a shame that you should have had to go and get this for me! I only wrote it fun about your not sending anything. I'm sorry you went and bought this, even though it is sc lovely." "You do not think that I only got it after you' letter came? Do you? " "I did think so."

"Silly little girl! Why, I have had it for ova a week, and have been longing for Co-day to coin( to give it to you." "I can't thank you enough!" she murmured. "How lovely it is! And how good of you to think of me!"

"As if I were not always thinking of you!" he said reproachfully. "I'm sorry I wrote—even in fun," she thought, when he had gone. "He'll think it was mean ol me, or begging, perhaps. But isn't it lovely ! " And the diamonds trembled and glistened in the light as she held up her arm.

"I shall love you for ever!" she wrote. "Nothing will ever make me change. I would do anything for you—dare anything for you—give m:c life for you, if you wanted it. Tell me again that you do—really do—love ens—poor little tne Oh, I do love you so much!"

div.head: VII.
div.p: VII.
"He is too old for you," they jeered. "A widower! An old man! Why, he's grey!"

"He isn't grey!" she said scornfully. "And besides, lots of quite young men have grey hair." "He's making fun of you!" they told her. "Making fun of me!" she repeated contemptu- ously, as the grave image of her lover flitted before her mind.
"The idea," they went on, "of a child like you making a fool and a show of yourself about a married man old enough to be your father! Why, you'll be the talk of the town!"

"What rot! "she whimpered impatiently. "You know perfectly well he's not a married man. He't been a widower for four years, and he's not 016 enough to be anybody's father! I wish you'd leave me alone!" and she cried miserably. "None of that game!" they shouted at her. "And don't let's have any of your impudence!"
"They will never let me marry him," Banjo said to herself despairingly, "and I daren't run away. Besides, .he hasn't asked me to ! " "Promise to stop this foolery!" they coin' mended.
"No—l can't!" she replied a 3 firmly as she dared.
"You don't stir out of this room till you promised not to see him again!"
A sob for answer.
"Little idiot! Throwing away all your chances like this! Why, you might marry anybody wia your face! The man doesn't care a pin about you; he's only fooling you."
Quiet. -"Promise to give him up and be a good girl, instead of making yourself and everybody else miserable like this. Promise."
"I can't." After four days. ."Promise not to -see him again."
"Very well," she said despairingly, and gave. in.

"I must see him once more," she thought, "just to tell him it isn't my fault; that they force me to it. Oh dear! How miserable I am—and I'm only sixteen! I wish people would leave me alone, and that I'd never been born! "

div.head: VIII.
div.p: VIII.
"So you cannot be faithful to me?" he said to her coldly. 1

"Oh, I can't help it! I can't help it! They won't let me; they torture the life out of me all day. I must have some peace. I've promised not to see you again, and yet here lam with you. If ria net they'll kill me. It he the hica time!" and she cried bitterly. "You don't pity, me a bit! " she went on. "It's easy enough for you who are your own master, but it's awful for me. l'm nagged at morning, noon and night, till I'm nearly driven mad. I can't help it, really. "Oh, do forgive me!"

"You cannot be faithful." he repeated. "There - is some other man."
"I assure you there is not ! " she said earnestly —"though I suppose you won't believe me."
"You cannot be faithful 4 After all your
promises! "
"Forgive me, and let us be friends," she wept, her face buried in her handkerchief. "Won't you? " she whispered timidly. But when she looked up he had left her. Ix.

He and she were present at the last dance of the season. Not together. He was alone. She was with an aunt, and a cousin almost as young and foolish as herself, with whom she had always carried on a milk-and-water flirtation.
"Do you know," giggled her partner to her, "we are supposed to be engaged ? " "Engaged ? " she repeated sharply. "How could such a ridiculous report have got about ? "

"I don't know, but it has. And don't you think we might as rell justify the report, darling? I'm awfully fond of you, you know." As they talked they had strolled slowly round the room, and had brought themselves up in front of a couple who had been eyeing them for some minutes. "It is he," she said to herself. "I wonder who the woman is?" And then she wondered if the man she loved had heard her cousin's last remark.

"Let us go' on," she said. "They are engaged!" laughed the woman to the man. "Don't they look a pair of turtle-doves! " He made no reply. "I must get to speak to him for a minute," thought the girl, "to tell him it isn't true." For nearly an hour she hunted him through the room. At the end of that time she •ilung herself passionately into her carriage and drove home, having failed to make him see her. "How could lie treat me so!" she thought angrily. "He has forgotten me already. Flirting with that mummy of a woman all night! And—oh, dear! Ido love him so!"
And she made herself miserable for a fortnight.

"She is absolutely heartless ! " he told himself that night as he settled comfortably down in his armchair. "Parading herself round the room with that little puppy she's engaged to! I knew she was !ying to me ! " Ile took carefully out of his pocket a rose which had been given to him by his partner of the evening, and held it in his hand for lb moment. Then flung it into the fire before him. "I must get married again," he said to himself. "She has twenty thousand a year." He was thinking of the woman who had given him the rose.

Padgate Minstrel Troupe. The members of the Padgate Nigger Minstrel Troupe had an excursion to Belle Vue Gardens, Man- chester, on Saturday. The weather was fine. Tea was partaken of at 5.30, and Padgate was safely reached later in the evening.

he Stockton Heath Tramway. The tram lines have now been laid and completed across the Swing Bridge and also into Victoria Square Stockton Heath. Gaughan, supervisor of the Inland Revenue, first class, Warrington district, is leaving for Cork (first class district). His suceessor will be Mr. N. Phillips who will be promoted from Bury district, second Class, to Warrington district, first class. Mr. Gaughan has been at Warrington since June, 1903. Bell-Ringers Entertained. On Saturday the Rev. G. B. Thurston, rector of Lymm entertained the ringers from the parish 'churches of Daresbury, Grappenhall, Warburton, and. St. Mary's, Lymm. The occasion was a branch meet- ing of the Cheshire Guild of Ringers, and during the afternoon the ringers from the different churches rang short peals on the splendid bells of the Parish Church. A vote of thanks was given to the Rector of Lymm for his hospitality. GREAT SALE OF BOOTS AND SHOES DOW On UNDER THE CLOCK.—Advt. Buckley-street P.S.A Society. On Sunday,the monthly open meeting of this society was held in the Methodist Free Church. The chair was occupied by Mr. A. Scott, Mr. H. Woolley read- ing the lessons. The musical part of the programme was given by the Legh-street Primitive Methodist Choir, under the leadership of Mr. A. Spruce, and was much appreciated. The items included choruses, solos, duets and an anthem. Mr. A. E. Trow presided was at the organ. H. M. ASHTON'S LIFF. TONIC is the RING OF TONICS. I 63. SANKEY-STREET, Warrington.—Advt. The New Free Church at Winwick.—Date of

- Foundation Stone Laying. The foundation stones of the intended now Free Church at Winwick will be laid on the 20th instant. The work has been inaugurated and carried out by the members of the Free Church Council, who have persevered most nobly with this work until success has crowned their efforts. The church will be of a unique character, and it will be unsectarian, and cannot but be of areat benefit and a boon to the grow- ing district of Winwick, as there is no Nonconformist church in the district.

Popular Health Lectures. The Health Committee are to be congratulated on the announcement which is made in another column that a course of three lectures is to be given in the Parr Hall during this and next month. The Council of the Royal Institute of Public Health who grant these lectures to a limited number of boroughs each year desire to awaken the public to a better appreciation of health questions and to the great necessity which exists of attention to public health measures, and by this means to strengthen the action of health commit- tees, throughout the country. It is hoped that the public of Warrington will avail themselves of the opportunity to attend and thereby show their appreci- a ton of the action of the Health Committee. A Soldier's Escapade. At the Borough Police Court on Thursday, William Dolan was charged with deserting from the South Lancashire Regiment stationed at Orford Barracks.— Superintendent Monaghan said that at two o'clock that morning the watchman of the Mersey White Lead Works, Sankey Bridge, noticed a light in the office. On investigating he found that the place had been broken into and prisoner was in the manager's office. He had discarded his military attire and was donning a suit which had been left on the promises. He had, it was alleged, broken open a book case— The magistrates handed prisoner over to the County Police, the White Load Works being outside the borough. Prisoner will be dealt with by the military authorities later.—Dolan was • subsequently remanded at the Occasional Court on a charge of stealing three pairs of trousers, a coat, a pair of goloshes, and a pair of socks from the office of the White Lead Works. The educational record for the past year is an exceptional ono, and has not previously, been equalled in the school's history. div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
OCTOBER Bth, 1904.
With Sir ' WILLIAM HAR- SIR WILLIAM COURT passed away the last HARCOURT. of the old stately school of

politicians. It is not only a life that has ceased, but a tradition that has perished. In this instance it may be said with con- fidence that we shall not look upon his like again. There was something characteristically dignified and appropriate in the manner of his death. He passed away quietly without pain or fear. The last enemy, coming as a friend laid his hand upon him as he slept. The Ration will now do justice to one who, throughout a long and most useful life, was in general harshly judged. It has been the fashion to say that as a politician Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT was lacking in convic- tion, that heavy as were his orslaughts on the opposing party, they were often histrionic and insincere. No politician is justly esteemed during his lifetime. We must be at the historical distance before we can see character in its true perspec- tive; but who among recent Statesmen, we may now ask, has presented a nobler example of con-

sistency and of high purpose than Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT ? He was at one time accused of having :placed himself in rivalry with Mr. GLADSTONE. The famous retire- ment from active leadership after the electoral defeat of 1874 was supposed to have been brought about in large measure by what was assumed to be the vaulting ambition of Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT. The best and the final commentary on the old accusation is supplied by .31r WILLIAm's subsequent career. In none of his Administrations had Mr. GLADSTONE a more faith- ful or devoted colleague. When the great dis- ruption came, when the present DUKE of DEVON- SHIRE, and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, and Sir GEORGE TREVELYAN, and so many men of less account fell away from the great leader's side, Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT remained staunch and unmoved. He was condemning himself to a long exclusion from office at the most important period of his life. If ambition had been a compelling motive in his character, he would have gone over to the other side,where he would in all probability have reached that supreme and commanding position from which on Mr. GLADSTONE'S retirement many years later he was debarred.

Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT was not merely a dis- tinguished political gladiator; he was also a great Liberal, and he adhered resolutely, to quote his own memorable phrase, to "the Grand Old Cause and the Grand Old Man." Though he was repeatedly in office, first as Solicitor-General, then as Home Secretary,and finally as Chancellor of the Exchequer and leader of the House of Commons, Sir WILLIA.7,I HARCOURT had only a comparatively brief administrative experience. His tenure of official positions bears quite a small proportion to the thirty-six years during which he was a leading member of Parliament. He was a member of Mr. , GLADSTONE'S four Administrations, and yet he sat on the Ministerial front bench for less than nine years in all. This is a considera- sion which should suggest a respectful tilence to those critics whose view of political life is that a Parliamentary career is little more than a struggle for the spoils of office. In the 2ase of a man so able and so distinguished as Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT, it is a career of sacrifice and unselfishness, with the good of the nation as its prime object, and the :old Radical demand for "Peace, Retrenchment, and Reform " as its guid- ing rule. From this point of view, Sir WILLIAM HARCJURT'S life has been one of the most effective service to his country and his countrymen. In apposition, he has been a keen, searching, high-minded, indispensable critic. In office, he has bean a man with a large grasp, bringing fine intellectual qualities to the solution of some of the most difficult problems of Statesmanship. His record is splendid. He was one of the best of our Home Secretaries. He passed the Ground Game Act against enormous difficulties, and the opposition of the whole landed interest. His really memorable achievement was the famous Death Duties Budget, under whose provisions, as it curiously happens, his own estates will have to pay large sums for succession duty for the second time in two years, The Budget of 1894 lightened enormously the work of all succeeding Chan- cellors of the :Exchequer, and entitled Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT to stand only second to Mr. GLADSTONE as a master of finance. The loss of a Statesman of such distinction creates a gap in the Parliamentary ranks such as is made by the falling of some great tree in the forest. Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT Stood for pro- foundly important and essential principles of Statesmanship. He was the resolute and immov- able opponent of the expenditure which, as he has so frequently warned us, is a great and threaten- ing danger to the nation. He was the powerful exponent of an ever-broadening Liberalism. He looked at events in the large light of practical , common sense. The country has lost much by reason of the fact that his opportunities of serving it in office were so circumscribed. A few more years with Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT as Chancellor of the Exchequer, ar.d the whole basis of the taxa- tion would have been reformed. It is equally certain that our expenditure could never have increased to its present formidable dimensions. The nation chose other advisers, with what dis- astrousi ry L resultsul fi t A R :beginning to realise- s spwublic services will be \ Ai is 0c onlyußno all the more esteemed as the years pass onward. He goes to his grave full of years and of honours. His life has been one of those on which it is a satis- faction on all good men to reflect. He has, in HEINE'S words, been a soldier in the War of the Liberation of Humanity. During these last few years, the tongue of detraction has no longer been busy with him, and now that he is no more among us, all parties will recognise in him a great, true, outstanding Englishman.

"If an irresistible force met an immovable object what would be the result r" This is a conundrum schoolboys are fond of asking one another. Just no w the ratepayers of Bewsey Ward in particular, and the town generally, are concerned with an interesting problem almost identical with the one over which they prob- ably exercised their ninds in childhood's days. And they are no nearer a solution, though fate has permitted them to come within measurable distance of seeing the effect of such a collision demonstrated. Bewsey Ward has narrowly escaped being thecentre of so remarkable a conflict, for the:"chief trader " and the leading Non-trader have both been nominated fur the existing Town Council vacancy, and both have since retired. The announcement that Mr. Henry Roberts J.P., had been adopted by the Bewsey Liberal Ward Com- mittee was followed almost immediately by the resignation of Councillor Dodds. That the two events had a close connection, was obvious, and the fact became unmistakable when both gentle- men were nominated for the vacancy, together with a Labour candidate in the person of Mr. T. Wright. The next item in this dramatic episode was the placarding of the hoardings by Mr. Dodds with a declaration ofThis reasons for taking such determined measures. Hardly had the excited public digested this com- munication when the news that Mr. Roberts had withdrawn became common property. Finally came the intimation, not unexpected con- sidering the course of events, that Mr. Dodds had also retired, leaving the field clear to the Labour Candidate who had been in imminent danger of being hopelessly involved in the strife of giants. The position of affairs to-day, therefore, is that Mr. Henry Roberts remains "as you were:" Mr. Dodds is no longer Councillor,and Mr. Thomas Wright will shortly succeed to that honour w ith - out incurring anxiety or further expense.

; The " whys and the Wherefores" for the final course adopted by each of the two gentlemen most prominently concerned are the points now most interesting to reflective and speculative electors. ' Mr. Dodds' position has been clearly and positively defined from the commencement. It was obvious that if Mr. Roberts entered the municipal arena n o ..Withouttrad i makinga declaration on the non trading question which was satisfactory to the opponents of municipal trading, there was no logical and conscientious course left for Mr. Dodds but to directly and uncompromising

oppose him. No one expected Mr. Dodds to do otherwise, and in his address to the Town Hall Ward electoes he was emphatic in his determina- tion to stand by the principle which carried him and his party to the head of the polls only two years ago. Mr. Roberts vouchsafed no explanation of the attitude he intended to adopt on the trading question, and the natural presumption is that he had no intention of making any concession to the public opinion which has been expressed so unmis- takably against trading by members of the Coun- cil with the Corporation through limited com- panies. The fact that he has avoided the issue is, it seems to us much more significant than any- thing he says in extenuation of his sudden with- drawal one minute from" time." There is much however, in the letter of explanation which he has addressed to the secretary of the Liberal Ward Committee which warrants some consideration. Mr. Roberts' first and primary reason for with- drawing from the contest is becauelP,to use his own words, "I decline to oppose the Labour candidate." Then why did Mr. Roberts allow himself to be nominated in opposition to the Lab -flir candidate when the latter was the only man in the field? This appears to us a question which naturally arises. But it is hardly worth while seeking to obtain further light on the reasons which actu- ated Mr. Roberts in his withdrawal from the contest. It suffices to say that he can hardly hope to re-enter the Council without first satisfying the public that he will not seek to place himself again in the invidious position of being a member of the Council and at the same time the predominant partner in a concern which trades extensively with the Corporation. Some such concession to public opinion :is demanded of Mr. Roberts under the circumstances, ;and we hope he will, :at the proper time, seek the suffrages of the electors on lines which will admit of his being unreservedly supported.

The information as to the prospects for the winter is anything but encouraging. From the large centres of population come stories of lack of employment and increase in poor-law relief which bode ill for us if the weather should be hard, and forms of outdoor employment, through the meteorological conditions have to be suspended. It behoves local municipal authorities and charit- able organizations to do what they can, both to provide work and to alleviate probable distres - It will not do to wait until the trouble be COM% acute; anticipative measures, at any rate should be taken in the next month or two. The Local Government Board's figures show how things are going, with £3,500,000 devoted to poor relief in the last half-year; and it would be well if the Local Government Board would move in the matter to at any rate the extent of giving local bodies a reminder of their imminent duty in what may well be a difficult situation. Of the state of affairs in London we have already heard. The Salvation Army, two months earlier than in previous years, has begun the provision of free morning bread and soup. It has been stated that at Manchester 5•4 per cent. of the heads of families are out of work; while at Leeds on the books of the unemployed bureau are 3,000 names, repre- senting persons for whom the Mayor says he does not know what to do. It is greatly to be hoped that municipalities and boards of guardians will see their way to establishing relief works wherever they are needed.

"The adventures of Mr. Gough" if they were ever printed under that title would,we think,make interesting read:ng. He has been a most success ful man—successful in getting across with the "powers that be': on almost every conceivable opportunity. Possibly it affords him amusement as well as excitement to do so. At any rate his escapades in public add to the gaiety of the people and for that much he deserves thanks. Since the ex-Councillor's conviction for using improper methods of persuasion at his election he has been —like some volcanoes—quiescent and people have been lulled into forgetfulness of his existence. To carry the simile further, Mr. Gough has unex- pectedly erupted.. At the Council meeting en Tuesday the eagle eye of the Town Clerk detected Mr. Gough seated calmly in his old place among the Councillors. Mirabile dictu. There was no questioning the substantial fact of Mr. Gough's presence, however, and the Mayor too was com- pelled to believe the evidence of his own eyes. His Worship lost no time in putting matters to rights, and the intruder was compelled to retire "under protest." Had he been given time Mr. Gough was evidently prepared to contest his right to the seat,for he had a goodly sheaf of formidable looking documents under his arm. Seeing that he I is disfranchised Mr. Gough's position admitted of no argument or extenuation, and the public benches were his habitat thenceforth. Here the eruption simmered down, and Mr. Gough's latest adventure was at an end. What, we wonder, will be his next?

The second report on the Non-Trading Inquiry has now been handed in by Messrs. Wilkinson, Peacock, and James. Evans, who have evidently profited by the experience of their predecessors,for they respectfully and very properly suggest to the Mayor that the contents of the report be not divulged until the Non-Traders have submitted their own summary and verdict on the inquiry. It is this latter report that the public anxiously awaits, for, while being last, it is also the most important. Th a non-trading members of the commission have sat 65 times haring evidence and supervising the examination of thousands of documents during a period extending over 12 months. The very nature of the charges they have publicly made requires that the utmost care and consideration . should be given to a report which must contain all the justification they have to offer. Councillor Pemberton inti- mates that the report is to be "very serious," a statement which few people will doubt. There is no room for loxity in the consideration of the sub • ject, and the Non-Trading Commissioners are right in taking every precaution in order to be sure of their facts. With regard to the minutes of pro-. ceedings at the inquiry we are sure the ratepayers will be glad to know that an opportunity is to be afforded of perusing the documents. They are in type, and will be reprinted for public reference.

Councillor A. Peacock is deserving of sympathy and commendation for his efforts to induce the Tramways Committee to give half -penny fares a trial on some of the routes. At present the tram service is expensive to its patrons though admit- tedly efficient. But it appears to us that if an experiment in reduced fares is to be tried at all it should be tried on routes that always pay well and not on those which are run at a loss. If the cars will not pay their way with the penny fares in certain districts it is hardly reasonable to suppose that a reduction in the charges will result in the much-desired profit. The Committee and Councillor Peacock are equally right in the course of action they have taken, but both will be ccmpelled to await the blarch of events before they can see eye to eye with each other. _

This excellent benefit f r waterway t et rhwe Manchester Hitherto Warrfngton has reaped little or no our shores has never been a commercial asset to Warrington, but better things may be in store for us. This week has witnessed :a new development which may have an important bearing on Warring- a with tou's commerce. For the first time, we under- stand, the lay•bye on the Ship Canal at Walton has been used as a stopping place by a passing steamer to Manchester for the discharge of a cargo for Mr. Edward Connor, and afterwards for the taking up of a parcel of goods of the Warrington Borate Company, Limited, for shipment to Belfast. This interesting operation occupied only a few hours, but it proved so successful, that we venture to think it will be .repeated. To local merchants and manufacturers it is purely a matter of business. If a saving can be effected by im- porting and exporting direct at Warrington, ther- vessels to stop a few hours at Walton for dis' charging or taking up cargo. The co-operation o the Ship Canal Company is necessary to the success of the scheme, but we do not think they will be found unsympathetic in listening to any proposals which will enable them to tap an hitherto undeveloped source of revenue.

The results are decidedly inter- esting and surprising, and afford a key to the sub- jects which loom largest in the juvenile mind. For instance, the candidates were asked to state certain celebrities were. Oily 47 per cent were cognisant of the fact that Mr. Arthur Balfour is the prime minister, and fewer still knew that Colonel Eielsten commands the Warrington Volunteers. But to the query " Wh„° is Mr. J. Fish ? " there was an 3"- round response, and 88 per cant. prcved them selves familiar with the deeds of Warria4coa crack footballer. The authol of "Sherlock Holmes," "The Ancient Mariner, "Woodstock,' and "The Charge of the Light Brigade" were quits unknown' whilst 4 per Cent:, , were aware that Defoe wrote "Robinson Crusoe•

0514§ King Edward's relationship to the Prince Of Wales was known to only 31 per cent and there was a surprising ignorance of the "rule of the road." Whilst very few boys could give a correct definition of courtesy, some of the elementary rulee of etiquette were very well known. One would have thought that every Warringtonian could clearlY indicate the position of the Town Hall, but the percentage of correct answers to this query wet but 84. The examination will no doubt have servea a useful purpose, and we hope it will encourage the boys to "keep their eyes open" so that wile° another test comes they will be able to give a better account of thems3lves.

div.head: Motor Accident in Church-street, Warrington.
div.p: Motor Accident in Church-street, Warrington.

-- Shortly after five o'clock on Saturday evening a serious motor-car accident occurred. Jr. James Lowe, 68 years of age, residing at 63, Padgate-lane, was standing on the footpath, near to Messrs. Rylands' works in Church-street, waiting for.an electric car. When the car was about twelve or fifteen yards away, he signalled it to stop and then stepped into the road- way to enter it. He failed to notice the approach of a motor car, which is alleged to have been going at a high speed, and he was knocked down sustaining a compound fracture of the right leg and injuries to the left•side of the head and face. He was conveyed to the Infirmary in a'. cab. The driver of the motor car which bore a Liverpool registration mark was shouted to, but refused to stop.

Local Bands at the Crystal Palace. Warringtonians will be gratified to hear of the success of two local bands in the national contest held at the Crystal Palace on Saturday. Messrs. Crosfield's band competed against 25 others in the junior cup section, the test piece being "Gems of Tachaikowsky." Mr. W. Halliwell, of the Wigan Rifles, wielded the baton, and so creditably did the members of the bancl acquit themselves that they carried off the first prize —a handsome 50 guinea silver cap. The band consists of twenty-six worknitn, and prior to last Saturday's success had attended eleven contests and won nine prizes in competition with 124 bands. The Cheshire Lines Railway band (Liverpool) took first prize in the preliminary shield :section, winning the " People " challenge shield, value 50 guineas, and £5 in cash. Twenty bands competed. The test piece was" Pinafore" (Sullivan), and Mr. R. Rimmer, Southport, conducted. The band secretary (Mr. Fred Molyneux) Lad in hand the arrangements:for the visit,which were successfully carried out. Most of the members of the band are from the Warrington Section of the railway. Both organisations are to be congratulated upon their splendid achievements. GREAT SALE OF BOOTS AND SHOES now lon UNDER THE CLOCK.—Advt. Spiritual Lyceum. At the Spiritualist Hall on Sunday and Monday the anniversary of this institution was celebrated. An open session was held on Sunday afternoon,which was attended by a fair number of friends, to whom the proceedings afforded much pleasure. The usual silver and golden chain recitations,music,al reading,marching and calisthenics were gone through, recitations by individual scholars, and a trio, "Glorious Apollo,' by the brothers Foster. Mr. S. S. Chiswell,of Liverpool, took part in the service and delivered an address. In the evening there was a large audience, when the scholars, arranged upon an extended platform, sang a number of special hymns, an anthem (" The Lord's Prayer.") and a choral march, the words and music of which were composed by Mr. Foster who had evidently taken great pains in the training of the members of the Lyceum, and pre- sided at the organ. A selection from the "Manuel," entitled "The presence of angels," was effectively given as a dialogue by Lily Shaw and John Turner. Mr. Chiswell delivered an address, and the service closed with the singing of "God be with you till we meet again." On Monday a public tea was attended by a large number of friends of the movement, and was followed by a social, at which a pianoforte solo " Fire ! Fire ! " was capitally played by Miss Bonner, followed by a skilful violin solo, Ever of thee," by Mr. Leopold Edwards. Mr. Frank Turner recited 'The burial of Sir John Moore," and Mr. Summers mused with "I burst out laughing," giving a recita- ion as an encore. The amusing sketch, "The bobby's ourtship," was well given by members of the Lyceum, causing roars of laughter.
Personal.

_ Writing in "St. Paul's Magazine," the Vicar ex- presses regret "that the people's warden Mr. A. H. Burgess, is about to leave WarriVon to take an im- portant position in Birmingham in connection with the firm (Messrs. Pearson and Knowles) he has worked with for so long." After paying a tribute to the valuable work of Mr. and Mrs. Burgess, the Vicar concludes: "We 6artily congratulate him on his appointment, but we greatly deplore the loss of .such staunch and true Church workers." Legh-street Brass Band. On Tuesday evening the members of the above band sat down to an excellent supper given by Mr. John Podmore. After supper songs were given by Mr. George Smith and Mrs. Mills and Mr. W. Dale gave excellent recitations. Hearty votes of thanks were proposed by Mr. Metcalf and Mr. Billingh.am and seconded by Mr. John Jones who urged upon the members to rallyjround their conductor,and encouraged them by referring to his connection with the old Legh- street band where he first received his training under Mr. Podmore, senior. Mr. John Podmore suitably re- sponded. Amongst those present were the President and his wife, Mr. and Mrs. Job S wales. The pro- ceedings terminated with the singing of" Auld Lang Syne." H. M.
