Mr. Halton pre- sided and there were also present :—Dr. Murray, Messrs. Ball, Thompson, Backhouse, Houghton, Brooks, Forshaw, Mather and Longton, together with Messrs. J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), B. S. Newcombe (surveyor), F. W. Ker- foot (inspector) and Dr. Sephton (medical officer.) —The seal of the Council was affixed to an agreement with the Warrington Corporation for an extended water supply to Burtonwood.— The Clerk reported that he had received a letter from the Bucklow District Council. with regard to the taking over of Warburton Bridge by the authorities in the adjoining districts. The Bucklow District Council declined to consider the matter until they had further information. Mr. Newcombe stated that further information could not be given. All the other authorities interested had favourably considered the matter, Bucklow District Council alone declining to consider it.—The matter was left over for a month, the :clerk in the meantime to approach the Clerk of the Bucklow District Council.— The clerk read a letter from the clerk of the Poulton Parish Council containing a resolution passed by the Parish Council approving of the scheme proposed by Mr. Newcombe for the treatment of the sewage.—Mr. Mather moved the adoption of Mr. Newcombe's scheme, and that it be carried out.—lt was however decided to postpone them until the Roads Committee of the Council have pre- sented their report on sewage matters generally.— Mr. Newcombe in his report recommended the con- struction of a precipitating tank at Blackbrook at a cost of £6O; the piping of the ditches in Orchard street, with intercepting trap, filters &c., at a cost of £150; and in Padgate-lane to extend th 3 existing pipe and treat the sewage in a similar manner as at Blackbrook. ..+••••••••••••011awa•am.g.ww~0. THE INFIRMARV CONCERT.

The annual concert of the Workingmen's Committee in aid of the Infirmary was of more than ordinary attrac- tiveness. A large audience therefore gathered in the Parr Hall on Saturday last and shewed in an unmistakable manner its appreciation of the best items in the pro- gramme. The performances of Mr. T. J. Down's orchestra, numbering some 58 performers,bulked largely in the programme and formed the backbone of the concert. The War March of the Priests from "Athalie" and the beautiful "Soldaten Leider " raise, were'pro- bably the most interesting of the orchestral items, as they were also the best from a technical point of view. Nor indeed was the "Willian Tell" overture much amiss having regard to its executive difficulties. The opening solo for the principal 'cello and the interplay of the wood-wind in this movement were highly creditable to all the per- formers concerned. It was rather in the brass instru- ments—a section usually so strong in Mr. Down's orchestra—that the most serious slips were noticeable. and this remark has, of course, particular refer- ence to the vivace movement. Considerable en- thusiasm was shown in regard to the orchestral items, and had "El Capaan " been played in any other part of the programme except the close, it would doubtless have been encored. Mrs. Arthur Booth and Miss Nellie Anderton were the solo vocalists, and the appearance of each on the platform was the signal for a welcoming round of applause. Mrs. Booth's rendering of the waltz-song "Star of Twilight" (Leslie Crotty) evinced an unmistakable advance in this gifted singer's management of a fine soprano voice which is now seen to be one of great flexibility. An encore ensued as a matter of course. Later in the evening Mrs. Booth's singing of "Love the Pedlar" served to emphasise the good impression made by her earlier effort and to confirm the favourable verdict passed upon it. The good old favourite "Kathleen Mavourneen " received a fitting interpretation from Miss Anderton and earned for her a well-merited recall. Subsequently Miss Anderton successfully essayed Blumenthal's "Sun- shine and rain" which we are inclined to think is a song better suited to her voice and style. With Mr. G. H. Ditchburn's singing Warrington concert-frequenters are already familiar. He is a bass of the profanclo type i and in nterpreting songs such as "Drinking" and "The Wolf" he but shews a shrewd judgment of the shortest way to the audience's favour. Certainly these songs were well sung and they may therefore- be fairly said to have both deserved and commanded the success which loud and frequent applause signalised. The humorist was Mr. Arthur Bearle whose character songs and whimsicalties mightily amused a section of the audience. We understand that financially the concert is likely to prove a record one —a fact to be hailed with unmixed satisfaction.

div.head: COUNCILLOR DODDS AND THE LANCASHIRE COUNTY RATE JOINT COMMITTEE.
div.p: COUNCILLOR DODDS AND THE LANCASHIRE COUNTY RATE JOINT COMMITTEE.
Letter to the Mayor.

Mt. James Dodds has written the following letter to the Mayor on the above-mentioned subject : Dear 'Mr. Mayor,—Having retired from the Council it is only through you that I can report the completion a few days ago of the quinquennial re-assessment of the County of Lancaster by the County Rate Joint Com- mittee, upon which I have had the honour to represent Warrington. The work of the preparation of a new basis or standard for fair and equal County rating, under 15 and 19 Victoria Chapter 81, for the five years commencing with August next, though highly interesting, has been onerous; nearly forty days in all have been spent upon it, and between December last and I September ultimo the new assessment of each ' of the 431 townships embracel in the 31 Poor Law Unions of the County Palatine has been carefully revised and settled. I have been able to attend about one-third of the meetings—rather over the average of my colleagues' attendances—at Lancaster, Ulverston, Preston, Manchester and Liverpool. Some most inter- esting variations of methods and of bases of valuation were submitted by the local assessment authorities, and much valuable experience was gained by the members of the Joint Committee. The Warrington Union was ably represented by Mr. J. C. Sutton and Mr. William Owen and the County Borough itself by that admirable financial officer, Mr. W. H. Woodcock. From the nompleted returns I find that the total new rateable value of the whole County for County rate purposes amounts to nearly twenty six millions, or to be exact £25,910,356, being an increase, as compared with five years ago, of £2,995,670 or 13 per cent. For the Warrington -Union, the corresponding figures are £489,628 an increase of £79,724 or a percentage increase for the five years of 19-4. Of this increase £17,980 has been provided by the County Borough and £31,714 by the townships in the Warrington Union which are part of the administrative County. Had I continued a member of the Council I should have been prepared at the next Council meeting to have given some interesting details and comparisons. I must not now further trouble you, except to add that believing as I do that any man who undertakes to give his services to the public, should'give them freely and fully, without any kind of pecuniary consideration and at his own expense, I have to-day therefore handed to the treasurer of the Warrington Infirmary twenty guineas, which will amply cover the amount of travel- ling expenses which lam to have recouped to me, and also my share of the pooled cost of hotel accommoda- tion and lunches Ste., which the County Treasurer directly defrayed. I am Dear Mr. Mayor, Faithfully yours, (Signed) JAMES DODDS. Penketh House, October 7th.

The Hon. Treasurer of the Infirmary and Dispensary writes acknowledging, with thanks, a donation of £2l from Mr. James Dodds, Penketh House, in respect of which he becomes a WelGovernor of the Institution.

IA Lloyd's Sydney (New South Wales) agent tele- graphs that the British ship Mount Stewart, from London, is on fire. Every means are being taken to ex- tinguish it. She is being beached and filled with water.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, October 8, 1904.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, October 8, 1904.
BEWSEY !WARD VACANCY.
A WEEK OF SENSATIONS AND SURPRISES.

, The bye-election in Bewsey Ward, caused by the en- forced retirement of Mr. Samuel Gough, promised at one time to bring the two chief local protagonists for and against municipal trading into an electoral conflict. When it became known that Mr. Henry Roberts, J,P. had been nominated by the Bewsey Liberal Ward Com- mittee as a candidate, Mr. Dodds decided to resign his seat as the representative of Town Hall Ward in order to be able to enter the lists against Mr. Roberts in Bewsey Ward.ln an address to the Town Hall burgesses he said:— "Two years ago I received a signal proof of your loyalty to the cause of Municipal Purity and of your confidence in me as its humble exponent. At that time I made it clear that I did not desire or seek a seat in the Council but that my sole object was to afford you the opportunity of recording your verdict as between pure administration and the trading which was then rampant, and which several members of the Corporation had practised. Your clear and emphatic decision had marvellous results, the chief trader accepted my election as notice to quit, and at once retired from the Council. Improper trading began to gradually decrease, until it is now practically extinct. Having attended every meeting of the Finance Committee daring the current year, and having seen all the accounts, I can con- firm what I stated in the Council Chamber a few weeks ago, that for the past twelve months there has been little if any trading between the members of the Council and the Corporation, but from Wednesday's issue of the " Warrington Guardian" I observe that the leaders of the Liberal party in the Bewsey Ward, to their lasting discredit, have invited a well-known leading trader to contest the vacancy which has just arisen in the Ward, and that it is understood the invitation has been accepted by him. As the leader of the Non-Trading movement, my duty seems olear, and I have therefore to ask you to release me as your representative, in order that I may enter the lists against the gentleman who two years ago, stood as the champion of the improper trad- ing, and who publicly boasted in the Parr Hall whilst Mayor of the Borough, that such trading should con- tinue. It is well that the ratepayers of Bewsey Ward should have the opportunity of saying definitely by their votes whether or no they approve the coarse I have pursued,and of the cause of which I have been,how- ever unworthily, the leader. Whatever may happen, and whether I be elected or rejected by my fellow townspeople I shall never forget how generously you supported me irrespective of party, in 1902, and how great a stimulus you then gave to the movement of municipal purity and thereby helped to remove from our good old town the stigma which had been brought upon it." Five o'clock on Thursday evening was the latest heOur at which nominations could be handed in and at that hour it was found that three candidates had been nomin- ated. The Labour Representation Committee brought forward Mr. Thomas Wright, a member of the Wire- drawers Association, and residing in Thewlis-street. One nomination was handea in on behalf of Mr. Henry Roberts J.P., and throe on behalf of Mr. James Dodds. This turn of events caused some surprise, and resulted in those electors who revel in the dust and heat of Et stiff contest looking forward with interest to a remark- able triangular contest. Yesterday, however, Mr. Henry Roberts, J.P., with- drew his nomination and Mr. Dodds has since issued an address to the electors of the ward stating that the reason which prompted him to seek their suffrages hav- ing been removed, he has decided to withdraw from the contest in favour of Mr. Thomas Wright, the labour candidate, who has satisfied him as to his views upon the Non-Trading question. Mr. Wright will, therefore have a walk-over.

div.head: WHY MR. ROBERTS WITHDREW.
div.p: WHY MR. ROBERTS WITHDREW.

Yesterday Mr. H. Roberts forwarded a letter to Mr. E. A. Sanders, who until a few days ago was secretary of the Bewsey Liberal Ward Committee, but which post he has now resigned. In the course of his letter, we understand, Mr. Roberts thanks the Ward Committee for requesting him to become their candidate, and adds: "Although the unwarranted statement that I had expressed my willingness to accept nomination was only Imade public on Wednesday last, I have already received so many offers of support from Conservative and Liberal electors in the Ward that my election would have been assured. 1 desire to thank these friends, and also the daily increasing number of those electors who are thoroughly sick of the trickery and dodges of the Non-Trading party, and who are convinced that the report of the Non-Trading Commissioners on the recent" Inquiry" has been needlessly and purposely delayed in the vain hope that it may serve in some measure to revive their dying cause at the ensuing November election."

In --giving his reasons for declining to stand, Mr. Roberts says :—" All my life I have supported the just and reasonable causes of workingmen and I decline to oppose the Labour candidate. Further lam strongly of opinion that it would be better to wait until the final Report of the Inquiry Commissioners is pub- lished (and which would have been in your hands by this time but for a deliberate breach of faith on the part of the Non-Traders) in order that the Burgesses may fully realise how absolutely unjustifiable the recent agitation has been. A mere defeat of Mr. Dodds at the poll would give me very little satisfaction,as I prefer to have the opportunity in the Council Chamber of compelling the Non-Traders through their self-con- stituted leader, to justify or withdraw the charges which he and they have made." Mr. Roberts then goes on to assert that the non- trading agitation is prompted by personal feeling and concludes :—" lam not the only man who in recent times has been the victim of injustice, but althou_gh the trials of the past two'years have lbeen severe, I have never lost my faith in the righteousness of the ulti- mate judgment of my townspeople or my belief that before long they would restore to me the confidence which it was my honour and privilege for so many years to enjoy, and which under the influence of an unscrupulous agitation, founded upon exaggeration and falsehood, they had in some small measure perhaps temporarily withheld."

div.head: MR. THOMAS WRIGHT'S CANDIDATURE.
div.p: MR. THOMAS WRIGHT'S CANDIDATURE.

On Thursday evening an open-air meeting in support of the candidature of Mr. Thomas Wright was held on the open spas opposite St. Paul's Church. There was a rather small attendance, presided over by Councillor Stott.

The CHAIRMAN said that as there had been a great deal of misrepresentation or misunderstanding with reference to the Labour Representation Committee, he desired to state exactly the true position of affairs. He pointed out that the Committee was formed two years ago, and consisted of representatives of the, Trades Council, trade union branches and Independent Labour party. Its object was to band together the whole of the trade unionists of Warrington for political purposes. Mr. Wright's candidature was the first that had been promoted by the committee, and they hoped it would be successful. He was surprised that neither of the two great political parties nor the other organiz- ation which had been in existence for some time for political purposes had seen fit to declare Bewsey Ward vacant. He (Councillor Stott) felt sure that if he had been a resident in the ward he would not have been con- tent to be without a representative for six months. He believed it had been stated by some of their opponents that this was an Independent Labour Party candidature. He could assure them that it was nothing of the kind for the Independent Labour Party had nothing more to do with its promotion than any of the societies affiliated with the Labour Representation Committee. It was not for them to say anything about the present position of affairs in regard to nominations, but they were pre- pared to fight on the straight labour ticket. They were entirely independent of the Liberal and Conservative parties and the Non-Trading Association. (Applause.) Mr. JAMES BALL. elective auditor, delivered an address on Labour politics, tie mentioned that at the annual meeting in connection with the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company, one of the directors stated that the firm was handicapped by the conditions of labour and employment which had been gradually gained for the workingmen by the action of trade unions in times gone by. He stated that nearly forty per cent. of the increased cost of pro- duction 'of iron was due to the minimum or living wage question which had been pressed forward by trade union officials for the past ten or twenty years. This employer, along with others, resented the success which had attended the policy of trade unionists,and he (Mr. Ball) thought the candidature of Mr. Wright gave workingmen an opportunity of showing their adherence to that policy which had obtained for them the minimum wage. (Applause). Mr. WRIGHT then addressed the meeting and advo- cated the Trade Union rate of wages and conditions of labour, direct employment of labour by all corporate bodies, and the establishment of a municipal works department, provision of artizan dwellings by the municipality, establishment of public institutions for .recreative purposes,lextension of municipal enterprise, free primary and secondary education, full and fair assessment of all property, the acquisition of power by municipal authorities to tax land values. He would do his utmost to further these objects if returned to the Council. He spoke of the need for housing reform in Warrington, and strongly advocated the taxation of land values. He also believed that when municipalities had obtained land they should not part with it, as the price would be considerably enhanced when they wanted to re-purchase. In Glasgow the Corporation sold some land for £BOO, and ultimately re-purchased it for no less a sum than £175,000. Mr. W. Edwardson and Mr. .T. Podmore, jun. (presi- dent of the Trades Council) also spoke. The latter remarked that Mr. Wright was a straightforward and honest man, and he was afraid that was more than could be said of some members of the Town Council. Coun- cillor Stott was doing more than one man's work on the Council, and he had been warned to take greater care of himself. It was therefore necessary that there should be other labour representatives to back him uP. He (Mr. Podmore) would like to see a majority of labour representatives on the Council. They had nothing to gain by the work they did, and had no axes to grind. They were simply workingmen, striving for the good of their fellows.

div.head: NOVEMBER ELECTIONS.
div.p: THE NOVEMBER ELECTIONS.

During the week several additional ward meetings have been held, but interest in the forthcoming con- tests has been somewhat dwarfed by the turn of events in Bewsey Ward. The only new feature to report is that Mr. William Furness has been invited by the Liberals to contest St. John's Ward. Councillor Brough has, we understand, expressed his intention of again standing for Whitecross Ward.

div.head: ST. JOHN'S WARD.
div.p: ST. JOHN'S WARD.

An enthusiastic— meeting of the St. John's Ward Liberal Committee was held in Brick-street Mission on Monday evening, Mr. William Furness chairman of the Committee presiding. The chief business of the meeting was to select a candidate for the forthcoming Municipal Election, and on the proposition of Mr. E. E. Dean seconded by Mr. G. Bailey it was unanimously decided to invite Mr. W. Furness to contest the Ward, and on the question being put to him, he thanked them for their kindness in giving him the privilege of accepting their invitation, which he promised to definitely decide in the course of a few days. A vote of thanks was passed to the Chairman for presiding, and the meeting was adjourned until Monday next, when the committee sincerely hope that Mr. Furness, (who has previously served three years in the Council) will favourably con- sider his dicision. ORFORD WARD. _ _

At a meeting of the Conservative Ward Committee on Thursday evening, it was decided to leave the selec- tion of a candidate in the hands of the chairman and secretary of the Conservative Association if it was deemed adinsable to contest the Ward. HOWLEY WARD.
A meeting of the Conservative Committee was held on Thursday evening under the presidency of Mr. John Fairclough, and Councillor Davies, the present repre- sentative was selected as the candidate.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football. (By " Ovalist.")
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football. (By " Ovalist.")

What a slump in" Warringtons " there was on Saturday night. Not many people expected such a tale of disaster as was outlined in the telegram : "Leeds, eleven points ; Warrington, three points," after the way the same fifteen had polished off Bradford at War- rington the Saturday before. It was generally thought that Warrington would come very near to beating the Leeds men on their own ground, but the fact has got to be realised, that very few teams in the Northern League will, this season, secure many points away from home. The standard of proficiency is so level throughout the League that, with the exception of one or two engagements, not even the top clubs in the Competi- tion can rely on winning away from their own particu- lar piece of turf. Since the opehing day of the season when six home clubs went down, there has been a general levelling up and not a single team has escaped defeat throughout the League. It seems a certainty that the fight for the championship will not only be keen,but prolonged to the bitter end.

The Warrington sfiectators were afforded an opportunity on Saturday of travelling by a cheap excursion to Leeds. The London and North- Western Railway Company granted special facilities and a fair number of enthusiasts availed thensselves of the reduced fares. Alas, however, for their faith in railway companies, and particularly the mighty London and North-West. What appeared a cheap trip eventually proved fu N the majority an expensive and bitterly disappointing one. I am one of those who have a bone to pick with the railway company, and for the benefit of my readers and the chastisement of the offending company, I propose to pick it here.

Some fifty or more of us botrdel the 12.18 train at Bank Quay under the impression that we should arrive in Leeds at 3.13 according to the published bills. This would just give us time to get up to Headingley for the match and like the old ladies who go to the Isle of Man, we prayed fervently for a safe and speedy passage. Vain were the prayers and likewise the subsequent anathema 3. The start from Bank Quay was delayed about ten minutes, which, deducted from the narrow margin at the other end caused some early anxiety. Once on the way, our spirits rose, conversation in the compartment I occu- pied becoming so general that at the first stop we nearly alighted ;under the impression that Manchester was relchecl. Only Newton! How we must have crawled! Alter that, close and anxious eyes were kept on the scenery. But it would not fly past in the way the novelist realistically pictures. We seemed to. be moving across the landscape at about the speed of an omnibus and I am sure that no self respecting tramcar would like to have been seen loitering on the way so disgracefully. Eventually we arrived at Kenyon Junction something like half an hour late, only to be further delayed by ticket- collectors who ambled gently from carriage to carriage and endeavoured to crack jokes with the surly occu- pants. To hurry the train off was about the last thing they thought of, and if language fails me here to describle the official laziness at this station it did not fail my fellow-travellers. Their eloquence was impressive, and I raise my hat in acknowledgment of the way they rose to the needs of the occasion.

That train reached Manchester nevertheless. It was forty minutes late, and had lost thirty minutes between Warrington and Manchester, but it got there, which was more than appeared probable at one time. Of course, the Leeds train had gone, and we were practically stranded. There was another at 2 o'clock, which gave hopes of our seeing some football, and for this we waited. At 2 o'clock came the crowning insult. The officials refused to take the excursionists on thir particular train. Red tape and regulations barred the way. A few of us rode roughshod over the official objections, but many turned miserably away. To those defrauded and hapless wights the Railway Company owes 3s. at least.

As for ourselves we landed at Leeds without further delay on the part of the Railway Company, but we boarded a tra,mcar which seemed to have it special and diabolic mission to stop at every standard and loop. The driver was a leather-faced individual who could hardly have been stimulated to activity if the whole of the motive current had been passed through him, but like the London and North Western train he got there !

We belated excursionists had hirdly , reached the confines of the enclosure before we were startled by an oninoas—to us—roar of cheering which was re- newed a few seconds later. The signs spelt a goal and a try unmistakably and as they could hardly be for Warrington, the amiability of the party was not increased. Our fears proved only too well founded for on entering the arena we learned that Warrington were no less than 8 points in arrears. The scene of battle was soon stretched before our eyes, and War- rington certainly appeared in dire straits. They were even then struggling desperately hard to clear the line, and but for a miraculous pick-up by Hallam from the feet of the Leeds forwards another five points must have been recorded. It was apparent at once that the forwards were being completely overplayed, and that the strong breeze and sunshine were factors in the comparative helplessness of the backs. Half- time soon arrived with Leeds leading by 8 points to nil.

There was just a hope that with the elements in their favour Warrington might put a bettor com- plexion on the game. They restarted strenuously and worked their way to the Leeds quarter, only to be twice repulsed through penalties against the half- backs. Good opportunities were thus wasted, but Warrington pluckily kept at it and at last success rewarded their efforts. Brooks made a strong dash for the line,only to be tackled by the legs. Before he was down however, the eveNready Thomas snatched the ball from his grasp and shouldered his way over the Leeds line in fine style. Fish failed at a some- what easy place kick, and Leeds rushed to the other
CRAWFORD'S
OVAL RICH TEA
BISCUITS.
(In in). Packets Etc.)
THE "CRAWFORD QUALITY.
end. Hallam was safe, but the ball coining out quickly on the Leeds side, the backs got going smartly and Hvans shot past Fish to score at the corner.

' This settled Warrington's chances, though they had a big share of the game. Fish was most foully tackled when following his own kick and had to be carried from the field senseless. The touch-judge drew the referee's attention to the affair but he con- tented himself with a penalty where the ball dropped. I should have thought an old threequarter like M'Cutcheon would have acted more drastically in the interests of good football. T. Llewellyn at least deserved sending off. Even the Leeds spectators con- demned the unfairness of the incident to the War- rington crack. Though shorthanded Warrington should have scored again, as Dickenson dropped an inside pass from Isherwood with only 5 yards to go. Leeds, however, won a handsome victory by. 11 points to 2 points. They defeated Warrington fairly and squarely—and in fact were just as much superior on the day's play as Warrington were the week before against Bradford. Not many teams will take points away from Headingley this season.

Behind beaten forwards Brooks and Davies could not be expected to shine. The pressure put on them revealed a want of experience and steadiness, and both would do well to have a few weeks in the "A " team before facing the music again in first-class com- pany. Hallam and Fish were the best of the War- rington backs, and both got a severe mauling at times. The forwards collapsed badly and Leeds were able to wheel and push them just as they pleased. This will not do. More backbone, Warrington !

To-day's encounter,with all due respect to theLinnets' should be a safe thing for Warrington. Preston and Di Davies afe back again, and if the available fifteen cannot account for Runcorn at Wilderspool I shall be surprised. The forwards ought to have a big pull, but there must be no slacking. Runcorn were never a side to despise, and they are just now flushed with the success against Salford.

Warrington will almost be at full strength, H. Harris being the only absentee. He, too, is getting sound again, and may be expected in the team to visit Oldham next week. The vacancy has been given to Short, who has also been on the injured list. He should do well with opportunity. The full fifteen is : Hallam, full back; Fish, Isherwood, Dickenson, and Short, threequarters ; Di Davies and flockenhall,half- backs ; Boardman, Preston, Thomas, Shugars, Belton, Cook, Naylor and Jolldy, ferwards.

div.head: Hockey.
div.p: Hockey.

The Heathens opened the season in fine style, both Ist and 2nd teams gaining on easy victory, but it must be admitted, that they had not much to beat. Although Bankfleld cut up so badly and were beaten by 11 to 1, yet they showed signs of making a fair team, after they get settled down.

The Heathen forwards played a grand game, the inside mon shooting and passing with great judgment, and with the two outside men banging the ball across the circle, instead of trying to do too much, the defending backs were kept very busy.

At the same time we should like to see the outside men use their inside partner more in beating a defend- ing half-back. For example B is threatened by the half- back A, then passes to his partner at 82, who plays the ball to 83. A having to follow the pass, Bis again able to obtain possession of the ball.
About the backs too much must not be said. Suffice to say, had they been playing against a good set of forwards, well. the Heathens might not have beon so joyful after the match.

The second team, playing at home, easily beat Bank- field second, the score being 8-4. Had Eric Fairclough been backing up the forwardsoand not been required by the first team, we fancy Bankfleld would not have got off so easily.

As in the first team match the forwards seem to have been the chief instruments of victory, Longdin and Skelton having quite a bag of goals, although the last- named might improve his game by using two hands.
This afternoon Huyton will be played, the First play- ing away by arrangement. This match is looked upon by both teams to be the match of the season.

The second team, although P. B. Hawtin is suffering from cold and will not turn out, ought to win; but the first team match is a very level thing, and a great deal depends upon H. Kirkconnel being able to turn out in place of B. Pierpoint who is also suffering from a cold.

div.head: Angling.
div.p: Angling.

The annual contest promoted by the District Protec- tion Society in aid of the Nursing Association was fished in the waters of the Bridgewater Canal at London Bridge, Stockton Heath on Saturday afternoon last. Though a good number of entriss had been received yet the number fell short of those who supported the con- test last year, and some of the local clubs, too, might have encouraged the contest more than they did in the way of helping to provide prize money. The amount raised last year was £26 135., but the amount this year to be handed over to the Nursing Association will only be about £l7.

However, there were 336 anglers who actually com- peted, and the drawing of the numbers was proceeded with in good time. The match had not long been in progress, before it was seen that small catches were likely to prevail and such proved to be the case. Result Ist, Sfr. 'Joseph Podmore sen., 9oz. Bdrs.; 2nd, T.

Buckley sun, Boz. 4drs.,• 3rd, Jos. Griffiths,7oz. 12 dm ; 4th, R. Naylor; sth, J. Nicholson; 6th, M. Evans; 7th, H. Martin; Bth, T. Nixon; 9th, B. Bradbury; 10th, P. Hoole• 11th, A. Maddock; 12th, W. Fish; 13th, J. SpeakLan; 14th, J. Tarrant; 15th, W. Wilson; 16th, C. Unsworth; and 17th, F. Dutton. The lowest recorded weight to win a prize was 3oz. sdrs., and 43 competitors weighed 81bs. 6ozs. sdrs. The total value of the prizes was a Bs. 6d. A very efficient committee drawn from clubs affiliated with the District Protection Society had conducted the arrangements, and the Chairman was Mr. P. Knight and the secretary Mr. S. R. Lodge.

The membera of the King Edward VII. Angling Association visited Vale Royal on the 2nd inst. to fish a contest and Messrs. A. Boscow, J. Mortimer, M. Chorley, J. Shepherd and Sam Foulkes,made all arrange- mants. There were 21 competitors. Result,- Ist. J. Mather, 11b. 50z. 11.drs. ; 2nd. T. Armitage, 11b. 3oz. 7drs. ; 3rd. G. Smith, 11b. 3ozs. 4drs. ; 4th. H. Owen, Senior, sth. C. Mather, 6th. J. Lawton, 7th, M. Charley, Bth, W. Shaw, 9th, J. Hampson,loth, S. Foulkes, 11th, J. Andrews, and 12th, J. Mortimer. The prizes were dis- tributed on Monday evening last at the head quarters of the club, the Ring o' Bells Inn, Wilderspool Causeway.

The Broadheath and District Angling Society fished a contest at Agden Bridge on Saturday last. Twenty- six members competed hnd the contest was rather novel in that no "ground-baiting" was allowed and only sizeable fish could be weighed. The match proved very interesting and enjoyable and though not a great quantity of fish were caught yet only two of the con- testants were unsuccessful in their catches. The catches were weighed at the club house, the Cheshire Cheese Inn, Broadheath and the result announced as follows in the order named. Messrs. Crossley,Mitchell, Crowther, Bradley, Harrison, Watson,Acton,Burslem, E. Piercy, J. Manby, R. Smith,Yeasley,Cassidy,Bebbington Tetlow, Parker, &c.

Items.—Anglers were not so numerous last week-end and the fishing results generally were only of a moder- ate character. The Bridgewater Canal was productive of little sport and the opinion is going round in some quarters that if anglers would only persevere with such baits as paste or potato, or perhaps even creed wheat some of the big roach would be accounted for. In the opinion of more than one very old angler "the fish are getting sick of maggots." The river Weaver yielded fair sport, but fish were on the small side, The War- rington Anglers' Association are about to lose one, if not the best, of their waters, the Old River at Lymm, it being required by the Ship Canal Company who pur- pose filling it up. The Past and Present Officers' Match in connection with the Association should be fished at Agden Bridge to-day. It is satisfactory to note that some fair catches:have been recorded just lately from the Old Quay Canal. The Committee of the Warrington Anglers' Association have decided that the weighing in of specimen fish from the Old River at Lymm be sus- pended from the present date, and permission be given to members to catch the fish by means of either rod and line, trimmers, or side lines. Two chub, respectively weighing 21b. 2oz. 13drs. and 11b. lloz. 10drs., have been registered in the catch book of the Latchford A.S. by Mr. Tom Starkey. A smaller design of medal than that presented with the Shield of the Warrington A.A. last year is to be provided this year for the winners, Victoria A.S. •

In connection with the Broadheath and District Angling Society, which is affiliated with the Warring- ton Anglers' Association, an open contest is announced in the Bridgewater Canal at Broadheath on Saturday October 15th. The entrance fee is is., but non-licence holders pay a bank fee of 3d. in addition. £5 will be given in eleven prizes, and the first prize will be £1 10s. The draw will take place below Broadheath Bridge at 2.30 p.m., and fishing will commence at 3 p.m. All fish weighed in are to be of standard size, except gudgeon and eels. The prizes will be distributed directly after the" weigh-in,", at the Cheshire Cheese Inn, Broadheath. Entries will be taken on the bank up to the time of the draw. Any further particulars may be obtained from Mr. G. E. Maltby, hon. secretary of the club.

div.head: NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS.
div.p: NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS.

Authors of letters intended for publication must in all cases send their namos and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith. Matter intended"for publication must be written on one side only of the paper and sent in, if possible, not later than Thursday.

div.head: "Republican " and his Letter.
div.p: "Republican " and his Letter.

Sir,—The Rev. Herbert Dunnico is not a lover of anonymous letter writers,but I think he will be glad to welcome this satellite in the form of" Republican " although he dares to write under the cover of a nom-de- plume. In the first place let me state that I know nothing of the workings and technicalities of the Inde- pendent Labour Party, but as an outsider I personally can see no object to be gained by debate as proposed by the Rev. Herbert Dunnico and therefore I think that Councillor Stott is perfectly justified in refus- ing to meet the reverend gentleman in a public debate Now to deal with the point of Nonconformists having received their education in church schools, I think if this member of the Baptist Church would only look around him he will find that he has made a wrong state- ment in saying otherwise. I contend that 80 per cent. of the people in Warrington in the past have been edu- cated either in Church or Roman Catholic schools. I don't think that " Republican " can prove otherwise. "Now if 'Fairplay' knows anything of the Rev Herbert Dunnico he knows that it is not his desire to cross swords with anyone Who honestly states his view on any subject." I quote from " Republican's " letter. Again I think that a mistake is made. If my friend has followed Mr. Dunnico's letters since he has been in War- rington and followed them honestly he would I think by this time have formed a different opinion, but then kis membership of the Baptist Church would debar him from holding an unbiased opinion. Mr. Duanico's motto in letter writing is "If you can't beat your opponent in argument then bully him." To prove this I have only to refer " Republican " to letters written by the Rev, gentleman in the " Examiner " the other week in reply to Mr. Bell and Miss Pemberton. Let it be understood that this is not said with any ill-feeling or animosity but simply to explain to my friend his mistake. '

How is it that Mr. Carleton has not crossed swords with Mr. Minnie° ? The answer to that query is very simple. It is because Mr. Dunnico has never published any contradictory letters in reply to Mr. Carleton's letters on the Education Question. I might as well ask how it is that Lord Rosebery or "Billy Jones" have not replied to my letters &c., on the fiscal question? I am afraid that" Republican "has not read the Educa- tion Act or he would not refer to the conscience clause as" Bosh." When I read his reference to this clause I formedthe opinion thathe could not be a fully educated passive resister or he would like unto the rest of this body have kept himself clear of that question.

As to "Republican's" mention of Mr. Stott and Mr. Dunnico in the last part of his letter I will say nothing for Ido not hold a brief for the Independent Labour party but Ido hope and trust that the teachings of the good Old Church which has done so much to educate this country of ours will never be abolished from our schools. - -
_ Apologising, Mr. Editor, for the length and disjointed- ness of my letter,—l am, Yours &c. "CHURCHMAN."
Warrington, Oct. 4th, 1904.

div.head: "Republican " and the Church Schools,
div.p: "Republican " and the Church Schools,

Sir,—From the nom de plume of your correspondent "Republican," it is plain to see that he is one of those who will be "Agin the Government." of whatever shade of politics it may be; so there is Halo use in trying to convince him. I may, however, give him my authority for stating that four-fifths of the congregation of the Baptist Chapel were educated in church schools. About a quarter of a century ago there were only two schools in Warrington that were not church schools— the People's College and Wycliffe, and they are not old schools, so that according to the law of average I cannot be far wrong in supposing that nearly all the older members have been educated in church schools. I know whole families who were educated at Heathside schools. Since then the Wesleyans have done nobly,led by such gentlemen as the late Alderman Shaw Green and others, 1 and by their efforts a great strain has been taken off the church schools. What have Baptists done?

From the" Guardian "almanack of 1902,1 find that at that date there were 16 schools in Warrington under Church of England management (some of them, such as St. Paul's may be counted as three—Rolleston-street girls, Kendrick-street infants, and Heathside boys ) ; Roman Catholic,and 4 Nonconformists. I do not count People's College, as it comprises all shades of belief. After breakfast in the place where I work, the conver- sation turned on the Education Bill. There were fifteen present. I asked each where he was educated. Thirteen said they attended Church schools, one began in a Church school and finished at People's College, and the other attended People's College. I think my estimate of four-fifths far too low. It seems to me that the so- called Free Churches among their hundred and one sec- tions, have only one feeling in common; and that is hatred of the Church of England, which is the only free church. We at every service pray" for all who profess and call themselves Christians.'' and they poison the minds of their hearers against a Church that tries hard to lead the people to morality, and to love Christ. I have been astonished in talking to Dissenters at their ignorance of Church history. One fallacy is, that they help to pay for the upkeep of our Church. I thought everyone knew that the property of the Church is theirs. Like Government bond holders,they receive the interest from the property left by pious Churchmen I do not say the church is perfect, there are many ,things we would like changed, but it contrasts favour-, ably with such awful scenes as were witnessed nea

!Wellington, Salop, where in a Primitive chapel, there was a fight for the pulpit. Oh! the pity of it, that religion should be so prostituted. Can we wonder at the spread of Agnosticism among our young people? Again we have the 11. F. Kirk, and the Wee Free in Scotland, holding a meeting to try and come to amutual agreement on a bill to be presented to Parliament for a settlement of their dispute. Oh! the irony of it. This and patronage were the very questions which Dr. Chambers in 1843 raised, and which led to the formation of the Free Kirk. Then look at my own part of the empire Wales. Here we have a people who have been educated for ages by the church. No sooner are they asked to help in the good work of educating their children, then Jo they find an elastic conscience. But we have con- science also and depend on it, we will never give up our rights to have the Bible, and the tenets of our faith,and love of our grand old church brought beforo our chil- dren. My own opinion is that if you banish the grand old Book and religious instruction from our schools, in one decade our churches and chapels will be empty. Think it over you Baptists , and do not be led by egotistical demagogues who are continually figuring as passive resisters, anti-vaccinationists, and anti-vivisec- tionists "Oh for the rarity of Christian charity under the sun." Yours etc.—
FAIRPLAY.

Sir,—l think I express the feelings of the body of your readers when I say that the literary style, fair and Impartial criticism of your occasional contributor, Mr. Edmund Osborne, on local and national events, is read with relish,appreciation, and admiration,lirrespective of the difference of opinion on the points raised. Although. differing politically,l am prepared to give credit to him for honesty and sincerity of purpose, and am anxious to prevent religious controversy from degenerating into a noisy harangue or Billingsgate vocabulary. Haying the above in mind, I confess I was rather surprised to find Mr.o4bome entering the controversial arena to defend and plead the injured innocency of a rev, gentleman who for inconsistency could not be equalled outside High- bury—a gentleman who attacked with vitriolic bitter- ness an organization of workmen who, from personal acquaintance and observation, I can faithfully attest, conscientiously believe the principles they hold so dear. I can give instances, if necessary where these MEM uncultured and untutored it may be, have sacrificed position, money, leisure and comfort on behalf of their socialism and trade unionism, and still they are sneered at by scholarly gentlemen as "little boys with tin cans." Ah well; this must be considered an unconscious tribute of honour to the exertions of the Independent Labour Party, when one thinks that the inception of all movements that had for their object the amelioration of suffering humanity, even Christianity, had their "tub orators "'sad " little boys with tin cans." I have just taken a glance over letters that appeared recently in the local press from five different correspondents who ventured to criticise the correctness of statements or utterances of Mr. Osborne's rev. friend. Permit me to give a few select phrases from Mr. Dennico's replies: —"A youth in his teens," "one who found variety stars and music hall ditties more palatable to his refined temperament than sermons," "I pity the smallness of his mind," "vulgar professional tub orators," "each fact a lie and a half," "not including extra cadges," "mount the tub," "Bridge Foot brigade,' "shut up shop," &c. I earnestly ask Mr. Osborne as an haziest opponent and a lover of public discussion being conducted decently and gentlemanly, if he is prepared to defend such effusions as the above, penned in deliberation and calmness by an educated refined follower, nay a shepherd of Him who said "He that would be the greatest among you let him be the least, the servant of all."—Yours etc., 5, St. Austin's-lane.
C. LEE.

Rev, H. Dunnico and the Labour Party. Sir,—Perhaps it is not a wise thing to interfere in this correspondence. Ido so only to point out the differ- ence in Mr. Dunnico's attitude now and his attitude a month or two ago with regard to the Labour Party. At the present time, so we are informed by the rev. gentleman, the Labour Party has no bottom to it, and that it is a narrow and exclusive party. This may be so of course, but it is open to doubt, and in fact in so far as the charge of narrowness is concerned, that same charge might with some justice be laid to Mr. Dunnico and one or two other gentlemen connected with him. It might however be interesting in the light of the "edifying "correspondence of the last two or three weeks to refer back to one or two statements made by the Rev. H. Dunnico at a meeting of the Liberals held to ask Mr. A. H. Crosfield to represent them_. At that meeting to judge from the tone of the rem/01Es made by him, Mr. Dunnico evidently did not think very badly of theLabour party and considered them a dangerous element if no compromise with them was arranged. He also admittei that there were some good broadminded sensible men within the folds of the Labour party, and went so far as to protest against someone at the meet- ing calling the Labour part,y anarrow one.(See copy re- port below). Whether this is consistent or not, with the recent utterances of the rev. gentleman I leave your readers to judge for themselves. For my own part I can come to no other con- clusion than that the Rev. H. Dunnico is annoyed— annoyed by the "tin cans and penny trumpets "—and angry with the Labour Men personally, and because of this he tries a few cheap sneers at the Party which so lately as June he to some extent supported and upheld. T enclose a copy of the report of the meeting referred. to so that your readers may see what was actually said. The report is taken from the issue of this paper of the 11th June, a reference to which will give the proceed- ings of the whole meeting. The greater part of the report below refers to the Labour Representation Com- mittee, but it can easily be seen that Mr. Dunnico's attitude towards all branches of labour, including the Independent Labour Party is one of sympathy and agreement except where the question of the candidate i for Warrington s concerned. And I would ask your readers to specially note the reference to the question of finance and what the Labour Representation Com- mittee are prepared and able to do. [CoPY.I REV. H DUNNICO ON THE SITUATION. The Rev. H. Dunnico said they must face facts. If the meeting thought financial considerations; would prevent the Labour candidate coming for- ward they were much mistaken. The National Labour Representation Committee would pay two- thirds of the election expenses, and give the candi- date a salary of £l5O a year if he got into Parlia- ment. On financial grounds, therefore, the Liberals must not run away with the idea that the Labour party could not run a candidate. He did not think it was impossible to come to a compromise. but that should be done before they adopted Mr. Cros- field as their candidate. Councillor Tinnion: No No. The Rev. H. Dunnico saidhe had had considerable discussion with the labour men. There were on the Labour Representation Committee men who took a broad view of things, and if they could win overa majority of the Labour Representation Committee, they would have no need to trouble. If Mr. Cros- field was adopted by the two parties combined, he believed they would be successful in returning the Liberal candidate. The Labour candidate had no chance if Mr. Crosfield put up, and Mr. Crosfield had no chance if a Labour candidate was put up. Of the two he thought Mr. Crosfield would poll most votes. If he failed in his endeavour to bring about a compromise, then he should support the candidate who was likely to poll the most votes. An effort must be made to bring about a compromise. If not they would be in a very awkward position and he would not promise what he would do. Why not go in for a compromise of this sort! Let them run Mr. Crosfield this time and if he failed to ' get into Parliament they would give the Labour party the opportunity of contesting the seat at the next election. He would suggest that they should come to a compromise of that sort. (Hear hear.) Mr. Cormdine said he was of opinion that the I other side were as much afraid as the Liberals were

The Labour party were too narrow, and in the best interests of Liberalism— The Rev. Dunnico : I protest against that." What has our friend to say to this? Did Mr. Dunnico consider himself virtually a member of the Labour party and that on this account the Labour party was not narrow, but has since become so through him securing connection with it and opposing the Labour men. The rev, gentleman is evidently in danger of deification. I trust the gods will not be jealous.—Yours &c., L.W.E.

A suspicious fire was late on Thursday night dis- covered in the hold of the American cruiser,Washington now building at Camden, New Jersey, when a heap of sawdust was found ablaze, but it was quickly extin- guished. The outbreak is a mystery. The annual report of the Metropolitan Commissioner of Police shows that the number of arrests for all offences in 1903 was 124,554, an increase of 12,349 as compared with 1902. One hundred and fifty- fourpersons were killed in street accidents during the year. Seven shopkeepers were yesterday summoned to the Manchester Police Court for selling bread otherwise than by weight,and fines ranging from half a guinea to a guinea were imposed. In each instance the bread was found to be short in weight. Mr. J. W. Robinson, chief in- spector of weights and measures. prosecuted. At Preston, yesterday. Tom Talbot, Leyland Scans- brick, ex-Mayor of Southport, was fined £5 and costs for driving a motor car at a speed dangerous to the public. On Sunday, September 25th. when the arrival of Buffalo Bill's show attracted large numbers of onlookers,defendant drove a motor at between 18 and 20 miles an hour. When told by Constable Whitby that this speed was dangerous to the public, defendant said he would report him for his insolence. It was stated that, it was a miracle that no accident occurred.

div.head: STRANGE DISCLOSURES AT AN INQUEST.
div.p: STRANGE DISCLOSURES AT AN INQUEST.
Runcorn Drowning Casa.

At an inquest at Runcorn on Tuesday, on a woman named Holland, who was drowned in the Bridgewater Canal on Saturday night, Thomas White, a boatman, from Worsley, clamed that the deceased was his wife. The Coroner (Mr. R. Dobson): .But she was known as Holland. White: Well, you see her husband worked on the same job, and when she earns to me the master said he must not insult her nor me,tor he would not let him have a job. The Coroner: Then she is not your wife at all? White: No, but we had to get married or else the master would not let us stop in the job. The Coroner!: Do you mean to say you married her? White: Yes sir lawfully.
The Coroner: Where ?- White : At Manchester.

The Coroner: At a church? White: Yes sir. She was married in the name of Margaret Ann Holland. The Coroner: What is her real husband's name? White: Thomas Holland. He lives somewhere in Manchester, but he is generally on the lighter 21 of the Bridgewater Collieries, Worsley. The Coroner: How long had the woman lived with you? White: Seven years. Witness stated that atlo p.m. on Saturday she went for threepenny worth of whisky for him. He did not want her to go, but she would have her own "road." In ten minutes he heard a splash and a scream. He was lame with rheumatism, but he went as quickly as he could with a boathook, and gave it to a man. Then a boatman came up, but the man re- fused to give up the boathook. He believed the boat- man would have recovered the body quicker. There were no lights, and the place was very dangerous. His wife to get to the boat had to walk up a narrow plank to a narrow boat and then lialk along the bank again. It was very dark. Detective Mottershead described the place where the boat was moored as the most dangerous on the canal. The Coroner said whoever the wharf belonged to, whether the Ship Canal Company or anyone else, if boats were allowed to be moored there, there should be lights. If there were no lights, boats should not be moored there. A verdict of •` Accidentally drowned" was returned. VI-COCOA MAKES MEN CHEERFUL.

div.head: WARRINGTON ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.
div.p: WARRINGTON ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.

A meeting of this committee was held in the Board room at the Workhouse yesterday. Mr. J. Billinge pre- sided and there were also present: Dr. Patterson, Messrs. A. Brooks, S. Davies, G. Mather, T. H. Ash- croft, W. Houghton, R. Forshaw, and J. C. Sutton (clerk). Mr. Owen (valuer) was unable to be- present owing to a slight indisposition. A VICAR'S APPEAL.

The Rev. J. D'a.-viEs, vicar of St. Anne's, appealed against the assessment of the new vicarage, Orford Avenue, which had been fixed at £4O gross, £34 rate- able. His objection, he said, was based on the ground that the vicarage was an official residence. It had cost a lot of money but it had to be built according to the specification. of the Ecclesiastical Commis- sioners who contributed more than half the expenses. As the Vicar of the parish he was bound to occupy the Vicarage. He was responsible for all dilapidations, and those were to be decided by the diocesan surveyor. The surveyor made his report and what he said he (the Vicar) had to perform, and could not appeal against the surveyor's award. Furthermore he (the Vicar) was responsible as tenant for the decora- tion, upkeep and ordinary wear and tear of the Vicar- age. It had also been decided that he was responsible Ifor the insurance of the Vicarage and tha diocesan Isurveyor's charges. The house, as it was, would be un- lettable in the neighbourhood in which it was placed to any other tenant. It was situated in a growing neigh- bourhood, where much smaller property was being erected.—The committee considered the matter in private and decided to make no alteration.—ln com- municating the decision to the Vicar, the Chairman said the committee were of opinion that if any change were made, the assessment ought to be increased.—The Vicar said he might mention that St. Peter's was put down at £3O and St. Barnabas' at £3s.—The Chairman: Prob- ably those are not sufficiently assessed. ICHE VALUER'S REPORT. Mr. OWEN (valuer) reported that since the last meet- ing he had made the following valuations and inspec- tions :—ln the township of Warrington, Smith and Son, Dallam-lane, gross £750. Rateable £6OO. The works had been practically closed for manufacturing since Ist August. The stock is being sold off as quickly as possible and it was thought the middle of October would see all sold. A portion of the premises consisting of the annealing room, and one small wire mill, had been now let off to Messrs Smith and Co., of Penistone, at a tem- porary monthly rental which amounted to £240 par annum. The portion of premises included in this lot, with the engine and boiler in connection, he had examined and was satisfied with the proportion of rent. If the present assessment was struck out, an assessment would be required of gross £240, rateable £192 on Messrs. Smithand Co. Another assessment would be re- quired on Messrs. Smith and Son for the use of the remainder of the premises as a warehouse. He suggests a fair figure for this would be gross £loo.,rateable £BO., but that whilst the premises were being used for the sale of stock the assessment should be gross £l5O, rate- able £l2O. . Joseph Dolan, Napier street, new 'works, gross £162, rateable £l3O. King's Head Inn, Winwick Street, dew inn, gross £l4O, rate- able £ll9. Red Lion Inn, Winwick road, : new inn, gross £llO, rateable £93 Ms. F. R. Pierpoint, new warehouse, Friar's Gate, temporary ' assessment, not yet completed, gross £2O, rateable £l7. In the township of Newton L. & N.W. Ry. Co. Earles- -1 town Station, additions, gross £124 10s., rateable, £lO6, after crediting removals. In the township of Haydock, St. Helens Tramways. The tramways having been settled in the adjoining union, it has been decided to , reduce these in the township of Haydock in proportion, ' and to repay the amount of over payment made to the 31st March, 1904.
