div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

DISGRACEFUL SUNDAY AFTER'SOOI4 SCEN'E. At the Warrington Police Court yesterday John and James Molloy, 201, Winwick-roitd, were summoned for _assaulting William T. Bate, 105, Winwick-road, on Sunday afternoon. Mary Molloy, mother of the other defendants, was charged with assaulting Madeline Bate, wife of the first complainant..—Mr. T. S. Steel appeared for the complainants and stid-the case was a sequel to a very disgusting scene which was enacted in Winwick- road on Sunday afternoon. There appeared to have been some ill-feeling between the parties, and as Mr. Bate's son was leaving the house Mrs. Molloy made use of abusive language towards him. He re- -seated this, and defendant made a rush at him. She called out her two sons and they commenced to thrash Bate. Mrs. Bate heard the disturbance and came to the pi otection of her stepson. Mrs. Molloy struck her a blow which caused her to fall in the gutter, and theh seized her by the hair and banged her head on the kerbstone. Mr. Bate then came upon the scene and was savagely assaulted by the male defendants. Had it not been for the interference of some passers-by the case might have been much more serious. Mrs. Bate lay uncon- -scions in the gutter, but eventually she was carried into the house and Dr. Adams attended her. She was suffer- ing from shock and severe contusions on the head and chest.—The defendant gave an entirely different version ot the affair. James denying that he struck a blow and the others alleging that they only acted in self-defence. —The case against James Molloy was dismissed, and he other defendants were each fined 10s. and costs.

div.head: Warrington Borough Police Court.
div.p: Warrington Borough Police Court.
Minor Cases.

MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (in the chair), Aldermen Smethurst and Francomb, Councillors Tinnion, Thornton, and -Wilkinson, Messrs. T. Birchall, W. Roberts, S.Wright,and J. W. Hayward. VIOLENT CI-lA.RACTERS SMARTLY FlNED.—Joseph Barry, Parr-street, and James Brennon Brown's-yard, were charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Market-street, refusing to quit the Cattle Market Inn, and assaulting Police Constable Whitby and James Hill, a civilian who assisted the officer.—The evidence showed that the prisoners went to the Cattle Market Inn in a drunken condition and had to be ejected. They returned and P.C.VVhitby was sent for. After a struggle he got the men into the street and they were extremely violent. The officer was struck about the chest and arms and when he closed with Barry, Brennon tried to rescue his companion. Whilst he was on the ground the officer received severe kicks. James Hill came to his assistance and had -a struggle with Brennon until P.C. Howard came upon the scene and the men were taken to the Police Station. Hill was kicked on the side of the face.—James Hill gave evidence and said he never saw two more violent men.—The Chief Constable said this case was a sample of what frequently happened on Saturday nights—A fine of £5 and costs, with the alternative of two months' imprisonment, was imposed, the magistrates thanking Mr. Hill for his services. AN OLD OFFENCE.—Thornas Quinn, 25, Bank-street, who was locked up for having been drunk and disorderly was further charged with committing a breach of the peace on March sth.—He was fined 10s. and costs in each case. SUSPICIOUS CoNDUCT.—Patrick Grady, last from Prescot, was charged that, being a suspicious character he was found on enclosed premises with intent to com- mit a felony at 12.40 ii.m. on Sunday.—The Chief Con- stable, in asking for a remand in order to inquire into prisoner's antecedents, said the prisoner was seen to enter the premises of Mr. Edward Gibson, forgeman, 169, Orford-lane. Mr. Gibson was sitting in the kitchen with his wife—the front portion of the house being in darkness—when he heard the front gate creek. He went into the front room, and saw the prisoner examining the window. Grady endeavoured to open it, but as it had been newly painted he could not raise the sash. Mr. Gibson returned to the kitchen and armed himself with the poker. 'When he again went into the front room, prisoner had evidently seen that he was detected, for he was standing with his head resting on the windowsill apparently to give the impression that he was partly drunk. Sergeant Smith happened to corn, upon the scene and took the prisoner into custody. Ultimately he gave the man into the charge of Sergeant Bell and P.C. Hamblett, and prisoner began to act like a maniac, striking and kicking the officers with considerable violence. With great difficulty he was taken to the Police Station.—The magistrates-remanded prisoner for a week. WIFE ASSAULT.—Patrick Macdonald, Ship-yard, was charged with having made use of obscene language in • Bridge-street at 945 on Saturday nightand with assault- ing his wife, Mary Macdonald.—Complainant said she asked her husband for some money, and he seized her by the hair, threw her to the ground and kicked her.—P.C. Metcalfe arrested the prisoner who made use of very filthy language.—Prisoner was sentenced to a Month's hard labour. CRUELTY To A HORSE.—Frank Bachegolupi,lo2, Win- wick-road was summoned for illtreating a horse by working it whilst in an unfit state, and John Monfredi was summoned for causing it to be worked.—lnspector Gibson, R.S.P.C.A., said the animal was very lame on both hind legs. The near hock was very badly diseased and just below the hock was an old suppurting wound. Monfredi gave an undertaking that the horse should be destroyed, and the magistrates fined defendant in the costs. TuEsDAY.----Before Aldermen Sutton (in the chair) and Hntchinson, Dr. Fox, and Mr. W. Richardson. • EXPENSIVE FLOUR.—Ernest Heaps was charged with stealing Gibs. of flour, value Bd., the property of James Fairclough and Sons.—Superintendent Monaghan said the prisoner was employed at the Bank Quay Mill and left his work at midnight on Saturday. Subsequently P.C. Bennett met him at Quay Fold, and as complaints of robberies of flour had been received, he stopped the man. He noticed something bulky under his coat, and prisoner replied that it was flour. At first he said that employ 43 were allowed to take samples, but afterwards he admitted that he had done wrong. The matter was reported to the firm, and as such thefts were so numerous they decided to prosecute.—A fine of 10s. and costs (Z in all) was imposed. WEDNESDA :—Before Mr. T. Birchall (in the chair) Alderman Hutchinson, Messrs. L. W. Reynolds and F. W. Monks. THEFT OF A BLOUSE.—Jane Sincup, 34, Bostock-street, was charged with stealing a lady's black blouse, value 4s. Gd. the property of Thomas Domville, pawnbroker, 35, Priestly-street. The evidence showed that the defen- dant went into the shop to get some pawntickets endorsed. As she was leaving an assistant named Cotterill noticed that she was carrying the blouse. He informed the manager, Mr. Evans, who visited the defendant's house and found the blouse lying on the table.—A fine of 20s. was imposed. THURSDAY.—Before Messrs. John Fairclough (in the chair), W. Roberts and C. White. REFRACTORY PAUPER.—SamueI Patterson an inmate of the Workhouse, was sent to gaol fer a month for re-

div.head: BENEFITS OF SCIENCE.
div.p: THE BENEFITS OF SCIENCE.
The Examiner, Saturday, October 8, 1904

WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. MR. S. GOUGH TAKES A SEAT IN THE COUNCIL CHAMBER. The Mayor Orders Him to Retire. COUNCILLOR STOTT AND THE CaNTRACTS QUESTION. There was an unusual scene at the commencemen of the Town Council meeting on Tuesday evening. It was noticed that Mr. Samuel Gough had taken a seat amongst the members of the Town Council and was poring over a number of documents which he had brought with him. The attention of the Mayor was drawn to Mr. Gough's presence, and his worship immediately asked him to retire. Mr. Gough demurred at doing so and made an endeavour to speak, but there were cries of "chair, chair." Bowing to the inevitable, Mr. Gough left his seat, remarking that he did so under protest. The following is the passage of arms which took place between the Mayor and Mr. Gough. The MAYOR: You have no right here, Mr. Gough. Mr. GOUGH: I claim I have a right; therefore I ask leave to speak. The M.A.YOR : You must accept my ruling. Your seat as a Councillor has been declared vacant, and another election takes place this week, as you prob- ably know. Mr. GOUGH: That is the reason lam here. The MAYOR : I cannot discuss the matter. I can only order your removal. Mr. GOUGH : I submit, if you will allow me that-- The MAvon ; I cannot. Mr. GOUGH: lam here on account of this election being declared vacant. The MAYOR: You must accept my ruling. It is a legal question, and I have ruled you are not a mem- ber of the Council, and there is an end of the matter. Mr. GOUGH : I protest. Tho MAvort : You must leave tile room at once. I shall not argue with you. You have ceased to be a member of the Council. Mr. GOUGH: If I dO" it will be under protest. The MAYOR : Very well then. You can go to the other seats if you like, but you must not take a seat in the Council. Mr. GOUGH: That is your ruling? The MAYOR Yes. Mr. GOUGH : Then 1 will leave. Mr. Gough then took a seat among the public at the far end of the CounCil Chamber. The following members of the Council were present: —The Mayor (Alderman Bolton), Aldermen A. Bennett, John Evans, T. Hutchinson, W. Pierpoint, 3. Smethurst, T. H. Sutton, Councillors T. H. Ashcroft, T. Barton, W. Brough, T. Burton, S. Davies, J. Dodds, D. S. Duncan, James Evans, L. Ellison, W. J. Forshaw, T. J. Hulse, J. Lord, J. Maginn, A. Peacock, P. Peacock, J. Pemberton, J. Roberts, W. Rogers, J. Sankey, F. Stott,H. Thornton, D. Tinnion, J. Wilkinson, W. J. Wilson, with Messrs. J. L.Whittle (town clerk), J.Fairhurst(borough treasurer), T. Longdin (borough surveyor),J.Deas(water engineer), W. S. Haddock (gas engineer),F.V.L. Matthias (electri- cal engineer), J. G. Gornall (medical officer), J. M. Murray (director of education). THE REPRESENTATIVE MANAGER OF ST. PETER'S SCHOOL.

AldermanBENNETT proposed that the Council confirm such recommendations of the Education Committee that required confirmation. Councillor ELLISON seconded. Councillor DODDS moved as an amendment that the following resolution of the General Purposes Commit- tee of the Education Committee :—" That Mr. John William Kay, of 112. Manchester-road, be recommended to the Town Council for appointment as a representa- tive manager of the St. Peter's School, in place of Mr. E. J. Guest, resigned," be referred back to the commit- tee for further consideration. He remarked that Mr. Kay was a member of the Church of England, and was churchwarden of St. Peter's Church. Mr. Guest was a Wesleyan, and dissatisfaction had been caused by the appointment. There had also been a little friction in regard to the Sacred Heart School, and in the circum- stances he •thought they should maintain the under- standing with which they began their work as an edu- cation committee, that for a Church school a member of some other religious body should be put on to repre- sent the Board of Management. He, therefore, moved Ithat the resolution be referred back to the Education Committee. Councillor TONION seconded, and said he thought it was a wise principle that was established that as far as they could, the management of a school at any rate should not be in the hands of the particular body to which it belonged. It was thought that while it might not be necessary it was desirable at any rate that some member of another church should be a member of the committee so that the whole of the managers sbouldnot be of one faith. The understanding come to at the commencement seemed to have worked very well, and he saw no reason for departing from it on that occasion Alderman BrarNerr said that, with the sanction of the Council, he was willing to withdraw the resolutionafter the opinions which had been expressed by Councillors Dodds and Tinnion. Their views were his. He thought they were right in carrying out the principles enunci- ated in Parliament when the Bill was passed. The obvious intention was that minorities should be repre- sented on the Board of Management and in this case it did not seem to have been done. Councillor Roberts rose to speak. The MAYOR: You are out of order. The resolution is withdrawn, but we will allow you a little latitude. COULIoiIIOrROBERTS said he wanted to be in order, and he knew he was often out of order. (Laughter.) It was unanimpusly decided in committee that Mr. Kay should be one of the managers of St. Peter's Schools. No objection was made at the meeting, and why the matter should crop up now he failed to understand. If it had been passed that a Churchman was not entitled to sit on the committee—(cries of " No, no ") he had nothing more to say. The MAYOR: Nothing of the sort. Councillor ROBEETS said it looked to him as if there had been something up the sleeves of the Dissenters. (Laughter.) The MAYOR: I think you misunderstand. Mr. Guest was a Wesleyan and he has retired, and it is thought by the Nonconformists that he ought to be succeeded by another of the same religious opinion. Councillor ROBERTS: There was no religious dis- cussion. The chairman asked me if I had a man to nominate andl nominatedhim, and he was unanimously carried. If that is not straightforward business I don't know what is. COllll6llol* ROGERS rose to speak. The MAYOR: You are all out of order. I allowed Councillor oberts to blow off steam. (Laughter.) That portion of the minutes objected to is withdrawn. If you want to do anything move that the matter be reinstated. Alderman PIERPOrNT contended ,that it could not be withdrawn without the consent of the Council. Alderman BENNF.TT : I said I was willing to with- draw it with the consent of the Council. Councillor ROGERS said that not a word was said about religious feelings at the committee meeting' There were gentlemen sitting round the table of all per- suasions, and when the Chairman asked for a name it was proposed by Councillor Roberts, and seconded by himself and carried unanimously, that Mr. Kay be selec- ted. If there had been any religious feeling against Mr. Kay he would have withdrawn from seconding the proposition. Alderman PIERPOINT thought Councillor Dodds ought to have nominated a Nonconformist at the committee meeting. Councillor Dorms: I wasn't present. Councillor JAMES EVANS asked if the resolution appointing Mr. C. E. Parker a member was also to be referred back. Councillor DODDS said he could assure Councillor Roberts that nobody had asked him to move in the matter. It was because he thought there should be a manager appointed of the same religious persuasion as Mr. Guest that he moved the amendment. Alderman BENNETT said Councillor Roberts was labouring under an entire misapprehension. If the whole of the managers of St. Peter's school belonged to the Church of England there would be no one to repre- sent the minority. The resolution recommending the appointment of Mr. Kay was then referred back. MR. C. E. PARKER APPOINTED ON THE EDUCATION COMMITTEE.

sth September, a letter was read from the Town Clerk of Glasgow with reference to the taxation of land values and asking for representatives to be appointed to attend a conference to be held at the Westminster
_ Palace Hotel on Friday, the 7th of October next. It was resolved, that no action be taken and that the letter
ie on the table.

Alderman BENNETT, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said he personally much regretted that they would not be represented at the conference with regard to the taxation of land values, as the state of the exist- ing law was an anomaly and unfair. He thought the Warrington Corporation ought to draw itself into line with other Corporations. _
Councillor FORSHLW seconded. Councillor STOTT asked whether the resolution meant . _ .

that the committee was not in sympathy with the pro- posal to tai c land values. The MAYOR: No, No! Thecommitteetid not wish to spend money on sending a representative. Mr. Fair- hurst will be in London on the 7th inst. and will attend this meeting. We shall therefore be represented, although not spending money on a deputation. Councillor STOTT said as their expenses increased they

must find some new source of revenue and the taxation of land values was one of them. Councillor P. PEACOCK said he should have proposed that a representative be sent if he had been present at the committee meeting. The MAYOR: The Town Clerk and the Borough Treasurer will be in London on business with the Local Government Board and•they will both attend this meet- ing. They could not have two better representatives. The minutes were adopted. WIDENING OP LIVERPOOL ROAD.

The Street Improvement and Lighting Committee met on the 15th September, when the Town Clerk sub- mitted the award of Air. William Owen 'with reference to the land required for the widening of Liverpool-road from which it appeared that the amount to be paid to 3lessrs. Joseph Crodield and Sons, Limited, was £876. The minutes were adopted, on the motion of Alder- man Sutton, seconded by Alderman Bennett. ALARMING INCREASE OF SCARLET FEVER. HOSPITAL FULL OF PATIENTS.

The Health Committee met on the 28th September, when it was resolved that a strip of land adjoining the Sanatorium, containing 700 square yards, be given to Mrs. Greenough in exchange for a strip of land con- taining 680 square yards, in order to straighten the boundary of the land and that legal costs amounting to £5 ss. and £8 Bs. surveyor's fees be paid by the Corpora- tion ; that the Chairman, Deputy Chairman. Councillors Burton and Wilkinson, together with the Town Clerk, Borough Surveyor, and Medical Officer of Health be appointed a sub-committee to consider and report upon the provision of an abattoir on land in Arpley adjoining the proposed cattle market, and that they be empowered to visit other towns to inspect the abattoirs there. Alderman SUTTON, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said he thought they were self-explanatory. He might, however, just tell them that he had received a letter from the I'Vredical Officer of Health, according to which Dr. Gornall said that the widespread attack of scarlet fever that he had anticipated in July last appeared to have taken place, as they now had 140 patients in the hospital—a record, the speaker believed —and it would be impossible to accommodate many more. The doctor added that they were doing their best in the circumstances, but the Council must not expect anything but the 'continued prevalence of scarlet fever during the rest of the year. The alderman added that the doctor told him that he had placarded the town with notifications with tespeet to the disease and hadsent hand bills throughout the borough. He was pleased to tell them that smallpox was over, at any rate for the present. Councillor EVA.NS seconded, and the minutes were carried without further discussion. CONTRACTORS' BIG MISTAKES. .

The Paving and Sewerage Committee have decided that Mr. Thomas Crompton, jun., be appointed tempor- aryassistant in the Borough Surveyor's department for a pniod of three months, at a salary of 30s. per week. Councillor TINNION moved the adoption of the report, and said they had had a good many tenders for a good deal of work, and when they had the sanction of the Local Government Board- The BORoUGH TREASURER : come. Councillor TINNION said he could understand that it had come for these particular streets, but when they got it for the other batches they would at once proceed further, and no one would have any reason to grumble. He would just like to explain two unfortunate incidents which had happened. People cox& not help making mistakes, and they would see that they had had to aocept a tender of £47 15s. 3d., by Mr. T. Stringer for paving a passage in Bridge-dtreet. Tn the first place the committee accepted a tender from Mr. Woodvine for £4l 15s. id., wh...n they afterwards received a notifi- cation from Mr. Woodvine that he had made a mistake of £lO. In the case of Porshaw and Laira Streets, they received a tender amounting to £241 9s. 6d., and the committee were pleased to have so reasonable a tender. (Laughter.) Mr. Hayes, of Seaforth, was the contractor. Since the tender was accepted, however, Mr. Hayes had informed them that he had made a mistake of £2OO. (Laughter.) A tender by Mr. Stringer amounting to £416 Bs. was accepted. He explained that the committee had bought 90 tons of cubes offered by Mr. A. Robinson at 20s. 6d., without advertising, although such a course was contrary to the Standing Orders. The committee considered that it was a bargain, as they were saving something like 3s. a ton. The setts were a job lot which had been sent to complete a cargo. With regard to the appointment of Mr. Crompton, he urged that it was very desirable that they should have a survey of the whole of the borough, as the borough had been extended, and they had no plan of the borough as extended. The Ordnance Department had offered to make a survey for them for £2,700. They had declined that as a luxury; but by the appointment, which was not intended to be permanent, of Mr. Crompton, they hoped to get the survey they wanted. Councillor JOHN ROBERTS seconded. The minutes were adopted. THE LIBRARY ASSOCIATION. MR. MADELEY'S REPORT.

Atte meeting of the Museum Committee held on the 9th September, it was resolved that a conference of persons interested in museums be held on Saturday, October 29th, that tea be provided, and that the Mayor be asked to allow the use of the Town Hall for the occasion. The Secretary of the committee (Mr. Charles Madeley) read a report on the annual meeting of the Library Association which he had attended at Newcastle- upon-Tyne. Among other things Mr. Madeley said: A report on the Bill to abolish the limit of the library rate, which was crowded out during the late session of Parliament, was presented by Councillor T. C. Abbott of Manchester, who impressed upon the association the necessity of local anthorities intimating to their Parlia- mentary representatives their desire for the removal of this, the only existing restriction on the liberty of the local authorities to manage their own affairs. Warring- ton was favourably mentioned in the report as one of the towns which, having taken steps to relieve itself of immediate restriction,has petitioned Parliament to make the concession general. Alderman BENNETT moved the adoption of the minutes They would see that Warrinzton was increasing as a centre of a.ttraction,<Lnd shortly a conference of persons interested in musenms would be held in their midst. Councillor ELLISON seconded, and the minutes were adopted.

t the Police Station and the Technical Szhool respec tively. The report was adopted on the motion of Alderman SMETHURST, seconded by Councillor DAVIES. THE SUPPLY OP WATER FOR TRADE PUKPOSES At a meeting of the Water Committee on the 22nd. September, the committee considered the question of the water supply for trade purposes, and the Engineer having reported that the water in the reservoir at Appleton was very low, and would run out in 30 days if the drought continued, it was resolved, that Mr. Deas be instructed to adopt all practical moans for con- tinuing the trade supply.—At a meeting on the 26th September the Engineer xeported the steps taken by him to continue the supply of water for trade purposes when it was resolved that he be authorized to hire an engine boiler and pump, at £l2 per month or part of a month, and to purchase the necessary 8-inch pipes from the Steepbridge Coal and Iron Company, Limited, at LI us. 6d. per ton. Alderman EviNG, in moving the adoption of the minutes, explained that the water in the reservoir at Appleton] had, dropped 16 feet 7 inches below normal. Something had to be done and as there were two or three million gallons running to waste at Winwick it was decided, but with some hesitation, to pump this into the mains. They had had the water analysed and declared to be fit for domestic purposes, and the Medi- cal Officer had also been consulted and made no objection to its use. Alderman HUTCHINSON seconded, and the report,was adopted.

THE GYMNASIUM. Councillor TINNION referred to the musical drill and gymnastic display to be held at the institution on the 21st November. He hoped the members of the Council would be in attendance. ABATING THE SMOKE NUISANCE. At a meeting of the Electricity and Tramways Com- mittee, on September 13th, the Town Clerk submitted the following letter from the Board of Trade with reference to the Corporation Light Railways Order, 1903 :—With reference to your letter of the 2.5 th ultimo, I am directed by the Board of Trade to state that under Section 33 (3) of the Order above named, they approve the plan which accompanied your former letter, dated the 10th ultimo, showing the size and design of the side poles proposed to be adopted on the Corporation Light Railways. Alderman SMETOIURST, in moving the adoption of the minutes;said he was pleased to inform the Council, and in particular his friend Alderman Bennett, that they had now put away that great smoky chimney at the Elec- tricity Works. Alderman BENNETT: Where have yoa put it? (Laughter.) Alderman SMETHURST, continuing, said he considered that the committee had accomplished something and that day he had watched the chimney for rather more than an hour and there was not a trace of black smoke. He hoped that they would never see that dense black smoke again as long as Alderman Bennett lived, at any rate. _ _

Councillor WILKINSON seconded. Alderman BENNETT: I must congratulate Alderman Smethurst.—The Mayor: What about? Alderman Bennett: About this smoke question. I have always felt— The MAYOR: It is not on the minutes and we cannot deal with the smoke question. The minutes were then confirmed. WARRINGTON BRIDGE IMPROVEMENT. THE THREATENED INJUNCTION BY MESSRS, FAIRCLOUGH.

At a meeting of the General Purposes Committee the tenders for the widening of Warrington Bridge were opened and considered whareupon it was resolved that the tender of Mr. Harry Fairclough to carry out the widening of the bridge in accordance with the plans and specifications prepared by Mr. J. J. Webster at £3,263 be accepted.—At a meeting on the 26th Sep- tember, Mr. J. J. Webster having rocommended the appointment of Mr. J. F. Jones, A.M.1.C.E., as clerk of the works during the alterations to Warrington Bridge, it was resolved that Mr. Jones be appointed at a salary ol £3 3s. a week.—A letter was read from Messrs. Alex- ander Wilson and Cowie on behalf of Messrs. James Fair- dough and Sons, Ltd., giving notice of the intention of that firm to take proceedings by injunction to prevent the alteration of Warrington Bridge by means of cantilevers and alleging that the proposed widening of the bridge would increase the risk and difficulty of navigating the river. The committee referred the matter to the Town Clerk. The MLYOR formally moved the adoption of the General Purposes Committee minutes. Alderman HUTCHINSON seconded. Alderman Strrrow asked for information as to the threatened proceedings by Messrs. James Fairclough and Sons, Limited. He wanted to know, he added, as to whether it was likely that they would carry out the threat, and whether or not it would not be better in these circumstances to put off this matter until they saw —(luterruptions of" No, no.") Councillor ROGERS : Has the report come? The Mayor: What report? The TOWN CLERK: I understand that it is the inten- tion of Messrs. Fairclough to proceed by injunction. Councillor TINN'ION : Let them " injunct." The TOWN CLERK (continuing) : But I do not think they will succeed. THE FAIR WAGES QUESTION. PENALTY CLAUSE REJECTED. INTERESTING DISCUSSION. In accordance with notice given, Councillor STOTT moved: "That this Council adopt the following Standing Order :—Any contractor having been proved by the Council to have broken the conditions of a con- tract, the Council shall not consider any tender sub- mitted by him for the carrying out of any work for a period of two years from the date of the contract hav- ing been broken." Councillor Stott stated that he had submitted a similar motion at the last meeting, but with a penalty clause of five years. A desire or opinion was expressed that five years was much too long, and he thought the feeling of the Council was such that if a period of two years had been fixed the resolution would have been carried. To meet these views the motion had been modified to two years. Councillor BARTON seconded. Alderman SMETHURST asked the members to reject the motion without fear or favour. It was, in his opinion, one of the most outrageous proposals that had yet been brought before the Council, and it simply mesh that tradesmen must be debarred if they made the slightest slip, and be. as in a court of justice, transpor- ted,and transported from the business of the Corpora- tion for two years. If any man thought that was English, then he would sooner be a Frenchman or a Dutchman. (Laughter.) The men aimed at were the respectable people of the town, the majority of whom sprang from the very ranks of those men who were now trying to cripple them ! There were scarcely one of these men who were aimed at, who had not belonged to the Trades Society. He had himself been a member of that society, and so had his relatives, and he could prove their certificates for 80 or 90 years back. To do this kind of thing against the men who were striving to get an honest living was wrong, and because they might employ some man who I did not belong to the society, they would , be debarred. Councillor STOTT: It is not a question of trade unionism. Alderman SMETHURST : It's a question of only employing men belonging to unions. Councillor STOTT: Not at all. Alderman SMETHURST said it meant that if a con- tractor did anything contrary to the standing orders he must be debarred in a manner to which he did not think there was any genfleman round that table would submit

div.head: PRECAUTIONS AGAINST _FIRE.
div.p: PRECAUTIONS AGAINST _FIRE.

The Fire Engine Committee met on the 26th Septem- ber, when it was resolved that the attention of the Watch Committee and the Education Committee be called to the want of appliances for extinguishing fires
Wood informed a Wood is a young

"Eczema broke out on my face, neck and arms, and my head was literally covered with sores." Thus Miss Elisabeth Ann "Belton. Chronicle " reporter when describing her marvellous cure through Zam-Buk after lifelong agony and disfigurement. Miss mill card tenter, and lives with her father, Mr. James Wood, at 3, Hopefield-street, Bolton. "The disease commenced in my youngest days," said Miss Wood. "It began directly after vaccination. div.head: SWIMMING GALA AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: SWIMMING GALA AT WARRINGTON.
The Local Championships.

Exponents and admirers of the natatory art assembled in strong force at the Legh-street Baths on Tuesday evening when the annual gala promoted by the War- rington Swimming Club was held. The programme embraced a series of highly interesting events, and the competitors, encouraged by the cheers of their friends, gave striking evidence of their skill and staying powers. The proceedings were presided over by Mr.H. Roberts, and among those present were Lady Greenall, Mrs. H. Roberts, Miss Roberts, Captain George Crostield, Dr. Adams, Messrs. E. Draper, Segar-Owen, Fulton Smith, Alderman Evans, T. Pemberton and J. E. Warren. The chief event of the evening was the 150 yards race for the championship of Warrington and district, the winner becoming the holder for the ensuing year of the handsome shield presented by the Licensed Victuallers' Association. Three gold medals were also offered. There were seven competitors but T. Pemberton held the lead thronghout and won a fine race by three yards. He is to be congratulated upon a splendid performance. R. Allen came in second and H. Ince was third. The contest for the 50 yards schoolboy championship for )Warrington and district excited keen interest, and as the competitors were well matched excitement ran high. Harold Partridge, of People's College, proved the winner, William Penketb, Silver-street, obtaining second place, and William Jolley,Heathside,third.By his victory Partridge becomes the holder of the Thornton Challenge Bowl for a year, besides receiving a gold medal. Penketh was awarded a gold-centred medal, and Jolley a silver medal. Other races resulted as follows : WORKS SQUADRON CHAMPIONSHIP.—I, Pearson and Knowles'; 2, Crosfield's ;3, Rylands's. It was announced that Sir Gilbert Greenall had generously given a trophy to be competed for each year by the works squadron teams. MEMBERS' HANDICAP.—Heat winners: B. Percival and F. Gardner; C. Woods and R. Field; G. Owen and J. Wainwright and F. Howard (dead heat) ; A. Ashton and P. Higham ; and W. Ashton and W. Sutton. Second round: Percival and Gardner; W. Ashton and W. Sutton. Final: 1, W. Ashton; 2, Percival; 3, Sutton; 4,Gardner Won by a foot; same. BLINDFOLD RACR.-1, A. Ashton; 2, G. Green; 3, H. Bowcock. The programme concluded with a polo match between Warrington, the champions of 'the Second Division of the Liverpool and District League, and Burslem, this year's winners of the Staffordshire Cup. Mr. A. G. Robertson, the well-known international,acted as referee and the teams were :—Warrington: C. Woods, goal; C. Ashton, and W. Ashton, backs • A. Ashton, half backs; W. Sutton, J. Peers and R. Allen. forwards. Burslem : C. Buxtoa, goal; W. H. Johnson and T. Foulkes, backs; F. Belfield, half-back; P. Ripley, (international), A. E Hill and E. A. Ball, forwards. A. Boscow, captain of the Warrington team, was unable to turn out owing to illness. The match was an exciting one, but Warring- ion were outplayed, and lost by four goals to two. C. Aston scored both goals for Warrington. During an interval the Chairman delivered a short address. He expressed on behalf of the members of the Swimming Club,as well as on his own behalf as a towns- man, their deep sense of gratitude to Sir Gilbert Greenall for the interest which he had displayed in.. that valuable institution by his promised gift of a trophy. He would also like to say how welcome was the presence of Lady Greenall,and he would ask her to kindly convey their thanks to Sir Gilbert. (Applause.) They had bad an exhibition of swimming of so satisfactory a character that he hoped it would carry the conviction to every parent of the absolute necessity that their children, both boys and girls, shou Id be taught to swim. Having alluded to the steps which had been taken to encourage the acquirement of art among the employees of Messrs.Crosfield, Mr. Roberts said the movement for the initiation of open-air baths had been revived in Warrington. (Hear, hear.) Fifteen years ago in the Council Chamber, his old friend, Mr. Jenkins, whose name was associated viiith more than one work in the town, pioneered the question. He regretted to say that theiklifficultres in the way of accomplishing their object obtained even now. Unfortunately, they had the eternal bogey of the rates to deal with. The heaviest rated towns were the most progressive towns, and he had always adv vated, and would always advocate, that if they got value for their money by seeing that it was properly spent, they need not be afraid of a little extra ' cost to the rates. Everything which conduced to the cleanliness, health and comfort of the people, and ' which improved their means of livelihood,added wealth of -a far more permanent character than could be economized by saving a few pence on the rates. These were days of high rates, and he was prepared to pay his share of them. He hoped when the question of open-air baths came up again they would not allow the financial aspect to set aside every other consideration. The health of the people was a most important thing for a governing body to consider, because with health every- thing else that was good would follow. (Applause.) Mrs. ROBERTS distributed the prizes at the close. On the motion of Mr. C. Wood, seconded by Mr. Draper, a vote of thanks was passed to Mr. and Mrs Roberts for their services. The officials were :—Judges, Messrs. John Evans, T. Locher and E. Draper; handicapper and starter. Mr. A. Barlow; checker starter, Mr. G. A. Scotson ; competi- tors' stewards, Messrs. R. T. Harding and F. Garside ; hon. secretary, Mr. C. Ashton; and hon treasurer, Mr. C. H. Wood. It may be added that Mr. Henry Roberts, J.P., has offered a trophy to be competed for at the next annual gala, for an event which is to be decided upon at a later late.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT
COUNCIL

This authority held its fortnightly meeting at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, under the presidency of Mr. S. Woodward. There were also present :—Admiral J. P. Jones-Parry, Messrs. J. Plllmg, C. E. Linaker, T. Baxter, J. Mounfleld, J. B. Chadwick, C. Roylance, J. Hallows, J. Whitley, G. Egerton-Warburton, J. Bolshaw, J. H. Davies, H. M. Davies, T. Antwis, J. L. Jones, A. Greenway, P. Mounfleld, A. Broome, E. Bretherton, H. Mawdsley, J. Smith, R. Billington, G. F. Ashton (clerk), A. E. Hulse (acting deputy clerk), Dr. Adams (medical officer of health), W. Diggle (surveyor), and J. Farrington (inspector of nuisances).

CHARGES FOR WATER. The Local Government Board forwarded notices of inquiries to be held on the 12th inst. at the Infants' school, Preston-o'-th'-11111 and the Board Room of the Workhouse to determine the cost at which water should be supplied at Preston-o'-th'-Hill, Aston-by-Sutton, and Dutton. The Council fixed the rate for Dutton at 10 per cent, which is the amount already decided upon for Preston Brook.

WALTON SEWAGE. Mr. J. Mounfield reported that the sub-committee appointed to deal with this question met that morning and examined the plans of a suggested scheme. It was decided to refer the plans to the Walton Parish Council and to the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee beiore finally sanctioning them. The minutes were approved.

FINANCIAL STATEMENT. Mr. Wright reported a balance at the last meeting of £9lB us. 2d.; receipts during the fortnight, £382 4s 9d; cheques drawn that day, £429 13s. 10d. ; leaving a balance of £866 ss. 7d. The total balance shown in the treasurer's book was £1,300 15s. 11d.

COMPLAINT FROM HELSBY. Writing from Brackenhurst, Helsby, Mrs. E. M. Dutton callo'd the attention of the Council to the fact that a bad smell was noticeable from Ivy Row in Raike Lane down to the main road on the side opposite to the Rail- way Inn, Helsby. The nuisance, she stated, had bsen in existence for some time and was particularly noticeable in warm weather. She requested the Council to take steps to secure abatement. Mr. Farrington prowised to give the matter attention as soon as possible.
HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT-THE PREVALENCE OF SCARLET FEVER. -

_ Dr. Adams reported a case of scarlet fever at Frod- sham and one of diphtheria in the same township. Eight scarlet fever cases were reported from Stockton Heath, and one each at Norley and Antrobus. A case of typhoid fever had occurred at Balton Brook. The Chairman remarked that the prevalence of scarlet fever was a serious matter. , Dr. Adams pointed out that there was generally an increase in the number of cases in autumn, but the rise was more marked in borough than in Rural Dis-rict. They were, he thought, to some extent indebted to the adjoining Borough of Warrington for the outbreak. Communication between the town and the district was free, and Warrington was as full as it could be of scarlet fever. The hospital there was quite full. The report was adopted. Considerable discussion took place with reference to the discharging of foreign manure at a wharf at Moore. and it was understood that the Medical Officer would make further inquiries into the matter.

div.head: BIG BLAZE AT WIDNES.
div.p: BIG BLAZE AT WIDNES.

About r.lo on Saturday the large dew colour depart- ment at the Orr Zinc White Company's works, Widnes, was found to be on fire. The tire spread with rapidity and within ten minutes of the discovery the whole of the building was involved in a .hopeless manner. The fire brigade set to work to srtve the adjacent portions of the works. On a works railway between the burning building and the other parts there were several vans and i waggons, and four of these were in flames, and very seriously endangering further property, before they could be shunted. The colour department which was completely gutted within threequarters of an hour, was a wooden structure covering the boilers and valuable plant used in grinding and making colours. A railway hut on the Widnes and St. Helens line adjoining also became involved and was gutted. A number of employes rendered good service in removing colour and other materials out Of range.

When such stroke is played at a fast pace the deviation If thB cue-ball from the line of aim (provided that the ball has been struck by a. horizontally held elle) is practically nil, simply because the 119,1$ ,f the cloth has no appreciable effect an a fast Call. When, however, a stroke is played at 14, edium or slow pace, the deviation of the cue ba.ll from the line of aim by the time contact .t 8 made with the object ball, can easily be a Rtlarter to half an inch and even .more. Play- from the baulk end of the table, that is ,with the nap, the tendency of right hand side to pull the ball to the right, and left hanit slde to pull it to the left. ,The ordirary player continually misses certain trokes (generally cannons off one or tete cushions) owing to the side which be has int- Darted to the cue hall causing it to diverge !rem the line of aim, yet the true cause 'ailtrre is seldom Or r.ever und.erstood.

div.head: DIAGRAM 16.
div.p: DIAGRAM 16.
two-cushion oanuon with running side. Unless stroke be played with " drag " as well as side object ball will be struck thinner than aimed

Diagram 16 shows a position for a cannon off ' two cushions played with plenty of running side. It the cue ball be struck about half-way tip with plenty of right hand side, and a half-hall stroke Ott to the object white be played at medium Pace, the object ball will be struck considerably finer than intended, and when this happens the ordinary player simply concludes that his aim was at fault, and repeated failures only confirm this conclusion. There, are, however, two methods by which the difficulty may be overcome. The first Is by aiming as though to hit the object ball a little fuller than is required. The allowance to be .roade must, of course, depend upon the amount of side whicleis going to be imparted to the cue ball and the speed at which the stroke is going 'to be played. As a rule, in playing a long dis- tance stroke from the baulk end of the table such as the cannon shown in diagram ~15, a quarter ball allowance 'would be the most that would be required, that la to say that if it were desired to hit the object 'hall half-ball, aim should be "taken to hit il about three-quarter ball. The second method of ensuring that the con- tact with the object ball be as desired is as fol- lows:—Aim should be taken without any allow- lace being made for the side, but the cue ball in addition to being it on the side must also be struck low down with what is known as ."drag." At some later date I intend to go very i fully into the nroperties of drag, but it It sufficient to state here that in the shot under discussion the drag causes the cue ball to slide or ' "drag along the cloth for a considerable distance instead of rolling forward, and that whilst this sliding or dragging continues, the nap of the cloth has little or no effect on the path of a ball, even though the ball has been struck with plenty of side. _;The distance that the ball drags Will depend upon the strength of the stroke, and Upon hew low the ball has been hit, but in a long shot such as shown in diagram 14i_if the Stroke be a drag stroke and not a screw, the Sliding or dragging action will terminate some considerable distance from the object ball, and the moment the drag becomes exhausted the ' joint action of nap and side comes into play. As however the cue ball has perhaps only half the original distance or even less to travel after the drag has disappeared, the side on the ball has not time to cause very much deviation from :the original line of aim. Nevertheless, if •the .stroke be a slow one, the deviation may still be fairly considerable .(i of an inch in an instance like this is considerable). The soundest way, therefore, of playing all these long shots that , require side and only medium pace is to play them with plenty of drag, aiming i .at the same time to hit the ball just a shade fuller than is required in the actual contact. It must not be forgotten, however, that when Playing against the nap of the cloth (that is, from the spot end of the table) side on the cue ball has just the reverse effect from what it has 'when playing with the nap, and therefore in Order to counterbalance the effect of running side against the nap before contact with an oh- ' ject ball, aim should" be taken as though to hit the ball just a little less full than the actual contact required. When playing a stroke with side, great "care should always be taken to hold the cue as hori- zontally as possible, for if the butt be appre- ciably raised a ball struck on its side will never .travel in quite a straight line, and the more the butt be raised the more marked will the ball's divergence be. This divergence is not caused by the nap of the cloth. It is, in fact, quite in- ldependent of the nap, and would occur just the same on a cloth without any nap at all. It re- sults from the more or less downward thrust of , the cue which- really masses the ball to a car-

fain degree. .; The following stroke can be tried to illustrate how the downward hitting on to the side of a ball affects the path of the ball:—Place the red on the spot and the cue ball touching the baulk cushion or the side cushion in baulk, the ball being in either case only a few inches from the left baulk pocket. Aim half ball on to the red on the side towards the right top pocket._ Raise the butt of the cue several inches and strike the ball on the right hand side, using a nice free stroke. Such a stroke will curl the cue ball so much edit of the line of aim • that the red will be mis,efl altogether. Even if aim be taken full • on to the red or even on to the other Side of the rod. thti red may still be missed as when a cue ball is struck in the way I have described, especi- ally if the butt is well elevated, the divergencek from the line of aim caused by the swerving of thA ball may easily amount toapveral inches. Players, therefore, when playing a stroke that requires no side should be extra careful in hit- ting the cue ball as near as possible in the centre when the ball happens to be touching a cushion or lying very close to a cushion. and the object ball is a considerable distance away. Also the cue should be. raised no more than necessary. Of course, when a. ball is dead or nearly dead on a cushien the cue must be Romewliat raised, but most players uplift the butt far more than they need to, though with very -11tt1e at fault may be easily got rid of. WARRINGTON BOARD OF
GUARDIANS.

The Prospects for the Coming Winter. A meeting of this Board was held on Wednesday morning at the Workhouse. Mr. A. Brooks presided and there were also present, Mrs. Clay, Mrs. Wilkinson, Messrs. A. J. Jolley, S. Davies,W. Hickman, G. Thomp- son, W. Houghton, J. Turton, G. Mather, W. Flannagan, M. W. Seton, R. Forshaw, T. H. Ashcroft, J. C. Sutton (clerk), J. F. Awbery (master of the Workhouse), A. Wright (superintendent of Padgate schools). THE A.CCEPTANCE OF TENDERS. Letters were read from Messrs. Pendlebury and Co., and Messrs Edwin Richardson and Co.pointing-out that their tenders, although lowest, were not accepted. Mr. HICKMAN moved that the tenders be referred I r back to the House Committee for further consideration, but the Chairman ruled this to be out of order as the tenders had been sent to the committee with power to accept. Mr. ASHCROFT remarked that the committee were guided by the guardians from Haydockin regard to the coal contract. The CHAIRMAN: This cannot be discussed as it is out of order. Mr. HicxmAN gave notice to move a reaolution at the next Board meeting with regard to future contracts, but Mr. JOLLEY pointed out that a committee consist- ing of the chairmen and deputy chairmen of the House and Padgate Committees and the Chairman of the Board had been appointed. Mr.HICKMALi thereupon withdrew his motion.

MEDICAL OFFICER. A letter confirming the re-appointment of Dr. Sephton as one of the medical officers of the Union was received from the Local Government Board. THE STATE OF TRADE IN THE UNION. VARIOUS OPINIONS OF THE BOARD. The following letter was received from Mr. Jenner- Fust, inspector of the Local Government Board :—I am directed to report upon (1) The condition of pauperism in this district at the present time ; (2) The prospects of employment during the coming year; (3) Thesubject of the unemployed. Can you kindly furnish me with Information on these subjects as regards your Union. Mr. BILLINGE said that in Haydock. and Newton trade was unfortunately not good and had been unfavourable for some time now. Work was at short time now and the prospects for the coming winter were not hopeful. He did not anticipate that things would , improve in fact the trend of circumstances was in the ' other dikOction in his district. A lot of property was unoccupied, and in many cases, two families were living in one house. Many able bodied men were out of employment and found it very difficult to get work. The Newton Relief Committee were compelled owing to sheer destitution to give relief in order that people might keep their homes together. The CHAIRMAN: Can you contrast it with last year? Mr. BILLINGE : Well I don't think the destitution is in excess of last year. The CLERK: May I write to the Local Government Board that you will be able to cope with the relief in your district without resorting to other measures that are available in the ordinary way. Mr. BILLINGE : I think so. The CLERK: You will not have to find means of em- ployment for the outdoor poor such as the opening of a stoneyard or such means? Mr. BiLLINOE : I think so. Mr. THOMPSON : I don't think things are any worse this year than last year. That is my experience. Mr. DAVIES : As far as Warrington is concerned, I feel perfectly sure we are in a better position than last winter. I don't think we shall have the slightest diffi- culty in pulling through the winter without any ex- traordinary measures being taken. The CHAIRMAN: That is if the winter is of an ordinary character. Mr. HOUGHTON: I think the relieving officers would be useful in giving information on this subject. Mr. MATHmR : The cheques they draw for out-relief have not increased. The CLERK: Most elaborate returns are sent weekly to Mr. Jenner-Fust and the Local Government Board and they arelfully aware how that stands. Observations are invited from members of the Board, and I think the , prospects are no worse than usual with a reasonable winter, as the chairman suggests. That appears to be the view of the Board and I will convey that view to Mr. Jenner-Fust. The CHAIRMAN : The staple trade of Lancashire is undoubtedly improving. For a long number of months the Lancashire cotton operatives have been working short time. There seems now to be a record crop or at any rate a very large crop of cotton in America,and so mills are already going on full time. If the state of the staple trade is good, it will re-act considerably on all other trades, not only in Lancashire but in the surrounding c guntriesi think we should look hopefully to the coming winter. Mr. HrcKmAN: I think the outlook is better all round if the weather is not severe. I don't think there Is any need for alarm. The matter then dropped. TENDER ACCEPTED. On the motion of Mr. BILLINGE seconded by Mr. PORSHA.W, the tender of Messrs. Monks and Fowler, Haydock-street,Earlestown.for the painting and decorat- ing of the relief offices at Earlestown, for £35 was accepted. This concluded the business.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD- OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD- OF GUARDIANS.

--- The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, Mr. A. R. Norman pre- siding. There were also present ;—Admiral J.P.Jones- Parry, Messrs. T. Baxter, C. E. Linaker, T. Wright, J. Hallows, J. Whitley, C. Roylance, A. Broome, J. Spruce, G. Egerton Warburton, J. Mounfield, J. Bolshaw, T. Antwis, J. Douglas, H. M. Davies, J. H. Davies, S. Woodward. J. L. Jones, W. M.Morris, J. W. Temperley G. Pilling, A. Greenway, P. Mounfield, A. Broome, J. Smith, H. Mawdsley, E. Bretherton, R. Billington, T. Cook, T. Riley and W. R. dePrez (relieving officers),J. Cuneah (master), G. F. Ashton (clerk), A. E. Hulse (acting deputy clerk.) MR. FLETCHER'S RESIGNATION. The Local Government Board wrote accepting the resignation of Mr. William Fletcher, from the office of parish councillor of Seven Oaks and Whitley. THE TIMES OF MEETINGS. I Mr. Woodward moved that during the winter months I the times of meetings should be as follows :—Asses- meat Committee, 10.30; Visiting Committee; 11.30; Relief Supervision Committee, 12 o'clock; Board of Guardians, 12.45; District Council Building Committee 11.30 ; Isolation Hospital Committee, 12 o'clock; Dis- trict Ciiuncil immediately after the Guardians,meeting. The Chairman said that was practically going back to the old system. If it worked well for six months he saw no reason why it should not be adopted during the summer. The resolution was carried _

FINANCE. Mr. Woodward reported a balance at the last meeting of £560 ss. id.; receipts during the fortnight, £llO 2s. Id.; payments that day, £1,083 3s. 4d.; leaving a balance of £412 16s. 2d. GIFT OF A PIANO TO THE INMATES. At a meeting of the Ladies' Visiting Committee a resolution was passed expressing sincere thanks to the Runcorn Co-operative Society for the gift of a piano to the inmates of the house. Mr. Roylance asked how it was that the Guardians received no intimation of the formal presentation of the instrument. The Chairman said that after the Board had risen at the last meeting Mr. Morris told him that the presentation was to take place on the following night and he attended the function. The arrangements , had been left in the hands of the Ladies' Visiting Com- mittee and that was the reason why the members of the Board received no invitations. Mr. Morris asked him, tas chairman, to attend the gathering and he felt it was his duty to go. They were very much indebted to the Co-operative Society for their gift. The piano was an 'excellent one; and he moved that the best thanks of the Board be accorded to the donors. The instrument I was not presented to them as Guardians, and that per- haps made the matter a little bit awkward. The inscrip- tion on the piano stated that it was presented to the 1 inmates of the house. However, the Board might very properly recognize the great kindness of the society. i Mr. Wright seconded. He pointed out that previous Ito the presentation from the Co-operative Society the ;Guardians were asked to contribute to a piano fund. He land others subscribed what they thought it was their duty to give and he suggested that the money should be handed to the Ladies' Committee to be used as they ' thought fit for any purposes in connectien with the ; house. IThe Clerk said the Board could bardly take that course , as some of the money was subscribed by former members. The vote of thanks was carried and it was decided that the subscriptions should be returned. I The Ladies' Visiting Commiti ee also expressed their :cordial thanks to the artistes who provided the recent enjoyable entertainment for the inmates.

CITY OF BII.I3FORD EXITIBITION.—MOrIday last was memorable in the history of the Bradford Exhibition by reason of the arrival of the two-millionth visitor. Though a check had been put upon all calculations by the withholding of the figures of attendance on Satur- day it was well known that the week's figures had been so good that all previous records for four days— Wednesday, Thursday,Friday and Saturday had been far exceeded, and thousands of people, putting two and two together in shrewd fashion, came to the conclusion that the after-business hours of Monday would be the time to try for the gold watch and chain which the Ex- hibition authorities had promised as a souvenir. At a quarter past eight Mr. Thomas Lee, pickle manufac- turer, of Otley-road. Bradford, was accosted by the Manager as he was entering, and informed that he was the fortunate individual, and he received the souvenir in due course.
