div.p: "BRITISH ISLES" BAZA.AR. GREAT LIBERAL EFFORT. PICTURESQUE SCENE AT THE PARR HALL. Interesting Speeches at the Opening Cerainonies. Thirteen years ago the Liberal ladies of Warring- ton and district rendered a distinct service to local Liberalism by carrying to a successful issue a grandl bazaar, the proceeds of which realised over :C1,200. A similar effort has been made this week,and although I the financial result has not been quite so satisfactory— due largely to the depression in trade—the ladies have every reason to congratulate themselves upon the result. The objects of the bazaar were "to provide funds for carrying on the important work of political education and organisation in the town; and to ensure the regis- tration of every person entitled to the Parliamentary and Municipal franchise." Since the passing of the Reform Act of 1832, Warrington has enjoyed the privilege of sending a representative to Parliament, and the local Liberal Association has never been without supporters who were willing to give freely of their time, energy and money for the advancement of the cause of progress in politics. But the wealthy then connected with the party have become fewer and fewer within the last two decades owing to death and removal, and it has been found necessary to look in other directions for the necessary funds t) defray the expenses of the politioal work of the Association. Encouraged by , the success of the bazaar of 13 years ago, it was decided to venture upon another, and this week Parr Hall has been the scene of the second Liberal bazaar held in the Borough. It has been conducted under the auspices of the Warrington Liberal Association and the Warrington Women's Liberal Association. I Members of both institutions have worked hard for the I success of the bazaar but the chief honours must fall to the ladies who have shown a willingness and self- sacrifice to work on behalf of the Liberal cause, which puts many ,of the Steiner sex to shame. For many months past, working meetings have been regularly held at the Liberal. Club, and in addition to attending these, all the ladies did work at home. A real and practical enthusiasm was displayed for the success of the bazaar and the results were seen in the heavily - laden stalls of useful and fancy articles which were offered for sale. •: THE SCENE IN THE PARR HALL. 'The British Isles" was the title given to the Bazaar, and the subject was illustrated by beautiful scenes depicting interesting places in England, Ireland, Scotland and Wales. Large as the hall is, it seemed comparatively small when the scenic effects had been introduced, but sufficient accommodation was found to meet the requirements of the stallholders and their patrons. The views gave a touch of colour to the surroundings, and the effect was considerably heightened when the declrators art was lit up with the bright soft light of numberless electric glow lamps. On enterincr,one naturally turns to the orchestra end of the Hall and there Wales was depicted in all its glory. If there is one spot in the kingdom that is politically prominent it is Hawarclen Castle, and towering in front of the organ was a presentment of the historic build- ing with its grey stone parapets and towers—a spot known and reverenced. At on side, pretty little Welsh cottages were seen rising one above the other on the hill side. Scotland was represented by Some Palace, which was selected on account of the Coronation Stone on which our kings have been crowned, corning originally from Scone, It is a link in our national history and a risible sign of our union and common 'interests. Ireland was represented by a characteristic old ruined abbey with an enormous square tower, and casement- less windows, but still preserving that perfection of outline that belongs to the old ecclesiastical buildings of the middle ages. The unique Rows of Chester were typical of old England. The stalls bore the names of the four kingdoms. The ladies in attendance also wore a distinctive dress. Their dainty cream holland dresses were relieved with a design of the national emblem of the particu- lar kingdom their stall represented. Cream-coloured caps were also worn. As viewed from the galleries, the scene was a picturesque and animated one. The scenic part of the bazaar had been created and arranged by Messrs. F. Le laistre and Company, of Manchester, and was in every way satisfactory. THE STALLS.

A glance at the stalls, heavily laden as they all were with an immense variety of articles, was sufficient to demonstrate how energetic had been the work of the ladies' working committee and with what gene roity their efforts had been backed up. So numerous were the articles to be offered for sale that at first the stalls were found inadequate to contain them. Great care was taken in the arrangement of the stalls and some of the stallholders were working late on Tuesday evening setting out their wares. By noon on Wed- nesday, however, everything was in readiness and the Ladies stood in attendance anxious to commence busi- ness. In front of the platform, was a stall devoted exclusively to the sale of flowers, and the display did much to grace the room. At the opposite end, imme- diately under the centre gallery, was the refreshment stall,heavily burdened with a choice collection of edibles and gracefully attended to by the ladies in charge. There were six stalls containing plain and fancy goods. It is impossible to particularise them, but here and there was to be seen a picture or a screen standing out prominently among an endless variety of other commodities. The two stalls bearing the name of England contained a large quantity of rich material and beautiful needlework. Mrs. Crosfield was in charge of an Ireland stall, and very appro- priately, she displayed a large quantity of Irish manu- factures, she having gone over to Dublin specially to make the purchases. There were some fine examples of Irish needlework, as well as numerous articles made of bog oak, including pipes, cigarette holders, Scc. Prominent on another stall bearing the name of Ireland, was a beautiful white satin cushion, relieved with the borough arms worked in silk and also containing the autographs of a number of distinguished local people. Amongst the pictures we noticed one by Oswald Garside, a local artist of much promise. The exhibits at the Scotland stall were exceedingly varied and contained a full assortment of plain and fancy work. It was originally intended to have a second Scotland stall in charge of Councillor A. Peacock and friends, but at the last, moment Mr. 'Peacock found himself unable to under- take the work, and kindly sent a donation to the bazaar funds instead. The members of the Liberal Club claimed the Wales stall as their own, and made a most effective display. Many of Messrs. Urns field's toilet requisites found a prominent place on this stall and there were many willing assistants to sell them. In addition there were two china stalls, crest china being a speciality at one of them. THE OPENING CEREMONY. When the bazaar Was opened at 2.30 the scene was one of great brilliancy, the only regrettable feature being that the body of the hall was not completely ' filled with sightseers. Amongst those present in addition to the Hon. Mrs. Emmott Sarlow,who per- formed the opening ceremony, were: Mr. J. Emmott Barlow, M.P., Sir J. T. Brunner, M.P., and Mrs. Brunner, Mr. A. H. Crosfield, Mr. and Mrs. C. E. Parker, Mr. T. Birchall, J.P., Mr. E. j. Guest, J.P., Rev. G. H. Carnson, Rey. R. Wilkins Rees, Rey. C. Harvey Cook, Mrs. Crosfield, Miss Crosfield, Mrs. Ziba Armaage, Mrs: Garnett, Alderman Bennett Councillors James Evans, W. Brough, D. Tinnion, L.' Ellison, T. Burton, T. Barton, Mr. and Mrs. C. Jackson Holmes, Mr. and Mrs. E. Osborne, Messrs. E. V. Walker, A. Browne, J. Longland, W. Furness, E. V. Morton, J. Critchley, T. Dale, J. Skelland, Thomas Locker, W. W. Winstanley, J. Briggs, E. A. Sanders, and the stallholders. SIR JOHN BRUNNER'S SPEECH. Sir JOHN•BRUNNER, who had a cordial reception on rising tel open the proceedings, said: It is a pleasure to me to find myself here for a good many reasons. The first is that I was Unfortunately obliged to dis- appoint an expectant audience in Warrington some months ago. I gave my excuse at the time, but I may perhaps repeat it to-day. It is that Mr. Herbert Glad- stone absolutely forbetde me from being out of my place in the House of Commons. I think that in spite of what appeared a discourtesy towards you you will I give me a hearty welcome to-day because my absence ' proved the loyalty of my Liberalism. (Hear, hear.) I I am very glad to help any gathering of Liberals,although I know that on occasions of this sort our good Con- servative friends come to help They know that we are very friendly people. (I.tittghter.) Nevertheless the object of the bazaar is to help the Liberal party. I have always delighted at all times to help those on the side of progress, peace and liberty. (Hear, hear.) No such gathering as this would be content unless we spoke a word of regret at the loss of our great leader, SIR WILLIAM HARCOURT and sent to his bereaved widow and to his mournidg sons a message of condolence and sympathy. Sir William has been known to me during the whole of the period I have sat in the House of Commons. I have lawns been a faithful follower of his. I have alway

regarded him with great admiration as a steadfast Liberal and with itrtense admiration for his powers of intellect and especially for his powers of debate. I He has been throughout his long career an. absolutely consistent Liberal and he has been besides theta great teacher. (Hear, hear.) fie has been a great , teacher in a very important field—the field of inter- !national flaw. (Hear, hear.) We English people are bound, especially now, to study international law. Sir i William Harcourt rendered great service to his country through the celebrated letters that he wrote in "The ' Times" over the signature " Elistoricus." (Hear, hear.) IVlay his nernory remain green among us for many a day. (Applause). lam heartily glad to come here to-day for many reasons, and one of them that is very attractive to me is this, that the bazaar is called a representation of THE BRITISH ISLES. I cordially approve of the clinic° of the subject of your bazaar for the reason that I think it is time we began to attend a little to the British Isles—(hear,hear)—and that we did not imitate the man who was spoken of in the scriptures as" The fool hath his eyes on the end of the earth." (Lartghter.) Let Ui have dons with these extravagant excursions into Thibet and Searaliland. (Hear, hear.) Let us abandon this policy of building railways in Uganda and making roads 700 miles long in Persia. Let us attend a little to our own affairs. There is only one way to obtain ett-mtion to our a.va,aff sirs and that is to get rid of the precast Government. (Hear hear.) I aeeell to you—l appeal to all level-headed men and all true-hearted ,vernea in Werrington—to give up this policy of push and swagger and will-rail enter- prises malt parts of the world andlet us adopt a policy of common sense. Common sense bids us—l am absolutely satisfied—to DEVELOP THE RESOTJRCE3 of the British Isles. (Hear, hear.) I have had my say pot' this subject for the last 15 years Fabliely, and for . good many years before that in private. -I want to develop the resources of the British Isles. It has always been a matter of deep interest and speculation to me what would have happened to Warrington and this district if Liverpool had been here instead of where it is. I will tell you what would have happened. The Nfersey would have been improved as the Clyde has been improved and I cannot see for the life of me why there should not be greatly improved navigation from this point down the river past Runcorn and Widass to Liverpool. (Hear, hoar.) Our cousins across the Atlantic, over 100 years ago adopted this policy of developing the natural reseurces of the country and they laid it down as a rule that the poverty of the immediate locality affected should never be a bar to a public improvement, provided that improvement could be shown to be for the National benefit—" All for all." Let us all join together and not inquire too curiously whether the people in a particular locality will get a little more benefit than the people of another locality. Never let the poverty of the immediate neighbourhood be a hindrance to national work. (Hear, hear.) I have spoken of the rule adopted by the Government of the United States and I might go on. I might tell you that the Canadians, who are in blood relationship no closer than the people of the United States, though they live under the same flag as ourselves—and let me remind you that if it had not been for a Tory Govern- ment, the people of the United States would have been under the same flag—the Canadians have adopted this policy I am referring' to. The Australians have also adopted it, for they build their own railways at the cost of the State. The New Zealanders have adopted the same policy, so that wherever We go in the world there we find English speaking people doine in their new homes precisely what I want the English, the Irish, the Scotch and the Welsh people to do in their own land. We have the example of all the English speaking people in the world before us, and on the continent, the French, the Germans, the Austrians, theNungarians, the Danes and the Belgians have sat themselves to work to develop the resources of their own country and always. with the idea of facilitating trade. lam through and through a FREE TRA.DER. (Applause.) lam absolutely convinced that freedom in this matter—freedom for each person and each com- pany—is absolutely the best policy for us in these two small islands. But I don't want to be content with this freedom of trade; I am extremely anxious that we should work together for the benefit of trade in our own country and I believe that any benefit to be got by a ten per cent tariff on imports will disappear entirely when compared with the enormous benefit we shall gat by spending our own money at home. (Applause.) I believe myself to be as true a patriot as any within the British Isles. A friend of mine sent to me a few days ago a local newspaper in which a writer under the name of " Imperialist " spoke of me as a little Englander. (Laughter.) There is no man amen; his Majesty's subjects—and " Gad save the King "—who is more anxious than I that England suould be great. (Applause.) There are more ways than one of attaining great- ness. I don't believe that avast military expenditure is the way to make our country great. 1 am absolutely convinced that we. have reached a point in our military and naval expenditure that has become a weakening and not a strengthening thing. I ask you to put a GOVERNNIENT OF CONI.VION SENSE government with ezonenricat views—into the place of those people who have doges') raaeh mischief in the last 15 years. I was blarned-in the letter I have alluded to for the opposition that I offered to the Beer War' I have no regret whatever in regard to anything I did in opposition to that war. I have n ) regrets, no apologies to offer on behalf of the Liberal party except this that we failed to stop it. Ala! how much better off we should boas a nation if we had stopped that war. Nobody except manufacturers of armaments have got any benefit out of it, not even the people who bought up the press in South Africa and flooded us with lies and fomented the quarrel. I am bound to say I don't sympathise with them in their trouble on account of the slump in the Stock Exchange. Not a whit! I am delighted to Corns here to help because want to get rid of snlash and muddle and put men of commonsense and lovers of freedom in the Government of the country. (Applause.) At this stage of the proceedings, Mrs. Ziba Armitage on behalf of the Warrington Women's Liberal Associa- tion and the Warrington Liberal Association presented the Hon. Mrs. Emmett Barlow with a lovely boaquet. The Hon. Mrs. E3I3IOTT BA.RLOW, who had a hearty reception, said: I am delighted to come to you to-day—it is my first visit to Warrington—because I have heard from my husband the many kind things that you did for him in bvegone days when he WAS contest- ing the Knutsford Division. (Hear, hear.) Although it is my first visit. I hope it may not be the lest. lam also glad to meet with the Liberal ladies of Warrington. It is a pleasure to meet Liberal women everywhere we go, and I feel it is most kind of them to have presented me with this bouquet to-day. Ve have not altogether the same opportunities in politics as men —some of us think we are very far behind in that respect—but we have in certain directions many oppor- tunities which they have not—(hear, hear,)—and may point out to you one especially that occurs to me? It seems to me that in the commercial world the women have a great responsibility in the bringing up of their children, because the husbands are away at work during the day and in the early years we have the entire management of our children—and how much rests with us in bringing up the next generation of voters. (Applause.) I firmly believe that in our earliest childhood it is pos-` sible to distinguish between a Conservative view of things and a Liberal view. I don't mean a narrow view when I say that—that Liberalism is right and Conserva- tism is wrong—but I mean the general broad views of what Liberalism means to us., I am quite con- vinced that it is possible and think what a splendid thing it would be if the next generatien that we are responsible for, grows up broad-minded,tolerant, anxious for freedom, and fighting as their fathers and grandfathers have done before them. (Applause.) I must tell you that two days ago I WAS reading Herbert Spencer's autobiography. He and Huxley were walking one Sunday afternoon as they - fre- quently did at Hampstead and Herbert Spencer said "Well I suppose one can expect nothing better than to make one's mark in life and die." Huxley said" Never mind about the mark. Everyone can give a push." (Applause). Lastly, it gives ma great pleasure to be associated here to-day with our chairman for the first time on a political platform. (Laughter.) Sir John Brunner is one of those Liberals whose Liberalism is the same wherever you find it. It is not the type that becomes luke-warm under some circninstances, and vigorous under others. Wherever he is, he is a staunch Liberal—and that I have experienced for many years— in fact Sir John and I are generally known wherever we inset as very decided Liberals. (Hear, hear.) I thank you for your kind reception of me to-daY, and wishing this bazaar every success, I declare it open. (Applause.)

MR. CROSTIELD AND HOPEFUL PROSPECTS. Mr. A. H. eItOSFIRLD, who was heartily received, slid: This is for me an unsonght honour. I think that the honour of proposing the vote of thanks that has been entrusted to m 3 would have been better discharged by somebody else, but at the same time' it gives me very great and sincere pleasure to propose a vote of thanks to our chairman for presiding over this ceremony and to the Hon. Mrs. Emmott Barlow for the most delight- ful and most charming address she has just given us. (Applause.) It certainly is a happy augury for the success of the bazaar that the opening proceedings should be initiated by two speeches so instructive and so delightful to listen to as we have just heard, and I hope that when the bazaar closes we shall all have great cause fur rejoicing in its success. Liberals are in a cheerful mood just now. (Hear, hear.) We have not had such bright times always for the last sixteen, eighteen, or twenty years—certainly not in Warrington. It has been really difficult for some of us who have been responsible for keeping the end up to make a proper fight of it, but if we have been under a cloud for a time, now the sun is shining. Sir John, Brunner has alluded to the reason, and fthink briefly it is this—that the Government, after all,has been found out. (Hear, ['hear.) The next fact that we have to anticipate is that the Government will be turned out. (Laughter and applause.) We have just had a very re- markable speech from our Premier. I am not going to take up time in criticising it. Mr. Balfour we know, is great on philosophic doubt. (Laughter.) He may, perhaps, sail on the seas of exploration, and he may be deep in the mysteries of metaphysics. Perhaps he may reach that condition of mind which Byron described when he said "there were men who doubted, if doubt

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, October 8, 1904.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, October 8, 1904.

itself was doubting." (Laughter.) Bat I think there is ono thing on which the Premier probably has no doubt whatever and that is the result of the neat General election. I think Mr. Balfour probably knows perfectly well—and his last speech indicates that knowledge too —that he is not going to have the country casting its vote in favour of Protection. (Elear, hear.)f-le may get a little retaliation,but I fancy it will be of a different nature to what he is advocating—(laughter)—.)oolll33 there are some old scores—not so very old either—that have to be reckoned with when the nation cornea to settle its account with the present Government. (Applause.) I am not going to detain you any longer, because, after aAI, we are met to-day not so much for the purpose of speaking as for the parpese of spending. (Laughter.) But I should like to give our Chairman and Mr. Ern.mott Barlow, who ha,re so kindly paid us a visit to- day, a reasoa why people who meddle with politics in Warrington should never be very loag-winied. (Laugh- ter.) It is an incident that occurred in the HOME, of Cenarnons, I believe before these gentlemen were dis- tinguished ornaments of that assembly, and it was at the expense of the Liberal or Radical member for War- rington of that day who bore a name which was honoured then, and is honoured newomi will always be honoured in our town. (hear, hear.) But lam afraid, Sir John, in the House of Commons they do sometikies have hard knocks if people overstep the line in re- gard to oratory. Whether the late Ar. Rylands had been trespassing upon the dinner hour or what he had done, I don't know, but it was in the days when Lord Beaconsdeld—who was then known by the name of Dizzy—was doing many things that were very much disapproved of by the Liberals. His policy, as you may be sure, underwent the purifying ordeal of Liberal criticism—Cl:Tear, hear)—but Mr. Rylands's criticism ay.aseatended perhaps a little too far, and,like Burke, he meat An purifying and thought of feaciag while other people thought of dining. (Laughter.) So four lines were passed down the opposition side about Mr. Rylands. ail this is my reasaa for not detaining you any longer Preposterous Peter, Prithee cut it short ; That "Dizzy" doeth what he didn't ought We know, but still life would be sweeter, With ten Disraeli's than one Peter! (Loud laughter.) Councillor TENSION' seconded. It was rather peculiar he said, that in the Chairman and in Mr. Eratnott Barlow they had two gentlemen nho. at any rate, owed to Warrington Liberalism some thanks for past services. He knew many very good Liberals who during the first contest that Sir John Brunner fought went and did a vary great arnonnt of work—(hear, hear)—and he was almost ~.oing to say that they were the means of his successful return. (Laughter). They would be very pleased to have SirJoha's services in future, and they would not lose the:n for the want of asking. (Hear, hear.) The inatiou was cordially agreed to. Sir JOTIN BRuNNER. said he was very mach obliged for the kind way in which Ar. Crosfleld and Councillor 'Final:on had spoken of him. Fle could assure both gentlemen that When the opportunity came for him to render what poor little service he could to the cause of Warrington Liberalism,he would be there.(Applause.)He now wanted to give the husband a chance—(laughter) —and he would call upon Mr. Emtnott Barlow to return thanks for his wife. He could not possibly acknow- ledge more fully than they could wish their grateful thanks to Mrs. Earnott Barlow for the delightful speech she had given.

M. ECIADTr BARLOW AND TORY TACTICS. Ar. E Ntorr 13 4. aLow, A.P., said: I thank you very much for the cordial appreciation which you have been so gool a. to show of my wife's efforts here to-day. I can assure you that it has been on her part a labour of love, coming to help Liberalism. She knows, and knows well, the uphill fight that you Libeeals in Warrington have had for a great many years, and no one hopes more heartily than she does that your efforts may be crowned with success at no distant date. (Hear, hear.) Speak- ing for m,yself, I can assure you that it gives me very great pleasure to come again to Warrington. If I I remember aright the Last occasion I was in Warrington on a political errand, if so it may be called, was when you had a bazaar here some thirteen years ago. But my recollections of Warrington, as has been I suggested, date somewhat farther back than that and I still remember with deep gratitude the hearty support which I had from many people in Warrington when I fought my first political contest as a much younger man. Tam afraid, than lam to-day. I shall never forget the sauport which I had from good friends in and around Warrington, and I hope the lessons I learnt in that held may have been of some use to me elsewhere, and possibly through ma in a small way, to the Liberal party. The prospects of the Liberal party are brightening. Let us hope they will continue to brighten. (Hear, hear.) We have had a dull and weary tirn,e in the House of Commons. We shall be charged with obstruction, but the obstruction in the House of Commons has not corns from us; it has come from the supporterslof the TorylGovernment when they could not get their other supporters back from the dinner table in order to support their own Government and what they are pleased to call the Constitution. The hours that have been wasted in the House during the last six or soften months by supporters of the Government because the Government were in a minority would be passed over, had they not been witnessed by some of us who have gone into the House and have seen Tory orator after Tory orator get up either in the afternoon or between nine and ten in the evening, looking nervously at the clock and talking about something that bore the faintest, possible connection with the subject under debate, and sitting down, after the Tory Whip had come into the House and someone had pulled their coat tails, with a sigh of relief and words,that so far as we could tell from the motion of their lips, sounded very much like "Thank God, the Government's safe this time." (Laughter.) That has been the sort of spectacle we have often seen in the House of Commons. I ask you whether any level- headed man, whatever his politics may be, can wish an effete and moribund party like that to continue to have the direction of our national affairs. The Tory party are divided among themselves. They are wobbling ; they are effete in the management of the country, and it is high time they were replaced by men who know their own mind, who have a single mind on the great subjects of the day, and who, we hope, will be able to conduct our national destinies on the lines of peace,retrenchment, and reform —(applause) —good old words we have heard sneered at, but which were never more necessary than they are to-day—looking after our own affairs, and in that way I trust in the future as in the past, the Liberal party will lead us on to success and to victory. (Applause.) When that day comes I trust and believe that you in Warrington will take your share by sending a good man to support us, a man whom we can rely upon, a good man who will bring Warrington to the front asa centre of Liberalism in the future as;it was in the old days which have been alluded to. In conclusion I must thank you most heartily, for though speech may be silven, silence is golden on an occasion of this sort—(Laughter)—and I must thank you most heartily for the vote of thanks you have been so good as to paws to nay wife for coming here this afternoon. (Applause.) The business of the day was then nroceeded with. THE ffrALLHOLDERS.

tions by Master Tom Barton's juvenile orchestra of six- teen performers have been much appreciated, and Miss Turner's mandoline band has submitted a capital pro- gramme at intervals in the refreshment room. A very successful side show has been the Queen of Sheba's Treasure Temple. Shoals of visitors have been pre- sented to her Majesty, and on shaking hands have received an electric shock—to their great surprise and amusement. The same "thril- ling touch " was imparted by the royal gift bestowed upon each caller on leaving. Miss Margaret Pierpoint, attired in gorgeous oriental I costume, has taken the part of the Queen of Sheba with ; due dignity, and her sister Miss Bessie Pierpoint has acted as her attendant. Mrs. F. Griffiths and Miss Walker have also assisted in the management of the I show which has done great business. Khan Telluca, the oriental character reader and impressionist, held a large number of consultations on Wednesday and Thursday. Mr. J. T. Reach (of Messrs, Le Maistre and Co.) who fulfilled this role, surprised many I by his remarkably good delineations of character. Sid IVlacaire, the society mystical merrymaker. ven- triloquist and court conjuror, has entertained numerous assemblies with his "Gems of naader magic" ii proved himself a very skilful exponent of sleight-on hand and other accomplishments. The musical item "Flora's Holiday" which has been nightly contributed in one of the ante-rooms by Miss Arline Harrison, Miss M. W. Collin, and Messrs A. Griffiths and E. Pownall, has formed quite a feature of the bazaar entertainments. The piece is a dainty collec- tion of partly traditional and mostly original tunes, worked up into an interesting and coherent cycle of sMos and concerted pieces, in which each of the artistes mentioned figures prominently in turn. And it is especially pleasing to record the uniform excellence with which the whole was presented to the audiences that gatherei nightly to listen to it, and who testified in no equivocal manner their appreciation of its attrac- tive points. The singing of the unaccompanied quartet and of the necessarily involved yet spark- ling catch, "Corns buy !" deserve special mention , as indicating by the nice balance of the parts and the ' crispness of the ensemble attack, how thoroughly the music had been rehearsed and the high intelligence ' brought to bear upon its interpretation by all concerned. Encores of the various numbers comprised in "Flora's Holiday "greeted all the performers in turn, during the run of the piece. The mechanical fish pond and shooting range have proved unfailing sources of amusement. Many of the sterner sex have resorted to the luxurious smoke room I and lounge, under the management of Messrs. T. Sudlow and Co., and have been able to enjoy a whiff of the i"fragrant weed" and a refreshing cup of coffee. ,

country. The first—which he was afraid people had I been rather inclined to forget of recent months because they had so many other things to think of—was the report of the Commission which sat to con- sider army matters. The mention of it would probably call up the terrible state of things which the Committee found. Even the Conservatives themselves made up their minds that, they ought to do something to put matters right, and a new army scheme was brought in by a valuable minister who had now been removed to a place where he would be less danger- ous. (Laughter.) That scheme was now dead and buried, and the only thing that remained was the soldier cap of entirely German manufacture. ( L-aughter.) Then they had another scheme brought in by an entirely new minister. Directly it made its appearance in the Rouse of Commons they were told that this was a little trial trip made by a new minister, and the Government had not the least intention of standing by it if it was dis- agreeable to the people of the country, and it was going to be withdrawn. After two such failures as that, he ventured to think that they could not have much con- fidence in the C4overnment to put army matters right. He was not going to say anything about education or temperance matters, except that he did not think there was a soul in that room who could believe that the Government had dealt wisely—and he might go so far as to say honestly—with either question. Alluding to the introduction of the

FISCAL AGITATION Mr. Nicholson said he thought it was about the worst 1 sin the Government had committed. When it was started they were told by Mr. Ch:aanberlain that the country was practically on the verge of ruin, that we were all going into the bankruptcy court. Another of Mr. Chamberlain's arguments was that the fiscal pro- posals were the only possible way of keeping the colonies loyal to the mother country. The first of those reasons had. been sufficiently disproved by the evidence of experts in political economy and by such a notable statesman as Mr. Asquith. The airsument as to the disloyalty of the Colonies was a most disgraceful thing to bring forward. He was a few minutes previously reading an extract from an article which appeared in the chief Ministerial journal in Canada, and which went straight to the point. It read: "Every self-respecting Canadian resents the argument, used on scores of platforms in Britain and published in scores of British papers, that NIT. Chamberlain's Protec- tionist polioy, even though it may raise the cost of the food to the millions of wage-earners in Britain should , be adopted by the British people because it would secure and retain the loyalty of the colonies. . . . Let no campaigner, even though he be Mr. Chamberlain him- self, slander Canadians in measuring their loyalty by , any tariff preference." That vv?s a sufficient answer to Mr. Chamberlain's arguments that the colonies were likely to prove disloyal. The other day he was talking to an old friend of his Sir Christopher Fnrness, a gentleman who had enormous interests in all kinds of businesses, but principally in 'steel and iron, and shipping. Sir Christopher told him that a few days ago he attended a meeting of directors which represented all shades of politics and ideas on the fiscal question. All, however, were agreed that what was doing damage to the country at the present time was the uncertainty of the people interested in commerce and business as to what the Government were intending to do. They could readily see that a man who was engaged in ship-building, for instance, could not possibly venture to enter into new contracts until he knew whether the Government was going to put a duty on imported steel or allow it to come in free as hitherto. The consequence was that work was lost, men were thrown out of employment, and pauperism began to increase. Tf they looked at the pauperism returns they would find that the number of people entering the workhouses during the past two months and the steadily increasing number getting out of work were simply appalling. One of the first duties of the Government was to see that before the winter was upon us the uncertainty as to whether to adopt the policy of Protection or Free Trade should be cleared up once and for all. (Hear, hear.) The matter had already been discussed four times in the House of Commons, but even now he did not think anyone could tell him what were Mr. Balfour's actual views on the subject. (Laughter.) The last definition that was given to him —and it was rather amusing—was that Mr. Balfour was "a Free-Trader with unabated sympathies with the Pro- tectionist policy for which he had no official recognition whatever." (Laughter.) He thought he had given suffi- cient reasons why they should feel a very considerable want of confidence in the Government. How were they to put things right? The Liberal party had always been the party of high ideals. It had always supported legislation in favour of the general population of the country. It would not recognize or support any class interest or monopolies whatever. What the interests of the present Government were,he need only refer them to the legislation of the past session for them to under- stand. Warrington was a good working class con- stituency and it essentially ought to be for that reason a Liberal constituency. If the policy of Protection was going to be adopted no one would be harder hit than the working class population. Besides being a man's question, as affecting wages,it WaS essentially a woman's and a housekeeper's question. During a recent election campaign a candidate was expressing sympathy with the working classes and remarked that he knew it was hard for them to " make both ends meet," whereupon a woman in the audience exclaimed " Both ends meet ! We have to be satisfied with one end meat and the other end bread." (Lend laughter.) If Protection came into force it would be a case of bread at both ends, and very dear it would be at that. (Hear, hear.) As he came along from the station, his cousin (Mr. Arthur Crosfield) said "Don't say anything about me on the platform," but he (Mr. Nicholson) winked the other eye and said "I know my business." (Laughter.) They had got an excellent candidate—(hear, hear,)—one who was a shrewd man, a fine speaker, and an excellent man of business—and those were three very important qualifica- tions for a member of Parliament. Above all, he was a man who was capable of discharging the duties,and he had no axe of his own to grind. (Applause.) They could not find a better man to represent them in Parliament, but to secure his return they would have to put their organization • into thorough working order. They did not know when they would be called upon to face a general election. Some people thought the time would come this year, but he was not of that opinion. Others prophesied that the election would have to be fought in March. He thought that was quite possible because he did not think the Tory Government would care to face what any Government would have to do—and that was to put on increased taxation with the next budget. They would no doubt prefer to leave that unpleasant work to the Liberals. In order to perfect their local organization funds were needed, and he asked them to support the bazaar liberally. He wished the effort every possible success, and trusted that its result would be the triumphant return of his cousin Arthur at the next election. (Applause.) This concluded the interesting ceremony. Downes and Mr. E. Osborne and Mr. E. V. Walker (hon. secs.): Mr. PARKER extended a hearty welcome to Mr. Lever, who, he observed, was formerly a resident in Warrington. It had been a matter of interest to Warrington people, continued Mr. Parker, to watch the magnificent developments and the commercial and social enterprizes whiah had been associated with Mr. Lever's name and the firm tinder his control. Mr. Lever was not only a Liberal in name but a Liberal in deed and in truth. (Applause.) Mr. Lever was firmly attached to the principles of FreeTrado, (Applause.) At a time when so many manufacturers, weak in nerve, and when SO many dilapidated industries were looking upon protec- tion as a sort of harbour of refuge which they would be able to enter and levy toll upon their fellows, it was a pleasing thing to find that Mr. Lever was firmly con- vinced that the policy of Free Trade was one which we ought to stand by. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: HANDBOOK.
div.p: THE HANDBOOK.

The Bazaar Handbook, which has been printed at the "Examiner" Office, is an interesting brochure of over 100 pages. It gives ithe fullest information relating to everything connected with the bazaar, and many of the pages contain apt quotations. In addition, there is a short history of the Warrington Liberal Association from the pen of Mr. E. V. Walker, and a brief sketch of Mr. A. H. Crosfleld, the prospective Liberal candidate. The booklet is embellished with portraits of Liberal leaders and officials, and altogether the handbook may be said to be an interesting souvenir of the occasion. It has been decided to present each visitor to the bazaar to-day (Saturday) with a copy.

div.head: THURSDAY'S PROCEEDINGS. THE LADIES' DAY.
div.p: THURSDAY'S PROCEEDINGS. THE LADIES' DAY.

The opening ceremony on Thursday was almost entirely in the hands of the ladies, and there was a good attendance. Mrs. Ziba Armitage presided, and the bazaar was opened by Mrs. Charles N. Nicholson. Others present on the platform were Mr. C. N. Nicholson (Liberal cajadidate for Doncaster division). Mr. and Mrs. Charles E. Parker Mrs. Crosfield, Mr. T. Birchall JP., and Councillor Ellison. Mrs. ARMITA.GE said she had a pleasing duty to per- form and that was to introduce Mrs. Nicholson to a Warrington audience. Mrs. Nicholson knew Warring- ton very well long ago but she had not been in the town now for some years. She (Mrs. Armitage) was sure the audience would accord her a hearty wel- come. She had come a long journey and unfor- tunately had a very bad cold, so she was not inclined to make much of a speech that afternoon. Mrs. Armitage having asked Mrs. Nicholson to declare the.bazaar open presented her with a handsome bouquet. Mrs. NICEIOLSON said it afforded her very much pleasure to be present. They must forgive her refrain- ing from making a speech, because speech-making was not at all in her line. She had much pleasure in declaring the bazaar open. (Applause.) Mrs. PARKER said she rose with!greafpleasure to pro- pose a vote of thanks to Mrs. Armitage and Mrs. Nicholson, and she thought they would include Mr. Nicholson, although it was ladies' day. (Laughter.) He had come to be quite a familiar figure among them in Warrington, and she hoped they would see Mrs. Nicholson more frequently. (Hear. hear.) There was nothing more delightful than to 'have a ready response to an appeal. The old saying was very true that "He gives twi 3e who gives quickly" and when they got Mrs. Nicholson to open the bazaar they were all more delighted than she could express. Past years had seen some deplorable divisions among their party and it. was a great deal to have the bazaar at a time when they were all feeling absolutely united. They had so much common ground at present, and she thought they had to thank the Government a great deal for that unity. They had had such a dose of unfair measures and iniquitous Bills and other things they did not like, that it had banded them together in a way that perhaps nothing else could have done. They were going to that" the Government by doing. their utmost to upset themselves—(laughter)—and bring in a Liberal Government. No legislature could do every- thing, but they hoped that when they got their Liberal Government in question a very great deal would be done, particularly to improve the social conditions of the poor. (Hear, hear.) That was one thing that every- body felt most deeply interested in. As John Burns said : "The swamps of human misery lie beneath thepeaks of wealth." That was very aptly and truly said, and they wan tod to do a great deal of levelling up to make the social conditions of the poor better and to give the workingclasses a fairer position in life. For all this money was necessary and 'their efforts that day were to further the Liberal cause. They were met not merely to sell a few things and make a pretty bazaar, but to help the Liberal party into power. (Applause.) Miss TRUDA. CROSFIELD seconded. She was Sure they would all work hapPily.together to the last hour of the last day of the bazaar when they thought of all that it stood Ifor. They were banding themselves together in the interests of true Liberalism—not rabid Socialism and little Englandism and an inability to see from more than one point of view—but a wide broad, and comprehensive Liberalism which aimed al doing the greatest good for the greatest number. (Applause). _ .

This motion' was carried- with acclamation. Mr. C. N. NtcHoLsom returned thanks. He was not at all sure in the first place whether he was the proper person to speak at the bazaar—in fact he rather thought that particular duty should have been left to his wife, for, after all, her connection with the town was very much longer than his own, • and he could assure the gathering that her interest in it remained un- abated. He wanted, if they would permit him, to call their memories back to past years. His connection with the town began twenty one years ago, and he was very grateful for the first visit he paid to Warrington, for it brought him one of the best and greatest blessings a man could possibly have, in a true and loyal wife. (Applause). Not only that, but it brought him ,some of the best and cheeriest friends he thought any man ever made in this world. His second visit to the town was a still more interesting one as • it was in connection with politics. Those were • the days of great Liberalism in Warrington, when Mr. Mc Minnies and Mr. Peter Rylands—(applause)— used to make the walls of the public hall ring with their voices. They were dead and gone but the memories of them remained. (Hear, hear.) To come down to later years, he would like to say a word about his own father. He looked upon him as being one of the best types of English citizens one could possibly meet with. He lived in Warrington for many years, he made his money here, and he spent it here, and he took care that the town should be very much better off for his presence. He was a stout and stalwart Liberal (Applause.) What should he (Mr. Nicholson) say of his uncle John? They all knew him and remembered him. If there was one other memory he would like to call back and it would be in the minds of many of them—his wife remembered it quite well—was when their great and revered leader, Mr. Gladstone came and spoke here on more than one occasion. He stayed at Mrs. Nicholson's old home, and that was a thing she could never forget. He would be rather out of place if he did not mention the great loss the Liberal party had sustained during the past week by the unfortunate death of Sir William Harcourt. The deceased statesman was a great politician, and a great advocate of temperance. In addition to that, he was a great financier and a friend of the people. In the House of Commons he was a hard hitter, but outside that House, even his enemies would no doubt admit that he was a kind and courtly gentleman. His loss would be a very great one, and they all felt it severely'. .(Hear, heal:). They must not let these things be memories only, but they should have the effect of stirring Liberals up, of stimulating them to greater efforts in the future. He would like to give them a few reasons why he thought the present Government had entirely forfeited the confidence of the

div.head: MR. LEVER'S SPEECH.
div.p: MR. LEVER'S SPEECH.

Mr. W. H. LEVER, who was heartily received, said it was a very great pleasure to him to come toWarrington. As he had been four times a Liberal candidate but could not induce enough people to vote for him on any of those occasions—(laughter)—he always liked to get near a winning man. (Hear, hear.) He thought he would come to that bazaar so that when Mr. Crosfleld was returned he would be able to say that, at any rate, he (Mr. Lever) had done his share to get him in. (Applause.) At one time he lived in Warrington and very happy days those were. He lived ma small house in Palmyra-squire and he well remembered alittle scene that occurred in a confidential conversation between the housemaid and a man he employed about once a fortnight to do some gardening. This man, leaning on his spade, confided to the housemaid that "Mr. Lever was no sort of a chap—(loud laughter) —but Mr. Crosfleid—well now there was a real gentleman! (Laughter and applause.) Mr. Crosfield kept six gardeners, but her gaffer ' (Mr. Lever) only employed him (the gardener) about an hour each fort- night." (More laughter.) The man thought that if the soap trade in Warrington could not afford to keep six gardeners there was something wrong with it. (Laughter.) He (Mr. Le.ver)hadthe happiest recollec- tions of his stay in Warrington, and the friends he then made had remained friends•ever since. With regard to the object of the bazaar, the money was wanted to further Liberal principles, for no political campaign could be conducted without funds. Alluding to the political situation, Mr. Lever said that at present they hardly knew where they were. With regard to

VIE FISCAL AGITATION, Aft. Balfour declared two months ac that we should not have a Colonial conference at all. Within the last few days, however, he had stated that such a conference was just the thing they wanted. The Premier had declared that he was not a Protectionist, and that Pro- tection meant raising the price of goods to increase the trade of the country. But he declared himself in favour of retaliation, and how he was going to make his retalia- tion effective without raising the price of goods he had not explained. How all the other countries in the world were immediately going to alter their interna

arrangements and adjust their tariffs to suit our I convenience—because that was what it meant I —he did not explain. If they did not, Mr. Balfour said they were going to retaliate, and how were we to retaliate without raising the price of goods? It was one of those things that no one could explain. It was more confusing still when they read Mr. Chamberlain's latest speech. He too declared that he was not a ProtectiOnist—(laughter)—but he said he was going to do something or other that was going to bind the empire together. He (Mr.Lever)had visited all our Colonies, and whilst he had no right to speak for any one of the colonies, hehad met a great many influential people in each of them, and it had always appeared to him that the colonies in their young life had none of their energy to throw away, and no oppor- tunities to lay on one side to help the mother country. He did not think the mother country, any more than a father or mother in real life, could depend for her own strength on sacrifices made by their children who were yet developing. When the colonies were full-grown and developed it might be a different thing, but to cripple the growth of the colonies by attempting to interfere with 'the free adjustments of their own tariffs appeared to him to be a very sorry way of making Eng- land strong and robust, and a way that would not com- mend itself to Englishmen. (Hear, hear.) Another side of the question was this :How were we—if we once committed ourselves to bargains with the colonies and to sanction an arrangement by which they made a tariff to suit us, and we responded with a tariff to suit them —going to have a free hand afterwards when neither one nor the other of the tariffs suited the colonies ar this co untry?We would not then be able to alter our tariff as we did now by a vote of the House of Commons. Our own House of Commons might be quite willing to vote the budget. in a certain way, but they could not do it if they had made a bargain with certain colonies. Nor could we alter the tariff if •only one of the colonies wished it. There would be all the others to consider. It was going to make con- fusion ten times confounded. (Hear, hear.) In the first place it was wrong that we should attempt to make manufacturers in England stronger at the expense of manufacturers in the colonies; it was also wrong that we should attempt to make colonial farmers stronger at the expense of English farmers. (Hear, hear.) The whole thing, to his mind, was a change for the worse. During the last fifty years under Free Trade conditions the love and affection of the colonies for the mother country had grown steadily each year. He remembered

div.head: VISITING CANADA
div.p: VISITING CANADA

in 1888 and at the time there was a distinct leaning towards fusion for fiscal purposes with the United States. What did the United States do? Because Canada was not going along quite as quickly as they wished, they made a retaliatory tariff against Canada. They did towards Canada exactly what Mr. Balfour proposed to do probably against the United States, Germany, France or some other country. What had been the effect? It had not drawn Canada any closer to the United States; it had simply made Canada come more closely to England. Instead of Canada climbing down merely because a big nation like the United States attempted to coerce her, she had gone further from the United States from that day, and she was more loyal and devoted to England to-day than at any previous period of Canada's history. He ven- tured to say that if we attempted to interfere with the developments of that great country by asking her, as Mr. Chamberlain had suggested, to start no new indus- tries that would interfere with the industries in the old country,or to interfere with the tariff which she thought —wrongly hesaid—to protect theindustries she had now got, he believed the present affection and love of the Canadians for the mother country would wane, and we would be in great danger of a revulsion of feeling against ourselves, and of that affection being transferred to the United States. He (Mr. Lever) felt when Mr. Balfour talked now of a Colonial con- ference which a few months ago he said he was not in favour of, that the "hand was the hand of Esau, but the voice was the voice of Joseph." (Loud laughter and cries of" Jacob.") No, in this case it was the voice of Joseph. (Laughter.) He might say that his firm had works in many countries besides England. They had works in the countries that were said to be more prosperous than England— the United States and Germany—and they had occasion- ally to send English workmen out there. They had yet to receive their first request from a workman in England to go to either of those countries or to any country out- side England. (Applause.) Whenever they had to send an Englishman abroad they had to pay him more than he received in England to induce him to go. If those countries were so wonderfully prosperous, did they not think that a firm with branches in them who moved their men about, would be deluged with applications? .There was no struggle on the part of any of their English workmen to go abroad. They knew the conditions of work there and they did not require Mr. Chamberlain to tell them that Protectionist countries were better off than England. They knew exactly the reverse to be the case. Protection was not the only point before the country. The Government promised a variety of

MEASURES FOR THE WORKINGMAN but where were they? The Government made very few promises, if any, to the brewer, the parson, or the capitalist, but they had managed to ignore all the promises they made to the workingmen and to do a great deal for the capitalist without any promise at all. They made a great fuss about the Alien's Bill. They managed to send it to a Select Com- mittee which was a polite way of shelving it. They did not send the Chinese Labour Bill to a Select Commit- tee. That was rushed through, and was now the law of the land. With reference to the Brewers' Endowment Bill, that had not been shelved, but had become law. Mr. Balfour said he did not submit to coercion in the Brewers' Endowment Bill. He said he belonged to a party and one of its traditions waste protect vested in- terests, and therefore he would see the matter out. Liberals had their traditions, and one of them was that it was not only capital and money that wanted pro- tection and legislating for. There was something higher to protect and legislate for, and that was men and women. The tradition of the Liberal party was human happiness and well-being,just and equitable laws,a good system of taxation which was to be the basis of sound Government—and without that all else was a failure. They WANTED FAIR TAXATION and they must make very radical changes. They could well understand, apart altogether from the natural leaning towards Protection of the Tory Party, that there was some misgiving with the Tories as to where the fifty millions additional national expenditure which they had incurred had to come from. They had to decide whether it had to come out of the bread and butter and meat of the workingman, or through the income tax on the incomes and land held by wealth and capital. They could either take it from the food of the people, in which case they would have a starved and stunted people not fit to cope with the other nations of the world, or they could take it fairly by a graduated income tax from those who were best able to bear it and distribute the burden. evenly over the shoulders of the people in proportion to their incomes. In addition to that, they wanted a fair and equitable system of land taxation. Mr. Lever referred to the strides which had been made in this direction in New Zealand, and commended the graduated scale 'of land taxation which was in force there. If that could be done in England the land would yield to the country revenue for the education of the citizens and carrying on of the Government.As it was the land- lord escaped entirely free, and those who worked and toiled to develop the land had not only to keep themselves but to provide an un- earned increment for the owner of the land. Again alluding to the fiscal question,Mr. Lever said our exports of manufactured goods were something like three or four times per head of people above what they were in the United States, and double per head what they were in Germany. It was only in food and raw materials which they sent to us, on which we wanted to feed our People and to make the very goods we export, that they could perhaps show a balance of trade against us. The whole thing would not stand examination. If we wanted to raise the country, let us have a fair and just system of taxation and give to everyone equal opportunities to develop the best that was in them. Let us have such burdens as had to be borne, distributed in proportion to the wealth a person had been able to acquire. That was a practical fair scheme, and one that would tend to the development and growth of the country and the more equal distribution of wealth. (Applause.) Mr. KING, in proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. Lever, related some interesting reminiscences of War- rington as he remembered it in the days of his boyhood. He could not claim to be a Warrington man, but his mother was a Warrington woman, and he therefore had a good deal to thank the good old town of Warrington for. Referring to the industrial progress of the town i during the last 30 or 40 years, he said Warrington was a standing example of the libellous statements of Mr. Chamberlain as to the condition of British industry. Mr. King proceeded to refer to the idbal conditions under which the workpeopleof Port Sunlight lived, and said the low deathrate of 9 per thousand showed what was possible in this country when the workers lived under good conditions. (Hear, hear). Alderman WILLIAM PIERPOINT, in seconding the vote of thanks, appealed to the young men to be loyal to their Liberal principles. Warrington, he said, was a depressing town from a political point of view, but he believed that by constantly pegging a t it, the justice of their cause and the earnestness of their labours. would bring about a condition of things which he hoped to see before he closed his eyes on this world's scene. (Hear, hear.)
The vote was carried with acclamation. Mr. LEVER acknowledged the compliment, and business was then re-commenced.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.

Church Society Anniversary. Theanniversary services in connection with the War-- ington Church Society was held at St. James' Church, Latchford,on Thursday evening and was 'well attended. The preacher was the Rev. E. Gordon Saville,secretary of the Church of England Men's Union, who spoke upon Christian fellowship. The service was conducted by the Vicar (Rev.H.B. Firth), the lessons being read by rhe Rector and the Rev. Morley Stevenson. Wycliffe P.S.A. Society. There was an average attendance at the meeting of this society on Sunday afternoon. Mr. Bannister, of Warrington presided, and delivered a brief address on the text" Grow up into perfection."—Mr. Butcher, of Urmston in speaking of the old gospel, which he said was ever new, observed that therein lay the source and inspiration of true and everlasting life. Life, he added, was an unsolved problem, and passed the comprehension of philosophers and scientists. A man really began to live when he allowed Jesus Christ to come into his life.- -Miss M. W. Collin very effectively sang two solos, entitled "The Promise of Life," and" A Soul's Awaken- ing."—Mr. B. Farrar, the secretary announced that 11. new members had joined, making the membership 525. It was decided to forward letters of sympathy to two members.—'2he lesson was read by Mr. Healey and Mr. Farrar offered prayer. Parr Hall Services. The Parr Hall was crowded on Sunday evening, when the first of the" Services for the People" were held. In the course of the sermon, Mr. Dunmco referred to. what he termed the absence of the serious note from modern life. The literature of to-day did not express that serious and noble view of life common to such writers as Kingsley, Browning, Tennyson, Arnold, Carlyle and Ruskin. Scrappy journalism which made no demand on thought was enormously popular. Another thing, it was a sad feature of to-day that many London and provincial theatres were being tranformed into music halls. Some present might taboo theatres but the narrowest Puritan must admit that there was a wide difference between those dramas which dealt with the great passions of human nature, and the vulgar and oftentimes unclean frivolities of the music hall, and it was the latter that held the foil to-day.—The service will be held as usual to-morrow evening. Mr. Evelyd Davies, the well-known tenor vocalist will sing.

The Rev. A. M. Mitchell on Alms Giving and Confirmation. The Rev. A. M. Mitchell, viear of Burtonwood,writes as follows in "The Guardian," the well-known Church of England organ: "Sir,—The administration of con- firmation without the opportunity of almsgiving is, it would appear, the rule which generally obtains in our Church. The question might be profitably discussed in the columns of a journal such as yours whether or not the rule is a wise one. Ought not almsgiving to be identified with confirmation? The only argument adduced against the confirmation offertory is that of consideration for the candidates—not r pockets, but their devotions; the offertory, it is smd, distracts the candidates' attention, if it does not actually worry them. Poor things! One would naturally think the duty and privilege of almsgiving on an important occasion like confirmation would far outweigh any momentary distraction during the service—if such. there be. What may be the experience of those incum- bents who have, with the sanction of their bishops, introduced the offertory innovation' at confirmation? Here, by permission, we always have the confirmation offertory, and our testimony is that it is highly appreciated by the candidates and also by the witnesses of the confirmation, and this appreciation is all the greater when the destination of their contributions has been determined beforehand by the candidates them- selves. Some little memorial of a confirmation in the form of a gift to God's house, or some act of charity to the sick and needy, ought never to be wanting in our churches. Complaint is con3tantly made, and with every reason, of the serious neglect of proportionate and systematic almsgiving. Are our confirmations in no way responsible? Have the bishops and clergy nothing to answer for? A great opportunity for instruction in almsgiving is presented to us and we allow it to pass by unheeded. Is it too much to expect our bishops to encourage the confirmation offertory, and thus in the, most practical of ways inculcate thankfulness to God and charity to man ?—A. M. MITCHELL. Burtonwood Vicarage, Newton-le-Willows, September 8, 1904."

div.head: Rev. E. C. E. Carleton on Creeds and Trust Deeds. ,
div.p: Rev. E. C. E. Carleton on Creeds and Trust Deeds. ,

At Holy Trinity Church on Sunday morning the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton preached on "The value of creeds in comparison with trust deeds." He pointed-Out that the Creed was an excellent guarantee for the stability and continuity of the Church's teaching; for they could understand it would not be an easy thing to tamper with a formulary that was being recited daily in the ears of the people. And as long as these standards remained and were given this kind of publication in the common tongue, the Church's faith was guarded, and the doctrine of the Scriptures from which that faith is derived was known by a most certain warrant, having behind it the assent of the whole Church catholic from apostolic times. Another method of securing stability and continuity of teaching, to which some had resorted in more modern times, was instead of creeds, to have trust deeds. He supposed that was the plan adopted in many of the Nonconform- ist bodies. Now that plan is not satisfactory, because by it the people were not brought in to have an interest in guarding the integrity of the faith. It might be that in the first instance they were consulted and had a hand in drawing up the deed, but the document had been put. aside, and it might be after a time forgotten. Trust deeds were very often put in a safe or locked up in it strong box ; and perhaps it was only some exceptional emergency that caused them to be unearthed and con- sulted. And when consulted it might happen, and often had happened, that the provisions and principles em- bodied in the deed had been departed from by the very people who were supposed to• be the custodians; and the people kept in ignorance were quite unaware that any change had taken place. And if the suspicion did. occur to someone that something was wrong, he might not care to raise a storm by performing a most unpleasant duty, and so the drifting continued. A deed was a very useful thing for securing the right ownership of pro- perty; but it was absolutely worthless for securing the soundness and continuity of Christian doctrine in any Particular congregation ; as had bean proved over and over again.

div.head: WARRINGTON LAY-BYE ON, THE SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON LAY-BYE ON, THE SHIP CANAL.

A Step in the Right Direction. On Tuesday afternoon the s.s. "Stanley Force" the Belfast steamer on her way to Manchester called at Warrington lay-bye to discharge cargo of Peat Moss litter from the Irish Peat Development Company, Ltd., and consigned to Mr. Edward Connor, Sankey-street Warrington. The steamer also took up a parcel of goods of the Warringtla Borate Company, Ltd., for shipment to Belfast. This is the first time says a corres- pondent that one of the passing steamers to Manchester has touched at the lay-bye,but it may be the commence- ment of a regular traffic. It would have been im- possible to bring this littor by either Liverpool or Manchester as the value of the material would no, have 'borne the extra charges. The "Stanley Force within one minute of making fast to the lauding stage was boarded by the shore gang, and cargo was being discharged in a few minutes afterwards. What is wanted at the lay-bye is a shed for accumu- lating cargo, a weighing machine, and either gas or electricity for night work. Another thing which re- quires doing is the filling up of the dangerous trench left between the stage and the solid ground. The owners of the Belfast steamer were able to telephone to their representatives in Liverpool and Manchester from the laybye. After a stay of a few hours the steamer left for Manchester. If merchants and manu- facturers who export and import goods would take the matter up they could get goods from abroad and send goods to home and foreign ports without the extra ex- pense of carriage and transhipment at Liverpool. Representations have been made to the Manchester Ship Canal Company from time to time as to the few' details that are wanting to make the lay-bye a success, but this needs to be backed up by a promise of traffic. It seems a pity that so much money should have been spent on the Transporter and wharf, and no covered shod provided to store the goods. Any number of workmen are available for porterage and could find employment at loading and discharging cargo, whilst the distance to the various places of bustness in town when once the goods are loaded on to carts in many instances is no greater than from the present traffic depOts. . ,

When the merchants and mannfacturers of Warrington realize the saving that can made by importing and exporting direct organized effort is required, for indi— vidually they may no have sufficient cargo to or from a home or foreign port, but collectively the supply to and the demand from a population of 60,000 would justify the stoppage for a few hours of each steamer; for London, Glasgow, Leith, Belfast, and Cork, ana possibly the principal liners from lJnite-i States, River Plate, South Africl, Mediterranean, North Sea and Baltic ports. The public could be advise 1 in the local prose of the times of arrival andsailing of steamers from the lay-bye' anda notice board at the Chamber ofCommerce and at the lay-bye would be useful. The provision of a she or warehouse (which is most important) at the lay-bye por receipt of goods and a clerk from the Canal Cea- fany to enter the goods would also be required. V"' necessities of business will do the rest.

THE INQUIRY REPORT. TO BE "VERY SERIOUS." Commissioners Not to be Hurried. --- Those members of the Warrington Town Council who weretexpecting on Tuesday to hear the report of the No- n Commissioners on the recent inquiry were dis- appointed. A question was asked as to when it might be expected, but no definite reply was forthcoming. The Commissioners are not going to be "rushed "says Mr. Pemberton,and this caused the Mayor to blandly remark "The report will arrive as soon as it comes !" The three Commissioners appointed by the Council—Coun- cillors Wilkinson, Peacock and Evans—have prepared their report, but they have requested that it be not made public until the report of the Non-Trading Com- missioners is received. This request was conveyed in the following letter to the Mayor which was read at the Town Council meeting on Tuesday: Town Hall, Warrington. 3rd October, 1904. Dear Mr. Mayor,—As you are aware, this inquiry was i closed on Monday, the sth ult. Herewith we send, n a sealed envelope, our report, which we respectfully suggest should not be made public until the receipt of the report of the Commissioners appointed by the Non- Trading Association. We consider that the shorthand notes of the proceedings of the inquiry are of sufficient importance as te warrant the reprinting of the same, so that any ratepayer who so desired coulfi obtain a copy at a nominal charge.—We are, dear Mr. Mayor, yours faithfully, JOHN WILKINSON, ARTHUR PEACOCK, JAMES EVANS. To his Worship. the Mayor, William Bolton Esq. The MAYOR: The envelope is initialled by the three Commissioners named. I take it that the reports should be presented all together. It is your wish I suppose, that the shorthand notes be printed, but I would like an expression of opinion from the members of the Council before that is done. Is it your wish that the evidence be printed? (Cries of" Aye, aye.") In answer to Alderman Pierpoint, ..; The MAYOR said the Commissioners had heard the evidence and they now gave it to the Council to enable them to form a correct idea as to what had been said and done. The Council would be in possession of the evidence which had been taken. The TOWN CLERK: The minutes of proceedings? Tne MAYOR: Yes; what we paid the shorthand writers to report. Councillor WILKINSON: I wish to explain, so that AldermanFierooint may understand, that our report is not to be opened until the other report has been received. The proceedings that have been going on for twelve months must be printed. The MA.von.: At the last meeting of the General Purposes Committee there was an expreSsion of opinion to the effect that the evidence should be printed as soon as the inquiry was closed,and, as we have not had the report of the Non-traders, I take it that the sooner we get this printed and put into the hands of the Council the better. I did not like to take upon myself the responsibility of ordering the work to be done, but I don't think that any member of the Council will object. Alderman BENNETT rose to speak. The MAYOR: I don't want a discussion to-night. Alderman BENNETT : I was under the impression the evidence had been printed. The MAYOR: Only 25 copies. Alderman BENNETT: It is a pity that stereos were not taken so that a larger number could have been printed. The MAYOR: We don't want any discussion now. Councillor TINNION : I think it desirable that every member of the Council, and every ratepayer in the borough, if he wishes it, should have an opportunity of reading not only the report of the whole of the evid- ence, but the reports ofithe Commissioners that may be issued, whatever the expense may be, if it be £lOO, £l5O or £2OO. or even more, in the best interests of Warring- ton. If it be in order I propose that that be done. The MAYOR: I will take the responsibility of having the evidence printed, but I wanted to take you into my confidence. J. take it for granted that the members are favourable to the evidence being printed. (Hear, hear.) The Council approved,ancl the subject dropped. At the close of the ordinary business Councillor ROGEFtS asked the Mayor if he had received the report of the inquiry from the Non-Traders. The MAYOR: I have not received anything person- ally. I understood they were going to send it in time for discussion to-night. It has not arrived yet. I understand it is being prepared,and that as so on as they think fit they will send it. Councillor ROGERS : . I was given to understand it was to be prepared for to-night. The MAYOR: I cannot give you any more informa- tion. Councillor ROGERS: It was promised for to-day. The MAYOR: Yes. Councillor STOTT : If possible. The MAYOR: It was an after-thought. I had it in my note book that it was promised for to-night. Councillor Dodds turned round to me at the meeting of the General Purposes Committee, and said it was im- possible to present it yet.. Councillor PEMBERTON: I think the question was put to me, and one memb or went so far as to get up and propose that it should be given to- night, and I told you then that it was almost impossible. I said if it was possible to present it to this meeting we should do so. Mr Mayor, it is a very serious report inde ed. The MAYOR: Can you tell us when it will be in? Councillor PEMBERTON : We have given a great deal of time to the matter—more time than .I shall ever give to anything of the sort again, and we are not going to be rushed with the report. It. is going to be a proper report, and in spite of all the twitting we are going to give the report in a proper manner. It is a weighty matter, and the interests of Warrington are very much concerned, and we are not going to be rushed for the sake of a few days. The MA YOR : Can you give us any idea when we shall get it ? Councillor PEMBERTON : We expect very shortly te be able to finish. The MAYOR: You will send it to me? Councillor PEMBERTON : Yes. The MAYOR: Before you give it to the Parr Hall meeting? (Laughter.) Councillor PEMBERTON: Certainly. It is all very well for Aldermon Sutton and Couucillor Hulse Alderman SUTTON: I never spoke a word. (Laughter). Councillor PEMBERTON : NO you didn't. Alderman SUTTON: Then what are you grumbling at? (Laughter). Councillor PEMBERTON : One can interpret what you mean. Continuing, he said that the Non-Trading Commissioners sat 65 times,and went through thousands of documents, and only since the inquiry closed had they hadan opportunity of going into the matter. The MAYOR: I thought you had been sitting eleven months. Councillor PEMBERTON: Yes, and during the whole of that time we have been taking evidence. We are doing the thing thoroughly. and not in a slipshod manner, as some people would like it to be done. The MAYOR (to the members) : I cannot give you any more information. The report will arrive as soon as it comes. (Laughter).

COVENT GARDEN BALL. The first of the series of fancy dress balls arranged by Messrs. Frank Rendle and Neil Forsyth has taken place at Covent Garden Theatre. It can be truly said that the evening was one glorious success and seldom has the initial ball reached so high a pitch of excellence. The bright faces and in- genious and artistic costumes rendered by no means easy the task of the judges in assign- ing the prizes. Since last season various improvements have been made, the most popular being perhaps the conversion of part of the balcony into a supper-room and the erection of a barrier round the dancing floor, which, by keeping back some of the promena- ders, gives the dancers more space. As was the case last season, Mr. Clarkson was the costumier of the principal prize-winners, the dress designed by him and depicting "Episodes of 1904" being particularly effective. The first priie, however, a diamond and opal brooch, was won by "When the Swallows Homeward Fly," a • beautiful con- fection created by Mme.
